milestone.description: Multi-repo workspaces and the hosted Registry sync. Gated on the taxonomy split and a finished M1.

items.body:
> ADR. Two questions: how state is partitioned locally, and what the hosted
> version runs on. The second was raised as "single-table design on DynamoDB —
> is that a fit?"

## Local: one database per repository, and the Registry is not in it

This is already how it works (`.atlas/atlas.db` at the repo root) but it has
never been stated as a decision, and sosalejandro/atlas#115 depends on it being one.

| Plane | Where it lives | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Index** (declarations, anchors, edges) | `.atlas/atlas.db` — **one per repo** | derived and disposable; rebuilding is a scan, not a migration. Sharing one DB across repos would couple their scan lifecycles and make a partial rescan a cross-repo transaction |
| **Evidence** (coverage runs, per-test rows) | same per-repo DB | tied to a run of that repo's suite |
| **Registry** (capabilities, specs, acceptance criteria, diagrams) | **files in git**, not a database | it is authored, reviewed in pull requests, and must diff. A database would make the one human-edited plane the one thing you cannot review |
| **Views** (matrix, scores, drift) | computed, never stored as truth | reproducibility (#119) requires they be a function of the other three |

That the Registry is git-versioned files is the load-bearing decision here. It
is what lets a spec change be reviewed like code, what makes the cloud sync a
mirror rather than a source of truth, and what keeps atlas from becoming a
system of record that has to be backed up.

## Cloud: per-tenant SQL, not DynamoDB

The instinct — a database per project in the cloud, as locally — is right. The
technology proposed does not fit, for four specific reasons.

### 1. The core screen is an ad-hoc query

The matrix is filtered by state, domain, owner, repo and freshness, and sorted
by score, churn or gap. In a single-table design every one of those is a new
access pattern: a new GSI, or a scan. DynamoDB is excellent when the access
patterns are known and few; this product's main surface is the opposite by
design.

### 2. Trends are aggregations

`atlas trend` (#92) and the regulated change-impact report (#119) roll up
across capabilities and over time. That is `GROUP BY` work. In DynamoDB it
becomes either pre-computed aggregates maintained on every write (correctness
burden, backfill problem) or an export to something else that can aggregate —
at which point the second store is doing the real work.

### 3. Self-hosting is a requirement, not a preference

sosalejandro/atlas-internal#23's buyers need air-gapped or self-hosted operation, and sosalejandro/atlas-internal#24 lists a
self-hostable sync server as a differentiator against Sourcegraph withdrawing
self-hosted. **DynamoDB cannot be self-hosted** (DynamoDB Local is a test
harness, not a deployment target). Choosing it forecloses the segment with the
clearest willingness to pay.

### 4. Two data models, one maintainer

The local store is SQL with migrations and sqlc-generated code. A single-table
design means a second model, a second set of invariants, and a permanent
translation layer between them — for the same domain, maintained by the same
person.

### What to use instead

| Option | Fit | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **libSQL / Turso — database per project** | **recommended** | SQLite-compatible, so the *same schema, same migrations and largely the same queries* as local. Multi-tenancy by database-per-tenant is the model it exists for, which is exactly the instinct behind the question. Embedded replicas make the desktop app's offline story simple |
| **Postgres, row-level tenancy** | solid fallback | more operational familiarity, better cross-tenant analytics, and the option every self-hosting customer already runs. Costs a dialect fork in the query layer |
| **DynamoDB single-table** | not now | correct choice for a different problem — see below |

### Where DynamoDB would earn its place

If runtime signal ingestion (#94) becomes a high-volume firehose — millions of
span-derived symbol observations per day, written constantly, read by fixed
key — that is a genuine fit: known access pattern, huge write volume, no ad-hoc
querying. That would be a **separate store for the Evidence firehose**, not the
home of the Registry and Views. Deciding it now would be premature; noting it
as the shape that would justify it is not.

## Consequences

1. `.atlas/atlas.db` per repo is a documented invariant; multi-repo (#115) fans out rather than merging stores.
2. The Registry format is a git-versioned file format with a compatibility promise, and the cloud mirrors it.
3. The hosted service is per-project SQL; the schema is shared with local, and divergence between them is a bug.
4. Self-hostability is a hard constraint on every storage decision from here.

## Revisit if

- The hosted matrix cannot be served in acceptable time from per-tenant SQL at a realistic workspace size (measure before switching).
- Cross-tenant analytics becomes a product requirement, which favours Postgres over per-tenant SQLite.
- Runtime ingestion (#94) reaches a volume where a purpose-built key-value store is the right home for that plane alone.

items.title: Closed set of document types and attributes extracted at ingestion

labels.name: data-extraction
labels.description: Document Tables / extract_records roadmap: every ticket of the data extraction effort

labels.description: Data extraction step 2/4: dates in paths, document types and attributes at ingest

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
Agents that pick documents from a knowledge database can only filter by path and text today. A closed set of document types, each with a fixed list of attributes extracted once at ingestion, lets them select documents reliably instead of guessing from paths or reading every document. Ingestion currently stores file timestamps, title and language, but not what a document is or its business attributes, such as the date on an invoice or the parties of a contract. The set is closed on purpose: a filter over a fixed vocabulary is reliable, an open set the model invents per document is not.

**In scope**

- Define the set: about ten document types common in enterprise knowledge (for example invoice, contract, offer, delivery note, letter, meeting minutes, report, policy, other), and for each type the attributes worth extracting (for example document date, period covered, counterparty, reference number). Working out and justifying this list is part of the issue.
- A step in the default ingestion pipeline that classifies each document into one type and extracts that type's attributes from its opening pages with one small-model call.
- Type and attributes stored on the document record and as filterable metadata in the vector store.
- An attribute the model cannot determine with confidence is stored empty, never guessed.
- A backfill for documents that are already ingested.

**Out of scope**

- Agents filtering by these attributes, see #2348.
- Custom types or attributes per tenant or per knowledge database; the set is closed for now.
- Choosing the model per knowledge database, see #1782.

**Planning decisions**

- Invoices first: the set starts as `invoice` or `other`, measured on the 106 invoices of #2312 before further types follow (#2485).
- Invoice attributes: issue date, invoice number, issuer, issuer tax ID, recipient, parties, total amount including VAT, currency, due date, service period and the numbers of related documents. Addresses, bank details, line items and tax breakdowns are left out: they are not filters, and line items are read at request time.
- Attributes are shared across types, each type lists the ones that apply and what they mean for it, and one primary type owns them while secondary types are labels only.
- The model copies values as written; code converts them to one stored form and keeps the original text, so a better parser can fill values later without a model call. A value not found in the document, or not applicable to the type, is stored empty.
- The values are filter metadata only: they stay out of embedded and model-facing text, so embeddings never change and a backfill never embeds again.
- Classification uses the knowledge database's own text model and is switched per database, on by default. A failed call leaves the document unclassified instead of failing ingestion.
- Names of people on invoices are stored like any other value: the PII guardrail keeps data from leaving the platform, not from being stored inside it.
- Targets agreed by the team: invoice recall of at least 95%, precision on documents resembling invoices of at least 95%, and wrong plus guessed values at most 2% per attribute, measured with the PII guardrail on.

**Sub-issues, one stacked PR each, merged in this order**

#2480 classifier and storage contract → #2481 evaluation → #2482 ingestion → #2483 backfill → #2484 UI request. #2485 extends the set beyond invoices after the evaluation.

items.title: Wave 1–3: RI ID → RINASPACE → RINPO Phone → Connector Gateway
items.body:
## Objective
Ship the narrowest reliable end-to-end loop from the proposed RI Platform Next Build contract (draft PR #223):

`RI ID → RINASPACE → RINPO → authorised action → audit → first value`

## Wave 1 — Identity / provisioning
- Ratify public `RINASPACE` naming through master-spec change control; retain legacy aliases temporarily.
- Audit existing auth/providers and map Google / email OTP / mobile OTP / passkeys into one RI ID.
- Personal RINASPACE creation on verified first login.
- Organisation create/join flow using existing `organization_id` boundary.
- Trial grants / entitlements / async provisioning / first-value telemetry.
- Fail closed on missing entitlement or tenant context.

## Wave 2 — RINPO Phone production shell
- Replace demo Today with authorised real data.
- Ground Ask in current RI ID + org/workspace/role context.
- Actions = proposals / approvals / executions / history.
- Growth shell uses existing campaigns/leads/content capabilities.
- Apps = capability registry + connectors + installed packs.
- Memory/permissions/settings surfaces.
- Avatar click should open the same authenticated RINPO Phone across eligible RINADS surfaces.

## Wave 3 — RI Connector Gateway
- Provider-neutral connection registry.
- OAuth + MCP client layer + webhooks/event ingestion.
- Provider scopes, health, audit, revocation and credential isolation.
- Priority adapters: Google Workspace, WhatsApp, Shopify, Wix, WordPress; logistics and Hootsuite/social after core gate.

## WhatsApp guardrails
- consent proof + category
- suppression/opt-out
- template enforcement where required
- human escalation path
- rate limits
- cost estimate before high-volume send
- approval + queue + delivery reconciliation + attribution + audit

## Acceptance
1. New verified user gets exactly one RI ID.
2. Personal RINASPACE is provisioned idempotently.
3. New business can create/join an organisation without a second account.
4. RINPO Phone reflects server-authorised context only.
5. At least one read-only connector is installable and revocable through the Gateway.
6. At least one approved write connector action flows proposal → approval → execution → audit.
7. No connector credentials are present in browser bundles.
8. Cross-tenant tests pass.
9. First-value event is persisted.
10. Existing production surfaces continue to build and pass release gates.

## Non-goals
- no World implementation in this wave
- no infrastructure migration
- no social-network clone
- no separate database per tenant
- no provider SDK direct from domain code
- no unrestricted L4 actions

items.title: Fivetran lineage binds same-named tables to the first service in dbServiceNames
items.body:
### Connector

Fivetran

### Feature area

Lineage

### Describe the bug

When several services in `lineageInformation.dbServiceNames` hold a table with the same database, schema and name, the Fivetran connector attaches every connector's lineage to the first listed service.

`_resolve_table` in `pipeline/fivetran/metadata.py` loops over `dbServiceNames` in order and returns the first service where `<service>.<database or *>.<schema>.<table>` exists. It never uses which source the Fivetran connector actually reads from. Sharded or per-tenant estates, where several databases share one schema, are the common case.

In our instance six MySQL services hold the same `evo` schema, one per Fivetran connector. With all six in one agent's `dbServiceNames`, all six connectors' 273 table edges were attached to the first service. Nothing was logged and the run reported success.

### To Reproduce

1. Two database services, A and B, each with table `db.schema.t`.
2. Two Fivetran connectors, one syncing from A and one from B.
3. A Fivetran agent with `dbServiceNames: [A, B]`.
4. Both connectors' lineage originates from A.

### Expected behavior

The source service is chosen from the Fivetran connector's own source (for example its configured host, or its database/service type), or the ambiguity is reported and the edge skipped rather than bound to the first match.

Our workaround is one Fivetran agent per source service, each with a `pipelineFilterPattern` and only its own service in `dbServiceNames`.

### OS

Kubernetes (ingestion-base image)

### Python version

3.12

### OpenMetadata version

2.0.6

### OpenMetadata Ingestion package version

openmetadata-ingestion==2.0.1.0; same logic on main.

### Pre-submission checklist

- [x] I searched for duplicate issues.
- [x] I removed credentials, hostnames, emails, and other sensitive data from logs and config.

items.title: Feature: tenant-bound Spanner database routing and composed pack activation
items.body:
### 2026-10-14 accepted tenant-isolation checkpoint

Public authenticated dispatch plus two pinned Spanner databases and 10 workers is verified for Core+User+Memory versus Core+PDLC+Memory:184 main + 12 restart assertions, independent audit and Astra acceptance. Final data retained; no database creation/deletion. [Verification and scope](https://github.com/arunmenon/Engram/blob/4bd47dd/docs/review/spanner-compatibility/tenant-isolation-verification.md).

This checkpoint does not close this issue. Tenant native webhooks/global metrics/import/cursors/prune/replay/reconsolidate, general pending/draining/forced termination and pilot readiness remain outside the accepted proof; hierarchy #49 remains parked. Earlier dated source observations below remain historical context, while the feature requirements remain open.

## Current agreed context — 2026-10-07

**Scope:** Confirmed target: one Spanner database per tenant, shared instance permitted; Engram routes authenticated context to that database and composed pack bundle.

**Required proof:** Define and implement minimal API/worker/search/retrieval/admin routing and scoped resource lifecycle, with colliding-ID isolation and no default-database fallback; a namespace or independent registry is not proof.

**Shared decisions:** Core is mandatory. Optional memory/user/domain capabilities compose through declared dependencies, without pairwise hardcoded flows. Authenticated tenant identity resolves its authorized Spanner database and pack bundle; processing and retrieval use that same context. Never infer authorization from agent_id, caller-chosen database or artifact IDs.

**Tracking and status:** Parent #34 holds the reconciled six-bucket scope; #35/#42 own composition/capability controls, #43 tenant routing, #39 exact conformance and #41 real-Spanner execution. This is a scope/context reconciliation, not a fresh runtime verification. The issue remains open; historical reproductions below retain their original revision, backend and run scope. Historical memory probes are diagnostic evidence, not cloud acceptance. No Redis/Neo4j runners or cross-backend migration are required. Pinned documentation links below are historical published snapshots; newer local reports/run artifacts remain unpublished unless explicitly linked to a published revision.

---

Parent: #34. Related: #35 activation/capabilities, #39 conformance, #41 Spanner verification. The database-per-tenant direction is confirmed. Define and implement the bounded tenant routing and activation needed by #34 using existing composition/storage patterns; no new multitenancy framework is presumed.

## Problem and evidence
Tenants may need different selected pack bundles (for example core+PDLC versus core+user+memory). Astra medium found one process-wide ontology registry at API startup; configured runtime caching keys configuration, not an authenticated tenant. API authentication checks shared keys without returning tenant context. Spanner ledger/graph/subscription keys and ontology active state have no established tenant dimension. Therefore different registry objects or different processes pointed at the same stores are not proof of tenant isolation.

Relevant source: src/context_graph/api/{app,dependencies}.py; ontology/{runtime,versioning}.py; adapters/spanner/{schema,subscription,log,graph}.py; ports/pack_graph.py; worker/extraction.py user identity construction.

## Confirmed direction and implementation boundary
Use one authorized Spanner database per tenant, with shared Spanner instance permitted. Authenticated tenant context selects the database and active composed pack bundle across API, workers and operations. A separate Engram deployment is not required by this decision; define minimal supported routing/client lifecycle and onboarding mapping before implementation. Separate configuration objects or caller-selected database names are not authorization.

## Acceptance
- [ ] Record the chosen deployment/tenant boundary, explicit supported customer scenarios and resource routing; distinguish today’s implementation from target behavior.
- [ ] Define ownership and scoping for ledger, graph/search, subscriptions/checkpoints, ontology/replay state, caches, APIs, admin/evaluation and retention. A caller-supplied header/agent_id alone is not a boundary.
- [ ] Define activation authorization, dependencies and interpretation-version agreement, plus disable/re-enable, historical visibility and catch-up policies with #35.
- [ ] Implement tenant-scoped ingress/handshake and required worker/read/admin routing from the reviewed boundary; split demonstrated missing work into bounded child tasks if necessary, preserving specialized processing.
- [ ] Specify adversarial tests using identical event/session/agent/artifact IDs across tenants, independent selected packs and admin/replay/cleanup operations. No cross-tenant reads, writes, acknowledgments or deletion.
- [ ] Verify database routing and complete API/worker/search/cache/admin separation even when the instance/application infrastructure is shared; prove failure isolation and no silent default database fallback.
- [ ] Add selected architecture’s acceptance to #39 and real-Spanner verification to #41; do not call local schema checks isolation proof.

Astra report and bounded schema probes are saved locally at docs/review/spanner-compatibility/2026-10-07-astra-pack-optionality-review.md and matching local-probe.py/.json; not yet published, no cloud tests performed.


## Required retrieval audit: only core may be assumed present

Confirmed product invariant: core is mandatory. Memory, user and every domain pack may be absent. Describing built-in schema in pack files does not mean all specialized retrieval code is already decoupled.

Current audit starting points include domain/pack_intents.py OPEN_PACKS partitioning, retrieval/engine.py intent/seed fallback, adapters/graph_ops.py user_profile and workflow_pattern seed branches, and retrieval/artifacts.py active domain seed/type/traversal selection. Specialized implementations may remain; availability must come from resolved selected capabilities rather than assumptions that all base packs are loaded.

- [ ] Inventory hardcoded type/edge/intent/seed/hydration/ranking/traversal/evidence and fallback dependencies in both event-memory and artifact retrieval paths, including storage/search adapter calls and any user endpoints.
- [ ] For core-only, core+PDLC, core+user, core+memory and combined selections, define supported queries and precise disabled/unsupported outcomes. No PDLC/user/memory presence may be assumed without active dependencies.
- [ ] Use the tenant's authenticated, server-resolved database and pack interpretation context for every retrieval call and cache, including search/vector results, graph expansion, evidence fetches and pagination cursors. Do not accept another tenant's supplied IDs/cursor as authorization or silently route to a default database.
- [ ] Test historical disabled-pack nodes and cross-pack edges: enforce explicit visibility policy rather than assuming seed filtering prevents traversal/evidence leakage. Define disable/re-enable/catch-up policy before executing affected tests.
- [ ] Verify unfamiliar compatible packs and unrelated-pack noninterference without combination-specific engine branches. A disabled required provider/capability must yield the defined error or refusal, not a misleading empty answer or hidden fallback.
- [ ] Bind concrete retrieval expectations to #39 fixtures and tracked #41 runs: exact typed artifact IDs, properties, relationships and supporting events; rejected/incomplete evidence behavior; colliding IDs across two tenant databases and negative isolation assertions.

This scope is required under #34. Local audit/checklists are not proof of implementation or real-Spanner acceptance.

items.body:
Parent: #352

## Outcome
Make speed and resource efficiency measurable product properties across SME single-node, managed enterprise and private-cloud deployment profiles.

## Principles
- Set budgets before optimizing.
- Measure p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, errors, CPU, memory, database pressure and per-tenant fairness.
- Do not trade correctness, auditability or tenant isolation for headline throughput.

## Child slices
<!-- axis-audit-children -->
- [ ] #361 — Performance: define workload profiles, SLOs and a reproducible baseline
- [ ] #362 — Performance: close database transactions before external model and workflow awaits
- [ ] #363 — Performance: enforce query budgets, pagination and index evidence
- [ ] #364 — Performance: reduce connector console request fan-out with a scoped read model
- [ ] #365 — Performance: benchmark ingestion streaming, concurrency and backpressure

## Done when
Representative workloads run reproducibly in CI or a controlled performance environment, regressions have budgets, and operators can diagnose bottlenecks.

items.body:
**Audit:** STATE_OF_THE_PROJECT 2026-07-03, service truth table (connector, CRITICAL).

services/connector/internal/repository/repository.go:214 (and the email/intake cross-tenant background scans) query the raw pool with no tenant context. Under prod NOBYPASSRLS, connector config and webhook reads return 0 rows — webhook delivery and email ingestion silently stop. Dev masks this via SEDOC_ALLOW_BYPASS_RLS=1.

items.title: eval: consider ClickHouse as primary store for billing analytics
items.body:
## Background

The current stack stores FOCUS 1.2 billing line items in PostgreSQL (`billing_line_items` table, 40+ columns, indexed on `billingPeriodStart/End`). This works for early development but PostgreSQL is an OLTP row-store — as billing data volumes grow into hundreds of millions or billions of rows, full-period aggregation queries will become the dominant performance bottleneck.

ClickHouse is a purpose-built columnar OLAP database with an Apache 2.0 licence that has become the de-facto standard for real-time billing and cost analytics at scale. Its design maps naturally to FOCUS billing data.

## Why ClickHouse fits FOCUS billing data

FOCUS 1.2 uses an **append-only correction model**: when a cloud provider discovers a billing error, it emits a new row with `ChargeClass = 'Correction'` — the original row is never mutated. This means billing data is structurally immutable from ingestion onward, which is a perfect fit for ClickHouse's MergeTree engine (which is designed for immutable sorted parts). ClickHouse's known weakness — expensive async mutations — is irrelevant for correction-model data.

Query patterns (aggregating `EffectiveCost` over time ranges, grouped by `ServiceName`, `ResourceId`, `Provider`, filtered by `BillingPeriod`) are exactly the columnar scan patterns ClickHouse is vectorised to execute.

Published benchmarks and real-world migrations show:
- 10–100x query latency reduction vs PostgreSQL on large billing datasets
- 10–30x storage compression (LZ4/ZSTD per-column codecs)
- Sub-second aggregations over billions of rows on modest hardware

## ClickHouse limitations to evaluate

- **Mutations are expensive and async.** `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE/DELETE` rewrites entire data parts in the background. No transactional consistency during mutation. This is a non-issue for billing data (append-only), but matters for any metadata co-located in ClickHouse.
- **Not suitable for OLTP.** User accounts, tenant configs, cost allocation rules, and workflow state require frequent updates and transactional guarantees — these must remain in PostgreSQL.
- **Operational complexity.** Self-hosting ClickHouse on Kubernetes (via the Altinity operator) requires managing ClickHouse Keeper (the ZooKeeper replacement), replication topology, and shard configuration. ClickHouse Cloud eliminates this at a cost premium.

## Recommended architecture: PostgreSQL + ClickHouse hybrid

| Data type | Store | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Billing line items (FOCUS) | ClickHouse | Columnar, analytical, append-only model, 10–100x query performance |
| App data (users, tenants, rules) | PostgreSQL (managed) | OLTP, full TypeORM/NestJS compatibility, CRUD/ACID |

The split is clean: the billing ingestion service writes directly to ClickHouse (dual-write, not routed through PostgreSQL). NestJS queries PostgreSQL for app state and ClickHouse for cost analytics via separate connection pools. No CDC or cross-system sync required for the core use case.

## Multi-tenancy in ClickHouse

Three patterns are supported; the recommended progression:

1. **Shared table with `tenant_id` in partition and primary key + ClickHouse row policies** — simplest to operate, good for early scale. Row policies transparently append `WHERE tenant_id = ...` at the database layer.
2. **Separate database per tenant** (`billing_acme`, `billing_globocorp`) — per-tenant TTL, partitioning, and data retention policies; clean GDPR deletion story (drop database). Suitable for large or regulated tenants.
3. **Separate cluster per tenant** — only for strict data residency requirements.

## Deployment options

- **ClickHouse Cloud** (recommended for early stage): managed, separated compute+storage, auto-pausing, no ZooKeeper/Keeper management. Note: 2025 pricing revision introduced egress fees — factor this into long-term cost modelling.
- **Altinity Kubernetes Operator** (v0.26, Apache 2.0): production-proven self-hosted K8s deployment, manages `ClickHouseInstallation` CRDs, rolling upgrades, replica management. Appropriate once the team has K8s DevOps capacity.

## Application integration

ClickHouse exposes an HTTP interface and a native TCP protocol. The `@clickhouse/client` Node.js SDK (official, maintained by ClickHouse Inc.) provides a typed query API. Billing queries are analytical SQL — TypeORM is not needed (and not appropriate) for ClickHouse; use the SDK directly in a `ClickHouseBillingRepository` service.

## Alternatives considered

- **TimescaleDB** (PostgreSQL extension with columnar compression and hypertables): viable up to ~100M rows with 10–100x query speedup over vanilla PostgreSQL. Simpler stack (one database). Does not close the performance gap for multi-billion-row datasets or sub-second interactive dashboards. Consider as a fallback if a single-database constraint is hard.
- **PostgreSQL with pg_partman + indexing**: reasonable for the current dataset; will not scale to the analytical query patterns expected in a production FinOps platform.

## Tasks

- [ ] Benchmark current PostgreSQL query performance on a representative billing dataset (1M, 100M rows)
- [ ] Evaluate ClickHouse Cloud vs self-hosted (Altinity operator) based on team capacity and cost
- [ ] Design ClickHouse schema for `billing_line_items` (partition by `toYYYYMM(billingPeriodStart)`, primary key `(tenant_id, billingPeriodStart, provider, serviceCategory)`)
- [ ] Implement `@clickhouse/client` adapter in billing ingestion service (replace/parallel to TypeORM insert)
- [ ] Implement ClickHouse row policies for tenant isolation (or per-database isolation if required)
- [ ] Migrate existing billing ingestion endpoint to write directly to ClickHouse
- [ ] Evaluate whether TimescaleDB is an acceptable interim step before committing to the hybrid stack
- [ ] Decide on multi-tenancy isolation level (shared table vs per-database) and document the decision

---
## Deutsche Fassung

## Hintergrund

Der aktuelle Stack speichert FOCUS-1.2-Abrechnungspositionen in PostgreSQL – Tabelle `billing_line_items` mit mehr als 40 Spalten und Indizes auf `billingPeriodStart/End`. Das funktioniert in der frühen Entwicklung, PostgreSQL ist jedoch ein zeilenorientierter OLTP-Speicher. Wenn das Abrechnungsvolumen auf Hunderte Millionen oder Milliarden Zeilen anwächst, werden Aggregationsabfragen über vollständige Perioden zum dominierenden Leistungsengpass.

ClickHouse ist eine speziell entwickelte spaltenorientierte OLAP-Datenbank unter Apache 2.0 und hat sich als De-facto-Standard für Echtzeit-Abrechnungs- und Kostenanalysen im großen Maßstab etabliert. Ihr Design passt natürlich zu FOCUS-Abrechnungsdaten.

## Warum ClickHouse zu FOCUS-Abrechnungsdaten passt

FOCUS 1.2 verwendet ein **Append-only-Korrekturmodell**: Entdeckt ein Cloud-Provider einen Abrechnungsfehler, erzeugt er eine neue Zeile mit `ChargeClass = 'Correction'`; die ursprüngliche Zeile wird nie verändert. Abrechnungsdaten sind damit ab der Datenübernahme strukturell unveränderlich – ideal für die MergeTree Engine von ClickHouse, die auf unveränderliche sortierte Teile ausgelegt ist. Die bekannte ClickHouse-Schwäche teurer asynchroner Mutationen spielt für dieses Korrekturmodell keine Rolle.

Abfragemuster wie die Aggregation von `EffectiveCost` über Zeiträume, gruppiert nach `ServiceName`, `ResourceId` oder `Provider` und gefiltert nach `BillingPeriod`, entsprechen genau den spaltenorientierten Scans, die ClickHouse vektorisiert ausführt.

Veröffentlichte Benchmarks und reale Migrationen zeigen:
- 10- bis 100-fach niedrigere Abfragelatenzen als PostgreSQL bei großen Abrechnungsdatensätzen,
- 10- bis 30-fache Speicherkompression durch spaltenspezifische LZ4-/ZSTD-Codecs,
- Aggregationen über Milliarden Zeilen in weniger als einer Sekunde auf moderater Hardware.

## Zu bewertende Einschränkungen von ClickHouse

- **Mutationen sind teuer und asynchron.** `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE/DELETE` schreibt ganze Datenteile im Hintergrund neu; währenddessen besteht keine transaktionale Konsistenz. Für Append-only-Abrechnungsdaten unproblematisch, aber relevant für gemeinsam gespeicherte Metadaten.
- **Nicht für OLTP geeignet.** Benutzerkonten, Mandantenkonfigurationen, Kostenverteilungsregeln und Workflow-Zustand benötigen häufige Updates und Transaktionsgarantien; sie müssen in PostgreSQL verbleiben.
- **Betriebliche Komplexität.** Selbst gehostetes ClickHouse auf Kubernetes mit Altinity Operator erfordert Verwaltung von ClickHouse Keeper, Replikationstopologie und Sharding. ClickHouse Cloud vermeidet dies gegen einen Preisaufschlag.

## Empfohlene Architektur: Hybrid aus PostgreSQL und ClickHouse

| Datentyp | Speicher | Begründung |
|---|---|---|
| Abrechnungspositionen – FOCUS | ClickHouse | spaltenorientiertes analytisches Append-only-Modell und 10- bis 100-fache Abfrageleistung |
| App-Daten – Benutzer, Mandanten, Regeln | verwaltetes PostgreSQL | OLTP, vollständige TypeORM-/NestJS-Kompatibilität und CRUD/ACID |

Die Trennung ist klar: Der Ingestion Service schreibt direkt nach ClickHouse – Dual Write, nicht über PostgreSQL. NestJS fragt PostgreSQL für App-Zustand und ClickHouse über getrennte Connection Pools für Kostenanalysen ab. Für den Kernanwendungsfall sind weder CDC noch systemübergreifende Synchronisierung erforderlich.

## Multi-Tenancy in ClickHouse

Drei unterstützte Muster mit empfohlener Entwicklung:

1. **Gemeinsame Tabelle mit `tenant_id` in Partition und Primärschlüssel sowie ClickHouse Row Policies:** einfachster Betrieb, gut für frühe Skalierung. Row Policies ergänzen auf Datenbankebene transparent `WHERE tenant_id = ...`.
2. **Eigene Datenbank pro Mandant** wie `billing_acme` oder `billing_globocorp`: mandantenspezifische TTL, Partitionierung und Aufbewahrung; saubere DSGVO-Löschung durch Löschen der Datenbank. Geeignet für große oder regulierte Mandanten.
3. **Eigener Cluster pro Mandant:** nur bei strikten Anforderungen an Datenresidenz.

## Deployment-Optionen

- **ClickHouse Cloud – für die Frühphase empfohlen:** verwaltet, getrennte Compute- und Storage-Ressourcen, Auto-Pause, keine Verwaltung von ZooKeeper oder Keeper. Die Preisänderung 2025 führte Egress-Gebühren ein; diese in langfristige Kostenmodelle einbeziehen.
- **Altinity Kubernetes Operator – Version 0.26, Apache 2.0:** produktionserprobtes selbst gehostetes K8s-Deployment mit Verwaltung von `ClickHouseInstallation`-CRDs, Rolling Upgrades und Replikaten. Sinnvoll, sobald das Team ausreichende K8s-DevOps-Kapazität besitzt.

## Anwendungsintegration

ClickHouse bietet HTTP und ein natives TCP-Protokoll. Das offizielle Node.js SDK `@clickhouse/client` stellt eine typisierte Query-API bereit. Abrechnungsabfragen sind analytisches SQL; TypeORM wird für ClickHouse weder benötigt noch empfohlen. Das SDK direkt in einem Service `ClickHouseBillingRepository` verwenden.

## Bewertete Alternativen

- **TimescaleDB:** PostgreSQL-Erweiterung mit spaltenorientierter Kompression und Hypertables; bis etwa 100 Millionen Zeilen tragfähig, mit 10- bis 100-facher Beschleunigung gegenüber einfachem PostgreSQL. Einfacherer Stack, aber bei Milliarden Zeilen oder interaktiven Dashboards unter einer Sekunde bleibt eine Leistungslücke. Als Rückfalloption bei harter Ein-Datenbank-Vorgabe erwägen.
- **PostgreSQL mit pg_partman und Indizes:** für den aktuellen Datensatz vernünftig, skaliert aber nicht auf die analytischen Abfragemuster einer produktiven FinOps-Plattform.

## Aufgaben

- [ ] Aktuelle PostgreSQL-Abfrageleistung mit repräsentativen Datensätzen von einer Million und 100 Millionen Zeilen benchmarken.
- [ ] ClickHouse Cloud und selbst gehosteten Altinity Operator anhand Teamkapazität und Kosten vergleichen.
- [ ] ClickHouse-Schema für `billing_line_items` entwerfen: Partition nach `toYYYYMM(billingPeriodStart)`, Primärschlüssel `(tenant_id, billingPeriodStart, provider, serviceCategory)`.
- [ ] Adapter mit `@clickhouse/client` im Ingestion Service implementieren – als Ersatz oder parallel zu TypeORM Insert.
- [ ] ClickHouse Row Policies für Mandantenisolation implementieren oder bei Bedarf Datenbanken trennen.
- [ ] Bestehenden Ingestion-Endpunkt auf direktes Schreiben nach ClickHouse migrieren.
- [ ] Bewerten, ob TimescaleDB als Zwischenschritt vor dem hybriden Stack akzeptabel ist.
- [ ] Isolationsniveau für Multi-Tenancy festlegen – gemeinsame Tabelle oder eigene Datenbank – und Entscheidung dokumentieren.

items.title: Per-knowledge-database pipeline status view

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
Dagster orchestrates ingestion for the RAG pipeline, including the sync pipeline from #1721, but has no concept of tenants or knowledge databases. Its own UI (`dagster.${DOMAIN}`) shows every run and asset across the whole deployment to anyone who can reach it, which is the wrong shape for a tenant-scoped, per-database view. This adds a light, purpose-built status panel scoped to one knowledge database at a time, instead of exposing or embedding Dagster's own UI.

**In scope**

- A backend client for Dagster's public GraphQL API (`dagster-webserver:3000/graphql`), not its internal Postgres run-storage schema, which Dagster does not guarantee to keep stable across releases. `dagster-webserver` already sits on the same `backend` Docker network as `api`, so this needs a new settings class and client plus an env var, no new network wiring.
- Run and partition status resolved by asset-key prefix rather than job name: the knowledge database name is already the first segment of every asset key the pipeline produces, and stays that way once #1505 lands a single shared pipeline, whereas job names aren't reliably scoped to one database.
- A new read-only endpoint on the knowledge API, guarded by the same per-database permission check the existing database-listing endpoint already uses. No new permission concept.
- A summarized response: the most recent run per ingestion stage (fetch, parse/embed) with its status and timestamp, plus counts of missing or failed partitions. Not per-partition logs or step-level detail.
- A small status panel on the knowledge-database page in the frontend: a handful of status indicators, the last successful sync time, and a link out to the full Dagster UI for anyone who needs to dig deeper.

**Out of scope**

- Triggering, canceling, or reconfiguring runs from this UI. Read-only status only.
- Deep step-level logs or the full Dagster run timeline. Link out to Dagster's own UI for that.
- The pipeline and model configuration work itself, covered by #1505, #1721, and #1782. This issue only surfaces status for whatever those configure.

**Accepted when**

- [ ] A knowledge database's page shows whether its most recent sync/ingestion run succeeded, failed, or is missing, without opening Dagster's UI.
- [ ] The status shown for one knowledge database never includes another knowledge database's runs or partitions.
- [ ] A user without access to a knowledge database cannot see its pipeline status.
- [ ] Failed or missing partitions are visibly distinguishable from healthy ones.
- [ ] `make test` passes in the affected scopes.

items.body:
## Current agreed context — 2026-10-07

**Scope:** Resolve declared dependencies/capabilities/versions into a consistent immutable bundle; core cannot be disabled and optional packs cannot be assumed.

**Required proof:** Check API/worker interpretation agreement and tenant-specific Spanner handshake before admission; no combination-specific dispatch or silent routing fallback.

**Shared decisions:** Core is mandatory. Optional memory/user/domain capabilities compose through declared dependencies, without pairwise hardcoded flows. Authenticated tenant identity resolves its authorized Spanner database and pack bundle; processing and retrieval use that same context. Never infer authorization from agent_id, caller-chosen database or artifact IDs.

**Tracking and status:** Parent #34 holds the reconciled six-bucket scope; #35/#42 own composition/capability controls, #43 tenant routing, #39 exact conformance and #41 real-Spanner execution. This is a scope/context reconciliation, not a fresh runtime verification. The issue remains open; historical reproductions below retain their original revision, backend and run scope. Historical memory probes are diagnostic evidence, not cloud acceptance. No Redis/Neo4j runners or cross-backend migration are required. Pinned documentation links below are historical published snapshots; newer local reports/run artifacts remain unpublished unless explicitly linked to a published revision.

---

A pack loading successfully does not establish that its required behavior is supported or that API and workers interpret accepted events consistently.

Acceptance:
- [ ] Define a small versioned capability/activation contract in existing pack/registry structures; refuse unsupported required behavior and expose optional inactive behavior.
- [ ] Define event owner versus permitted subscribers/dependencies, namespace collisions and unloaded-owner refusal, with explicit legacy exceptions.
- [ ] Choose persisted contract/binding/bundle metadata, available immutable historical interpreter artifacts and required consumer/profile obligations.
- [ ] Before new metadata is accepted, prove supported N/N−1 compatibility or controlled refusal/defer across API and applicable workers; digest alone is not an interpreter.

items.title: Governed SQL: dedicated ClickHouse settings profile and workload scheduling for governed queries

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: Improvement to existing functionality (performance, UX, capabilities)

labels.name: P3 - low
labels.description: Polish, nice-to-have, rare edge case. Backlog.

items.body:
## Finding

Governed SQL queries run without a dedicated ClickHouse settings profile or workload class. A heavy governed query competes with product-critical queries (ingestion, dashboards, evaluations) on equal footing for threads and memory. The per-query ceilings that exist today (scan rows/bytes, threads, the 10-second cap) bound a single query, but nothing isolates the governed workload as a class or deprioritises it against product traffic.

Constraint carried from the decision record: per-tenant fairness does **not** belong in the database layer — it belongs at route-level rate limiting. The remaining database-side work is the settings profile / workload scheduling piece only.

## Evidence

- Governed queries execute under per-query ceilings but no `SETTINGS PROFILE` or workload/priority class distinct from product queries.
- Noted as a deliberately deferred remainder in the governed SQL API review discussion ("max_threads is one line" — the scheduling/profile question is the open part).

Surfaced in https://github.com/langwatch/langwatch/pull/6486.

---
