- [ ] All baseline assertions pass through Engram on real Spanner, including previously failed, partial and blocked scenarios; no silent exclusions.
- [ ] Agreed #34/#40 acceptance extensions have explicit expected artifacts, relationships, versions, evidence and retrieval answers, and pass on Spanner.
- [ ] Failure/recovery, retries, duplicates/conflicts, ordering, concurrency, pagination, deadlines, retention, replay and upgrades are exercised wherever applicable in the matrix and feature acceptance.
- [ ] Every confirmed defect has a linked disposition and a passing cloud regression; local-only fixes remain identified until verified.
- [ ] Run ledger, checklist, matrix and issue statuses agree; redacted evidence is published and independently reviewable.
- [ ] Final review records residual limitations explicitly. Any proposed scope exception requires an explicit decision and does not count as a passing scenario.

This umbrella remains open until these acceptance criteria are satisfied. It does not assert Spanner compatibility today.


## Entity-only native ANN follow-up (#44)

Track #44: the Engram Spanner adapter currently searches embeddings across all GraphNodes and returns those IDs as Entity IDs. This is a source-confirmed integration defect, not an executed cloud failure or a Spanner service bug. Repair must restrict the ANN corpus before top-k, preserve stored embeddings, validate schema/index readiness, and pass real Engram→Spanner differential tests with inactive/non-Entity vectors and colliding IDs. Local post-filtering is insufficient. Baseline scenario status remains unchanged until registered cloud reruns prove acceptance.

items.title: PRD: Multi-tenant — per-user accounts + data isolation (row-level + Supabase RLS)

labels.name: ready-for-matrics-ai
labels.description: Fully specified, ready for Matrics AI to action

items.body:
## Problem Statement

Today Metric AI is single-user. Whoever opens the app sees and queries the same single pool of uploaded data — there is no notion of "my data" versus "someone else's." If Alex and Rogi both used the system, Alex's questions would run against Rogi's sales records and vice-versa, and either could overwrite or delete the other's uploads. There is no real login either: authentication is disabled by default and backed by a single hardcoded admin credential. As a result the product cannot be handed to more than one business. We need every person to sign up / log in and reach only their own data, with all of it stored in our Supabase database.

## Solution

Turn Metric AI into a multi-tenant product. Each person signs up (or logs in) with their own account. From then on every upload, KPI, dashboard, chat session (Recents), and natural-language answer is scoped to that person's own **Tenant**. Alex sees only Alex's data; Rogi sees only Rogi's — enforced at the database layer by Postgres **Row-Level Security (RLS)** in Supabase, so even the Agentic loop's generated SQL physically cannot cross tenants. The existing upload form and the whole question → answer → chart flow look and behave exactly as they do today; the only visible change is a real login/signup gate and the fact that what you see is now yours alone. When auth is left disabled (local dev), the system runs as a single implicit tenant — identical to today's behavior. Nothing is hardcoded and nothing crashes.

## User Stories

1. As a new user, I want to sign up with an email and password, so that I get my own private workspace in Metric AI.
2. As a returning user, I want to log in, so that I can reach my own data.
3. As a user, I want to stay logged in across page refreshes, so that I don't have to re-enter credentials constantly.
4. As a user, I want to log out, so that my account isn't left open on a shared computer.
5. As a user, I want my password stored only as a secure hash, so that a database leak doesn't expose my credentials.
6. As Alex, I want to upload my sales/purchase workbook, so that only I can see and query it.
7. As Alex, I want my questions to run only against my own data, so that I never accidentally see Rogi's numbers.
8. As Rogi, I want assurance that Alex cannot see my data even if the AI writes raw SQL, so that my business data stays confidential.
9. As a user, I want my dashboard KPIs computed only from my data, so that the figures reflect my business.
10. As a user, I want my chat sessions (Recents) private to me, so that my questions and answers aren't visible to others.
11. As a user, I want to delete my own dataset/upload, so that I can manage my workspace without affecting anyone else.
12. As a user, I want my cached answers to be mine alone, so that I never receive an answer computed from someone else's data.
13. As a user, I want the "data changed" banner / data version to reflect only my own uploads, so that another user's upload doesn't make my chat look stale.
14. As a user uploading via the same form as before, I want the upload experience unchanged, so that there's nothing new to learn.
15. As a user, I want the question → answer → chart flow to work exactly as today, so that the multi-tenant change is invisible day to day.
16. As a developer running locally without auth, I want the app to behave as a single implicit tenant, so that local development continues to work unchanged.
17. As an operator, I want no credentials hardcoded in the source, so that the product is safe to deploy.
18. As a new user, I want a fresh, empty workspace on signup, so that I start clean with no one else's data.
19. As a user, I want my session token to expire after a period, so that a stolen token has a limited blast radius.
20. As a user, I want an invalid or tampered token to be rejected, so that nobody can impersonate me.
21. As a user, I want to see only my own list of uploads/datasets, so that the dataset manager reflects my workspace.
22. As a user, I want forecasts/enrichment (where available) computed from my data, so that insights are about my business.
23. As a user, I want other tenants' activity not to interfere with my requests, so that the system behaves predictably under concurrent use.
24. As a user, I want my Google Drive sync (if I use it) to import into my own workspace only.
25. As a security reviewer, I want the database to refuse cross-tenant reads at the engine level, so that an application bug cannot cause a data leak.
26. As an operator, I want the app to refuse to boot insecurely when auth is enabled but secrets are missing, so that we never deploy an open system by accident.
27. As a user, I want signup to reject a duplicate email, so that accounts stay unique.
28. As a user, I want clear errors when login fails, so that I know whether to retry or to sign up.
29. As an operator, I want the multi-tenant change to be additive, so that the existing single-user deployment keeps working through the transition.

## Implementation Decisions

- **Tenant model.** A *Tenant* is the unit of data ownership. Each signup creates one Tenant with one owner user (1:1 for now), but the schema keeps `users` and `tenants` separate so a Tenant can gain multiple users (teams) later without migration.
- **Isolation model — row-level `tenant_id` + Postgres Row-Level Security (RLS).** Every data-bearing table gains a `tenant_id` column. RLS policies restrict each row to the current tenant. The app sets the current tenant per transaction via a session setting (`app.current_tenant`); policies reference `current_setting('app.current_tenant')`. Because enforcement lives in the database, the Agentic loop's generated SQL is constrained automatically — the SQL the LLM is allowed to write is unchanged and table names stay identical, so KPIs, the Schema tool, and dashboard aggregates work exactly as before.
- **Critical RLS prerequisite.** The runtime must connect to Supabase via a role that is *subject to* RLS (the table owner / `service_role` bypass it) — or RLS must be `FORCE`d on the tables — and `app.current_tenant` must be set on every pooled connection/transaction before any tenant query runs. This is the single most important correctness/security requirement of the epic.
- **Identity module** (grows the existing HMAC-token auth). A `users` table (id, unique email, password_hash, created_at) and a `tenants` table (id, owner_user_id, created_at). Password hashing via a vetted algorithm (bcrypt/argon2). The stateless HMAC token payload is extended to carry `{ user_id, tenant_id, iat, exp }`. Interface: `signup(email, password) -> Principal`, `authenticate(email, password) -> Principal | None`, `mint_token(principal) -> str`, `verify_token(token) -> Principal | None`, where a `Principal` is `{ user_id, tenant_id, email }`. The legacy single-admin / hardcoded `Mansuri/182012` fallback is removed.
- **TenantContext module** (the linchpin). A FastAPI dependency `require_principal(request)` validates the Bearer token and yields the `Principal` (401 on missing/invalid). A tenant-bound connection helper acquires a DB connection and sets `app.current_tenant` for that request's queries — the single chokepoint through which all tenant data access flows. When `AUTH_ENABLED=false` it yields a single well-known implicit tenant, preserving today's local/dev behavior.
- **Tenant provisioning.** On signup, create the `tenants` row and link the owner user. KPI *definitions* stay global templates (not duplicated per tenant); KPI *values* derive from the tenant's own data through the existing KPI fast-path / MetricSqlBuilder against tenant-scoped tables.
- **Tenant-scoped ingestion.** The dynamic ingestion path stamps `tenant_id` on every inserted row and on the uploads-registry (`uploads`) row, and ensures the `tenant_id` column + RLS policy exist on each `u_*` table (created on demand). Sheet → table naming is unchanged (tables remain shared; isolation is by `tenant_id` + RLS). File-hash dedup becomes per-tenant.
- **Per-tenant cache + versioning.** The Response cache key incorporates `tenant_id` so identical questions from different tenants never collide. `data_version` becomes per-tenant; `invalidate_all` becomes `invalidate_tenant`. The PresentationEmitter's `data_version` reflects the requesting tenant.
- **Conversations / chat sessions.** The `conversations` + `conversation_messages` tables already carry a nullable `tenant_id`; it becomes populated from the request `Principal`, their three endpoints + the runner's persist hook scope to the current tenant, and RLS policies are added to both tables.
- **API contracts.**
  - `POST /auth/signup { email, password } -> { token }` (new).
  - `POST /auth/login { email, password } -> { token }` (extended to the users table; returns a tenant-bearing token).
  - `GET /auth/me -> { user_id, email }` (extended).
  - All existing data routes (`/upload*`, `/uploads`, `/datasets`, `/dashboard`, `/kpi*`, `/conversations*`, `/query_stream`, etc.) gain the `require_principal` dependency and operate within the resolved tenant. Request/response shapes are otherwise unchanged.
- **Frontend auth.** The existing `LoginGate` (already rendered when the backend reports `AUTH_ENABLED=true` and there is no token) becomes a real login + signup screen. The token (already persisted) is attached to every REST and SSE call via the existing auth-header helper (streaming already uses `fetch`, so the Bearer header applies). On logout, per-user store state is cleared. No backend URL or credential is hardcoded.
- **Backward compatibility / safety.** With `AUTH_ENABLED=false` the whole system runs as one implicit tenant — byte-for-byte today's behavior. With `AUTH_ENABLED=true`, the backend refuses to start when the token secret or admin bootstrap is missing (extends the existing startup guard). SQLite (local) has no RLS, so multi-tenant *enforcement* targets Postgres/Supabase; SQLite remains the single-implicit-tenant local-dev path.

## Testing Decisions

- **What makes a good test:** it asserts externally observable behavior (inputs → outputs, HTTP responses, token validity), never implementation internals, and is deterministic with no dependency on a live LLM or network.
- **Module under test (per the developer's choice): Identity / auth.** Cover: signup creates a user + tenant and returns a usable token; duplicate-email signup is rejected; login with correct credentials returns a tenant-bearing token; login with a wrong password is rejected; `mint_token` → `verify_token` round-trips to the same `Principal`; an expired token is rejected; a token with a tampered payload or signature is rejected; `verify_token` never raises; a stored password hash never equals the plaintext and verifies correctly.
- **Prior art:** mirror the existing pytest suite style (e.g. `test_schema_mapping.py`, ~20 behavior-level tests passing today) — interface/pure-function assertions, no network.

## Out of Scope

- Schema-per-tenant or database-per-tenant isolation (row-level + RLS was chosen).
- Teams / multiple users per Tenant, roles & permissions, sharing/invites (the schema leaves room; not built now).
- Automated tests for tenant isolation, per-tenant cache, and ingestion (recommended, but tests were scoped to Identity/auth this round — see Further Notes).
- Password reset, email verification, OAuth/social login, MFA.
- Per-tenant billing, quotas, and LLM rate-limit partitioning (the shared LLM key remains; fair-use limits are a follow-up).
- Migrating the legacy SQLite enrichment/hierarchy substrate to be multi-tenant (it already no-ops on Postgres today).
- Per-tenant object storage for raw uploaded files (current disk-path behavior retained).

## Further Notes

- **Security recommendation:** tenant-isolation tests are the highest-value safety net for this epic (they prove Alex cannot read Rogi's rows even via raw SQL). Tests were scoped to Identity/auth this round; strongly recommend a fast-follow that adds an RLS isolation test before this ships to real multi-tenant traffic.
- **RLS bypass footgun:** confirm the Supabase connection role does not bypass RLS (`service_role` and the table owner do). Use a dedicated app role and/or `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`, and verify `app.current_tenant` is set before the first tenant query on every pooled connection.
- **Existing NULL-tenant rows:** `conversations` / `conversation_messages` rows from the chat-sessions feature (and any other pre-migration data) have `tenant_id = NULL`; decide whether to assign them to a bootstrap tenant or purge them during migration.
- **Prod engine divergence:** on Postgres the post-ingest enrichment chain already no-ops, so per-tenant inventory/margin/legacy KPIs depend on the `@builder` concept-resolved path; unchanged by multi-tenancy but worth remembering when validating per-tenant KPI coverage.
- Resolves constraints **C2** (no authentication) and **C1** (hardcoded credentials) in CONTEXT.md.

items.body:
## Situation

#8 wires the OpenTelemetry `MeterProvider` into every Go service and defines the initial RED metric surface. What does not exist is the platform that receives those metrics: a time-series store, a recording-rule layer, a cardinality budget, per-tenant and per-country routing, and a query API the consoles and alerting can build on. Without it the metrics are emitted into an OTLP endpoint that has nowhere to put them.

The consequence of that gap is that the platform has no quantitative view of its own behaviour:

- **Per-tenant rate limits and resource quotas cannot be set or enforced empirically.** The brief requires them to prevent noisy-neighbour degradation across a shared-schema, RLS-isolated estate. A quota chosen without a distribution of observed per-tenant request rate and database time is a guess that will either throttle a legitimate hospital during morning OPD peak or fail to contain a runaway integration.
- **EmergencyConnect's mandated capacity headroom is unverifiable.** "Isolated, highest-SLA" is a commitment. Without saturation metrics for its pods, JetStream consumers and connection pools, nobody can say whether the headroom exists on the day an ambulance dispatch surge arrives.
- **Business-critical operational signals have no home.** Bed occupancy, OPD queue depth, pending pathologist approvals in LabConnect, cold-chain excursions in SupplyConnect and open P0 work orders in FacilityConnect are all countable and all currently invisible outside the transactional database — and the architectural rule that analytics must never run on the live clinical DB means they cannot be dashboarded by querying it.
- **Capacity and cost decisions are unevidenced**, which for a platform billed per tenant is a direct commercial exposure.

Affected: SRE on-call, platform engineers sizing services, product owners for each of the eleven products, and the hospital admin who has been promised an availability commitment.

This story delivers the metric storage, cardinality governance, recording rules and query surface. It is a sibling of #605 (centralised logging) and #607 (distributed tracing), and it is a hard dependency for #609, #610, #611 and #612.

---

## Task

### User or System Story

**As a** platform SRE and product owner
**I want** a per-country metric store that ingests OTLP metrics from every service with governed cardinality, tenant attribution and derived recording rules
**So that** I can size services, set defensible per-tenant quotas, verify EmergencyConnect headroom and drive dashboards and alerts from a single queryable source.

### Scope

**In scope**

* Metric storage per country deployment, ArgoCD-managed, ingesting OTLP push from the collector established in #8, with long-term retention in downsampled tiers (raw 15 days, 5-minute rollup 13 months).
* A **metric naming and semantic-convention standard** for HMS: OpenTelemetry semantic conventions where they exist, and an `hms.` namespace for domain metrics, enforced by a CI validator that rejects non-conforming names and unbudgeted attributes.
* **Cardinality governance**: a declared per-metric attribute budget, a collector-side limiter that drops and counts series beyond the budget, and a weekly top-cardinality report so growth is caught before it becomes an outage.
* The four golden signals per service and per JetStream subject: traffic, errors, latency and saturation — the last including connection-pool utilisation, JetStream consumer lag, Temporal task-queue backlog and Redis memory.
* **Domain metric registration**: a small Go API (`metrics.RegisterDomainGauge`) so a product module can publish counts such as `hms.beds.occupied`, `hms.opd.queue.depth`, `hms.lab.reports.awaiting_approval`, `hms.facility.workorders.open` with the priority as an attribute, and `hms.supply.coldchain.excursions` — sourced from the module, never from an analytics query against the clinical database.
* Recording rules for the expensive aggregations dashboards and alerts need (per-service availability, per-tenant request rate, p95/p99 latency), so query cost is paid once at write time.
* A query API with OpenFGA-scoped access, so a tenant-facing consumer cannot query another tenant's series.
* Per-country routing and residency enforcement; no cross-country metric replication.

**Out of scope**

* **Log ingestion, retention and search** — owned by #605.
* **Trace storage and sampling** — owned by #607.
* **Alerting rules, thresholds, escalation policy and on-call rotation** — those are consumers of this store and are defined once the golden signals exist; owned by the SRE reliability epic.
* **Dashboard composition, SLO definitions and error budgets** — owned by #610.
* **Per-tenant health scoring and noisy-neighbour attribution surfaces** — owned by #611; this issue provides the series, #611 builds the tenant view.
* **De-identified analytical warehouse and product analytics** — a separate OLAP path owned by #613.

---

## Recommended Solution

### Storage and ingestion

A Prometheus-compatible time-series store per country deployment, receiving OTLP push from the OpenTelemetry Collector DaemonSet rather than scraping pods directly. Push is preferable here because Knative scales services to zero and short-lived pods are missed by scrape intervals; the collector holds the delta and forwards it.

Retention is country-profile configuration on the same pattern as #605:

```yaml
# country-profile: IN
metrics:
  raw_retention_days: 15
  rollup_5m_retention_days: 400
  residency_region: asia-south1
  cardinality_budget_total: 2_000_000
```

### Cardinality governance

This is the single most likely way a metrics platform fails, so it is designed for rather than discovered. Every metric is declared in a checked-in registry:

```go
// pkg/metrics/registry
var BedsOccupied = Declare(Spec{
    Name:        "hms.beds.occupied",
    Kind:        Gauge,
    Unit:        "{bed}",
    Attributes:  []string{"tenant.id", "facility.id", "ward.type"},
    MaxSeries:   50_000,
})
```

The CI validator fails a build that emits a metric absent from the registry or carrying an attribute outside its declared set. At runtime the collector applies a per-metric series limiter that drops beyond `MaxSeries` and increments `otel.metrics.series_dropped`, so overflow is visible rather than silently distorting dashboards. High-cardinality identifiers — `patient.id`, `encounter.id`, `work_order.id`, ABHA numbers — are structurally impossible because they will never pass the validator; that correlation belongs on traces (#607) via exemplars.

### Domain metrics without touching the clinical database

Architectural rule 7 forbids analytics on the live OLTP database. Domain gauges are therefore maintained from the module's own event handling rather than by periodic `SELECT COUNT(*)`: MediCore's bed module increments and decrements `hms.beds.occupied` on `PatientAdmitted`, `PatientTransferred` and `PatientDischarged` consumed from NATS JetStream, with a low-frequency reconciliation sweep (hourly, off-peak, on a read replica) that corrects drift and emits `hms.beds.occupied.drift` so the correction itself is observable.

### Query API and authorisation

| Method | Path | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `POST` | `/api/v1/metrics/query` | instant query, OpenFGA-scoped |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/metrics/query_range` | range query for dashboards |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/metrics/registry` | declared metrics, units, attributes, budgets |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/metrics/cardinality` | current series counts against budget |

```
type metric_scope
  relations
    define tenant_reader: [user, group#member]
    define estate_reader: [user, group#member]
```

The query layer rewrites every submitted expression to inject a mandatory `tenant.id` label matcher derived from the caller's OpenFGA scope. Rewriting server-side, rather than validating a user-supplied matcher, means a crafted expression cannot escape the filter.

### Events consumed

`PatientAdmitted`, `PatientDischarged`, `AppointmentBooked`, `LabResultReady`, `MedicineDispensed`, `StockLow`, `AmbulanceDispatched` — each feeding a declared domain gauge or counter. No module reads another module's tables to produce a metric.

### Sequencing and dependencies

#8 must land first. The collector deployment and country-profile abstraction are prerequisites. This issue must precede #609, #610, #611 and #612. The domain-metric registration API should land early so product modules adopt it as they are built rather than being retrofitted.

### Risks

- **Cardinality explosion** — the dominant risk, mitigated by the checked-in registry, CI validator, per-metric limiter and weekly report.
- **Domain gauge drift** from missed or duplicated events — mitigated by idempotent event handling keyed on event ID and the reconciliation sweep with an explicit drift metric.
- **Metric store outage cascading into request failures** — the export path is asynchronous and bounded; a black-hole test asserts service latency is unchanged when the store is unreachable.
- **Cost growth from 13-month rollup retention** — mitigated by downsampling at ingest and a cost review at the 30-day mark.
- **Metrics becoming a PHI channel via a label** — structurally prevented by the attribute allowlist in the registry; a CI test asserts no declared attribute is a patient-level identifier.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

### Primary Scenario

**Given** MediCore is admitting and discharging patients across three facilities of one tenant, and the bed module maintains `hms.beds.occupied` from JetStream events
**When** an SRE issues a range query for `hms.beds.occupied` grouped by `facility.id` over the past 24 hours
**Then** the series are returned for all three facilities with 15-second resolution and p95 query latency under 1 second, the values match the transactional bed state within one reconciliation interval, all series carry `tenant.id` and `country.profile`, and no series carries a patient-level identifier.

### Failure or Validation Scenario

**Given** a developer adds an attribute `patient.id` to `hms.opd.queue.depth` without updating the metric registry
**When** the change is pushed and CI runs
**Then** the metric validator fails the build with an explicit message naming the undeclared attribute and the registry file to amend, the change cannot merge, and no unbudgeted series is ever created in the store.

### Edge Cases

* A Knative service scales to zero between collector export intervals — the counter's last delta is still forwarded, so a burst on a scaled-to-zero service is not silently lost.
* A tenant on the schema-per-tenant premium tier — metric attribution works identically, and the tenant's schema name never appears as a label.
* A per-metric series budget is exhausted mid-day — new series are dropped with a counter increment and a rate-limited alert, existing series continue unaffected, and dashboards display a staleness indicator rather than an apparent decline to zero.
* A JetStream consumer replays a backlog after an outage — the domain gauge does not double-count, because handlers are idempotent on event ID, and the replay is visible as consumer-lag recovery rather than as a spike in clinical activity.
* A query is submitted by a caller with no resolvable OpenFGA scope — the rewritten expression matches no series and returns empty, never the unfiltered estate.
* Clock skew between a node and the store causes out-of-order samples — samples outside the accepted window are rejected and counted, and the affected node is identified by `k8s.node.name` rather than silently corrupting a series.
## Engineering Guardrails

Complete the applicable items before the story is closed.

### Code Quality

* [ ] The change is limited to the agreed scope.
* [ ] Existing behaviour remains backward-compatible unless explicitly approved.
* [ ] Code follows the team’s agreed standards and architecture.
* [ ] No temporary code, debug output or unnecessary complexity remains.
* [ ] Error handling is explicit and does not silently ignore failures.

### Test-Driven Development

* [ ] Acceptance criteria were converted into test scenarios.
* [ ] New or changed business logic was developed using Red–Green–Refactor where practical.
* [ ] Bug fixes include a regression test that fails before the fix and passes afterwards.
* [ ] Tests validate behaviour rather than private implementation details.

### Automated Testing

* [ ] Unit tests cover new and changed logic.
* [ ] Positive, negative and important boundary scenarios are covered.
* [ ] Integration or contract tests are updated where service boundaries change.
* [ ] Critical user journeys are covered by Playwright or an equivalent E2E framework.
* [ ] Existing tests pass.
* [ ] No new flaky or skipped tests are introduced without justification.

### Security and Access

* [ ] Authentication and authorisation are enforced at the appropriate layer.
* [ ] Users and services can access only the data and actions they require.
* [ ] Input is validated and sensitive information is not exposed in logs or errors.
* [ ] Secrets and credentials are not stored in source code.
* [ ] Security and dependency scans pass.
* [ ] Tenant, account or customer isolation is tested where applicable.

### Accessibility and User Journey

* [ ] The primary user journey works from start to completion.
* [ ] Loading, empty, success and error states are handled.
* [ ] Keyboard navigation and focus behaviour work correctly.
* [ ] Controls have clear labels and accessible names.
* [ ] The change meets the team’s agreed WCAG accessibility level.
* [ ] The experience works across supported devices and browsers.

### Performance and Reliability

* [ ] The change does not introduce unnecessary API calls, database queries or processing.
* [ ] Timeouts, retries and failure behaviour are defined where applicable.
* [ ] Duplicate requests do not create inconsistent data.
* [ ] Performance-sensitive changes are tested against an agreed threshold.
* [ ] Partial failures do not leave the system in an invalid state.

### Observability

* [ ] Important failures are logged with useful diagnostic context.
* [ ] Logs do not contain sensitive information.
* [ ] Metrics or traces are added where the change affects a critical workflow.
* [ ] The team can determine whether the feature is working correctly after deployment.

### Documentation

* [ ] Relevant README, API or technical documentation is updated.
* [ ] Configuration or environment changes are documented.
* [ ] Deployment, migration or rollback steps are documented where required.
* [ ] Known limitations are recorded.

---

## Result

* **Expected user or system outcome:** Every service, JetStream consumer, Temporal worker and product module publishes governed, tenant-attributed metrics to a per-country store queryable through an authorisation-scoped API, with cardinality held inside a declared budget.
* **Expected business or operational outcome:** Per-tenant quotas and rate limits are set from observed distributions rather than guesswork; EmergencyConnect capacity headroom becomes a measurable claim; dashboards, SLOs and alerting have a single source of truth; infrastructure spend is attributable and defensible.
* **Success metric or validation method:**
  - **100%** of deployed services report all four golden signals within 5 minutes of rollout, verified by a conformance job that cross-checks the deployment inventory against the metric store.
  - Total active series stay **below 80%** of the declared cardinality budget, with zero unplanned series-limit drops over a rolling 30-day window.
  - Dashboard range queries return at **p95 under 1 second** over 24 hours of data and **under 3 seconds** over 30 days, backed by recording rules.
  - Domain gauge accuracy within **0.5%** of the transactional source at each hourly reconciliation, measured by `hms.*.drift` staying inside that band.
  - Metric ingestion adds no more than **2 ms to p95** on instrumented endpoints, measured with export enabled versus disabled.
  - Cross-tenant query attempts return empty in **100%** of adversarial isolation tests.
* **Monitoring period:** 45 days after production rollout, with a cardinality and retention-cost review at day 21.

---

## Pull Request Evidence

The pull request should include:

* [ ] Link to this story.
* [ ] Summary of the change.
* [ ] Test evidence.
* [ ] Screenshots or recordings for UI changes.
* [ ] Security, accessibility or performance evidence where relevant.
* [ ] Deployment and rollback notes for higher-risk changes.
* [ ] Known risks or follow-up work.

---

## Definition of Done

The story is complete when:

* [ ] All acceptance criteria pass.
* [ ] Required tests pass locally and in CI.
* [ ] No critical or high-severity security or quality issues remain.
* [ ] The critical user or system journey has been validated.
* [ ] Documentation is updated.
* [ ] Code review is complete.
* [ ] The change has been deployed or is ready for deployment through the standard pipeline.
* [ ] Post-deployment validation is defined or completed.
* [ ] Any exception is documented with an owner and reason.

---

## Exceptions

**Guardrail:** Accessibility and User Journey — the primary user journey, WCAG level, keyboard navigation and accessible names.
**Reason:** This story delivers a metric store, ingestion path, cardinality governance, recording rules and a query API. It ships no user interface. The dashboards and tenant views that render these series are owned by #610 and #611, where the accessibility guardrail applies in full.
**Alternative validation:** The query API is exercised by contract tests covering the loading, empty, partial-result and error responses that downstream consoles must render, so #610 and #611 inherit well-defined states rather than inventing them.
**Residual risk:** Low. The risk of an inaccessible surface is deferred, not removed, and is explicitly carried by the consuming issues.
**Approved by:** SRE Team lead (owner of the Observability epic).

**Guardrail:** Automated Testing — critical user journeys covered by Playwright or an equivalent E2E framework.
**Reason:** Partially applicable. There is no browser journey in this story, but end-to-end metric flow is a genuine integration concern that must not go untested.
**Alternative validation:** An integration suite runs a Go service, the OpenTelemetry Collector and the metric store as test containers, emits declared metrics through the registry API, and asserts that series arrive with the expected names, units and attributes, that undeclared attributes are dropped by the limiter, and that the scoped query API filters by tenant.
**Residual risk:** Low — the failure modes with real consequence are ingestion and scoping, both covered.
**Approved by:** SRE Team lead.

items.title: Ejecutar migración completa del dashboard a login integrado en ocpp-abb-1 (sin autorizaciones intermedias)
items.body:
## Objetivo y autorización
Completar **de extremo a extremo, sin pedir autorizaciones adicionales**, el despliegue y la migración del dashboard de `arthexis/ocpp-reports` desde Nginx Basic Auth al login integrado en `customer.gelectriic.com` (`ocpp-abb-1`), cubriendo tenant-b, tenant-a y administración. Este issue es una orden explícita de ejecución: desarrollar correcciones mínimas necesarias, CI, fusionar PRs propias cuando estén verdes, desplegar por el mecanismo Ansible/Bastion existente, provisionar cuentas y completar el cutover. No detenerse tras diagnóstico o una PR.

Relacionado: #185 (inventario, evidencia, seis registros y tres accesos directos). #187 ya fusionada en main, commit `698be0ae94517da0e27a9d4e3d526caf5cbb71a2`. El último release documentado en destino era `eedc4115bbc1054ede544b41559fcd26aac41689`; comprobar estado actual antes de actuar.

## Ejecución requerida
1. Localizar y reutilizar la ruta **Bastion SSH + instalador Ansible propio de Reports** que ya funcionó en #185; no depender de que `ssh ocpp-abb-1` resuelva directamente desde gway-001. Verificar HEAD de main, CI, despliegue automático existente para evitar duplicados, y release instalado. Desplegar el código integrado primero. Comprobar unidades de dashboard, Collector e ingestión, HTTPS, Nginx y allowlists.
2. Implementar **el cambio mínimo idempotente** en Ansible y templates para que los tres hosts de dashboard utilicen el login integrado sin `auth_basic`; configurar `OCPP_REPORTS_AUTH_DATABASE` y `OCPP_REPORTS_AUTH_TENANT` por instancia y permisos privados. No cambiar la autenticación del Collector ni de descargas diagnósticas. Mantener los límites de origen tenant-a/tenant-b y la administración conforme al inventario.
3. Inventariar las seis entradas de cuentas actuales, sin revelar hashes ni contraseñas. Crear seis cuentas funcionales en los tenants correspondientes, con nombres únicos cuando se repitan usuarios entre instancias; roles admin/operator correctos. **No es necesario convertir hashes APR1/bcrypt ni preservar contraseñas antiguas**: crear credenciales nuevas mediante ingreso/entrega segura, nunca en issue, argv, logs o MCP. Si un usuario no puede recibir su contraseña, documentar el bloqueo preciso y continuar con las demás tareas seguras.
4. Actualizar y probar los tres accesos directos existentes en gway-001 para abrir el login integrado (sin credenciales incrustadas). No crear sistemas permanentes de importación, herramientas remotas auxiliares o frameworks de pruebas.
5. Ejecutar pruebas representativas sobre HTTPS real: visitante sin sesión, cookie inválida/expirada/revocada -> /login; login válido/inválido, logout, perfil y cambio de contraseña, revocación, persistencia tras reinicio, roles y 403 de API, aislamiento entre tenants y source allowlists, y acceso administrativo de recuperación. Probar los tres dashboards y sus accesos directos.
6. **Completar el cutover** retirando Basic Auth solamente de los dashboards una vez que las cuentas y el login sean funcionales. Validar Nginx y acceso final. No se requiere implementar ni ensayar rollback; tampoco conservar las contraseñas anteriores. Evitar en todo momento dejar un dashboard públicamente accesible sin autenticación. No interrumpir Collector ni diagnósticos.
7. Registrar en este issue y en #185: SHA de main y release instalado, CI, Ansible, comprobaciones por dashboard, cuentas funcionales (de seis), accesos directos (de tres), estado final de Basic Auth, incidencias concretas y pruebas sanitizadas. Cerrar el issue **solo al completar** el cutover.

## Política de ejecución
Autorización del operador ya otorgada para código, PR, merge, Ansible, despliegue, creación de cuentas y cambio de autenticación del dashboard. **No solicitar confirmaciones intermedias.** Resolver problemas menores de forma autónoma. No cambiar contraseñas de servicios ajenos ni revelar secretos. Si hay una dependencia externa imposible (por ejemplo, entrega segura de contraseñas), documentarla con precisión, sin declarar éxito prematuro.
