items.body:
**Parent epic:** #2 (Project Foundation & DevOps)
**Iteration:** Iteration 2 (due Oct 20, 2026) · part of Release 1 (Iteration 4, due Nov 17, 2026)
**Story points:** 3

## Goal
Record the stack and architecture decisions the team has made, and why, as ADRs D1 to D7, so the whole team builds on one agreed foundation.

## Context
The rubric asks for a justification of frameworks and libraries (UET-2) and looks at how the design evolved (DE-2). Most decisions were made with Omerlo's CTO at the Oct 14 technical sync and now need to be written down with the alternatives that were rejected:

| # | Decision | Choice |
|---|---|---|
| D1 | Hosting | Fly.io app plus managed Postgres (not AWS; Omerlo is leaving AWS) |
| D2 | Pipeline language | Python (Elixir rejected: learning curve) |
| D3 | Search | Deferred to Iteration 5 or later; then Meilisearch or Typesense rebuilt from Postgres by a job, never dual-written |
| D4 | Storage | Postgres plus a raw payload archive; no Databricks, Snowflake or Elasticsearch |
| D5 | Tenancy | `tenant_id` on every table, enforced in the query layer, proven by a CI test |
| D6 | Ingestion | Scheduled pull with an `updated_at` watermark per source, behind a webhook-ready interface |
| D7 | Deployment shape | PULSE is a standalone service (own database, auth and UI) that reads Omerlo through its APIs |

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] Backend (FastAPI), frontend (React with Vite and TypeScript) and database (PostgreSQL) chosen and set up (#16, #19)
- [x] One ADR per decision D1 to D7 on the Architecture wiki page, each with context, the options considered, the decision, its consequences and the date
- [x] Each ADR names the alternative rejected and why (for example AWS for D1, Elixir for D2, Elasticsearch for D3, one database per tenant for D5)
- [x] Libraries chosen and recorded for: migrations, HTTP client, fuzzy matching, phone number normalization, logging, test mocking
- [x] ADR template committed so later decisions follow the same format
- [x] Decisions confirmed by the team in a meeting and recorded in the meeting log

## Tasks
- [x] Create the ADR template
- [x] Write ADRs D1 to D7
- [x] Pick and record the remaining libraries
- [x] Review with the team and link the ADRs from the Architecture page (#28)

## Dependencies
- **Blocked by:** None
- **Blocks:** #17 Configure linters, formatters and pre-commit hooks, #19 Containerize the application with Docker Compose, #21 Set up test framework, mocking and coverage tooling, #25 Implement data model v1 with tenant_id on every table, #28 Create the architecture and layer diagram

## Out of scope
- Product direction decisions (scoring, statuses, target users): they wait for sponsor validation

## Rubric coverage
`UET-2 Select appropriate tools` · `DE-2 Idea generation and selection` · `Code: Using best practices for framework`

## Definition of done
- [ ] Decision and reasoning documented in the wiki
- [ ] Reviewed with the team (and the sponsor where relevant)
- [ ] Follow-up issues created for the work it unblocks

items.title: Spec: PulseIntel v1 collaborative market intelligence dashboard

labels.name: ready-for-agent
labels.description: Fully specified, ready for an agent

items.body:
## Problem Statement

Small teams that track competitive intelligence, market signals, and internal performance data usually stitch together spreadsheets, news feeds, ad hoc scraping, dashboards, and team chat. That makes it difficult to keep observations trustworthy, collaborate around changes in real time, preserve historical context, and act quickly when something meaningful changes.

These teams need PulseIntel: a shared, real-time market intelligence product where a Tenant can organize Workspaces, attach Sources, monitor Metrics and Observations, create Insights, annotate Dashboard trends, and receive Alerts with clear provenance.

## Solution

Build PulseIntel as a multi-tenant SaaS for collaborative market intelligence. Each Tenant has global Users with Tenant Roles and Workspace Roles, a Tenant Home for navigation, tenant-owned Sources, and one or more Workspaces. Each Workspace owns Dashboards, Custom Metrics, Alert Rules, Insights, Annotations, and subscriptions to tenant Sources.

The v1 product will provide:
- Tenant/workspace collaboration with Invitations, memberships, and role-based access control
- Widget-based Dashboards with a Dashboard Time Range and optional widget-level overrides
- Tenant-owned Sources with Source Kinds for RSS feed ingestion, price tracking, KPI ingest, and Manual Source entry
- Immutable Observation History with Evidence and Evidence Snapshots for trust and auditability
- Base Metrics plus workspace-scoped Custom Metrics with strict Unit Validation, Formula Function Set guardrails, and asynchronous Metric Materialization
- Rule-based Alerts with Alert Severity, per-rule Alert Cooldown, durable Alert Events, per-user Alert Subscriptions, in-app history, and email delivery
- Insights and Annotations with Comment Threads, required Insight Evidence Links, and soft locking for finalized findings
- Revisions, Snapshots, archive/restore, Activity Feed, and Audit Trail behavior that preserves history instead of hiding it

## User Stories

1. As a tenant owner, I want to create and manage a Tenant, so that my company has a dedicated market intelligence boundary.
2. As a tenant admin, I want to invite users by email, so that teammates can join the correct Tenant and Workspaces.
3. As a user, I want a single global identity across multiple Tenants, so that I can work with different customer or internal accounts without separate logins.
4. As a user, I want to land on a Tenant Home after accepting an Invitation, so that I can choose the right Workspace quickly.
5. As a tenant admin, I want to assign Tenant Roles and Workspace Roles, so that administration and day-to-day collaboration stay separate.
6. As a workspace admin, I want to manage membership within a Workspace, so that the right people can view, edit, and administer shared intelligence.
7. As a team member, I want to create a Workspace, through tenant administration, so that different initiatives can collaborate without mixing dashboards and alerts.
8. As a workspace member, I want to open a Dashboard with a shared default time range, so that the team sees the same market picture.
9. As a workspace member, I want certain Widgets to override the Dashboard Time Range, so that a single Dashboard can show both short-term and long-term views.
10. As a workspace editor, I want to arrange Widgets on a fixed grid, so that Dashboards are flexible but still structured and versionable.
11. As a workspace editor, I want to clone a Dashboard as an independent copy, so that I can reuse setup without creating hidden linkage to the original.
12. As a workspace editor, I want to create Insights tied to supporting evidence, so that durable findings stay trustworthy.
13. As a workspace member, I want to annotate Widgets, Observations, and time ranges, so that I can add context exactly where a change appears.
14. As a workspace member, I want Comment Threads on Insights and Annotations, so that collaboration stays attached to the relevant evidence.
15. As a workspace editor, I want to lock an Insight after finalizing it, so that the finding stays stable while discussion can continue.
16. As a workspace editor, I want tenant-owned Sources to be reusable across Workspaces through Source Subscriptions, so that we avoid duplicate setup.
17. As a workspace editor, I want Subscription Filters on a Source Subscription, so that each Workspace can focus on the subset of data it actually needs.
18. As a tenant admin, I want to define Source configuration once per Tenant, so that feed and price tracking logic is consistent.
19. As a workspace editor, I want Manual Sources, so that I can capture intelligence even when automation is not ready.
20. As a workspace editor, I want Manual Source entries to require a Citation Note, so that manually entered values are still explainable.
21. As a system operator, I want RSS feed items normalized into Observations with article evidence, so that news fits the same trust model as other signals.
22. As a workspace member, I want repeated sightings of the same article deduplicated into an Article Identity, so that feeds are readable without losing provenance.
23. As a workspace editor, I want price tracking Sources to capture extracted values plus evidence snapshots, so that pricing changes can be verified later.
24. As a workspace member, I want broken source collection to surface Source Health problems, so that missing data is not mistaken for stable conditions.
25. As a workspace member, I want Collection Runs recorded separately from Observations, so that failed collection is distinguishable from no change.
26. As a tenant admin, I want Base Metrics to be tenant-owned and reused, so that source-backed definitions stay consistent across Workspaces.
27. As a workspace editor, I want to define Custom Metrics inside a Workspace, so that each team can build derived intelligence on top of shared data.
28. As a workspace editor, I want Custom Metrics to reference other Custom Metrics through an acyclic Metric Dependency Graph, so that complex derived analysis remains stable.
29. As a workspace editor, I want strict Unit Validation in formulas, so that derived Metrics do not combine incompatible values incorrectly.
30. As a workspace editor, I want a guarded Formula Function Set with arithmetic, comparisons, conditional logic, and time-window helpers, so that formulas are useful without becoming arbitrary code execution.
31. As a workspace member, I want Custom Metric values materialized asynchronously, so that dashboards and alerts remain fast and predictable.
32. As a workspace editor, I want KPI ingest credentials scoped to a Workspace, so that internal metric ownership matches the collaboration boundary.
33. As an integration system, I want to push KPI Observations with optional Metric Dimensions, so that teams can track segmented business performance.
34. As a workspace editor, I want to create Alert Rules on Observations and Metrics, so that meaningful changes are surfaced automatically.
35. As a workspace editor, I want Alert Severity on Alert Rules, so that high-priority changes stand out from routine monitoring.
36. As a workspace member, I want Alert Events recorded durably, so that I can review alert history in-app and not rely only on transient notifications.
37. As a workspace member, I want to acknowledge an Alert Event, so that the team can see that someone has seen it.
38. As a workspace member, I want Alert Cooldown configured per Alert Rule, so that noisy conditions do not overwhelm the Workspace.
39. As a new workspace member, I want alert subscriptions to start unsubscribed, so that joining a Workspace does not immediately flood my inbox.
40. As a workspace member, I want to subscribe only to the Alert Rules I care about, so that notifications stay relevant.
41. As a workspace member, I want Alerts delivered in-app and by email, so that I can respond quickly whether I am in the product or away from it.
42. As a workspace member, I want realtime updates for Alerts, Annotations, Comment Threads, and dashboard content refreshes, so that collaboration feels live without requiring full concurrent editing.
43. As a workspace member, I want immutable Observation History, so that I can trust what the system actually captured at a given time.
44. As a workspace member, I want long-term historical analysis to transparently use downsampled data when needed, so that old trends remain explorable without keeping infinite raw detail.
45. As a workspace editor, I want every change to a Dashboard, Custom Metric, or Alert Rule to create a Revision, so that restore behavior is simple and auditable.
46. As a workspace editor, I want named Snapshots, so that important milestones can be restored intentionally.
47. As a workspace member, I want restoring a Revision or Snapshot to create a new current Revision, so that history is preserved instead of rewritten.
48. As a tenant admin, I want Workspaces archived before deletion, so that shared intelligence is not lost accidentally.
49. As a tenant admin, I want Workspace Restore to recover the full Workspace state, so that archiving acts as a safety measure rather than a teardown.
50. As a workspace member, I want an Activity Feed for collaboration, alert, and source health changes, so that I can understand what the team and system are doing over time.
51. As an administrator, I want an Audit Trail for security, admin, and restore actions, so that accountability exists without exposing everything as user-facing noise.
52. As a product team, I want PulseIntel to treat evidence and provenance as first-class concepts throughout the product, so that trust remains a core differentiator.

## Implementation Decisions

- Build the product as a modular monolith with separate worker processes for ingestion, metric materialization, alert evaluation, and other asynchronous jobs.
- Use a multi-tenant SaaS model from day one with a single global user identity and shared-schema tenant isolation enforced at the application and query level.
- Implement authentication with Auth0 rather than custom JWT infrastructure.
- Target AWS for v1, running the application and workers on ECS Fargate.
- Use PostgreSQL as the primary store with TimescaleDB for time-series workloads.
- Use Redis and BullMQ for background job orchestration.
- Store Evidence metadata in PostgreSQL and Evidence Snapshots in S3.
- Model the core domain around Tenant, Workspace, Dashboard, Widget, Source, Source Subscription, Observation, Metric, Custom Metric, Alert Rule, Alert Event, Insight, Annotation, Revision, Snapshot, Activity Feed, and Audit Trail.
- Keep Sources tenant-owned, with workspace-level Source Subscriptions and Subscription Filters controlling how each Workspace consumes shared Sources.
- Support first-class Source Kinds for RSS feed, price tracker, KPI ingest API, and Manual Source in v1.
- Represent each collection attempt as a Collection Run, distinct from the Observations it may or may not produce.
- Model Observations with a shared envelope for timestamps, provenance, and analysis, plus kind-specific payloads and evidence details.
- Keep Observation History immutable; corrections and recaptures must create new or superseding records rather than overwriting history.
- Deduplicate repeated news items into a stable Article Identity while preserving collection history.
- Define Base Metrics at the tenant level and allow Workspaces to define Custom Metrics locally.
- Support Custom Metrics over workspace-visible Metrics only, with an acyclic Metric Dependency Graph and strict Unit Validation.
- Materialize Custom Metric values asynchronously when upstream Observations or Metrics change.
- Require explicit Metric Unit metadata and support optional Metric Dimensions on ingested metric values.
- Implement Alert Rules as rule-based conditions only in v1, with per-rule Alert Severity, per-rule Alert Cooldown, durable Alert Events, and user-level Alert Subscriptions.
- Evaluate Alert Rules both on relevant data updates and on scheduled sweeps so missing-data conditions can be detected.
- Default new workspace members to an unsubscribed Default Subscription State for Alert Rules.
- Support in-app and email alert delivery in v1, using user acknowledgement rather than a full incident-resolution workflow.
- Allow Viewers to contribute Annotations and Comment Threads, while structural changes remain limited to Editors and Workspace Admins.
- Require every Insight to carry at least one Insight Evidence Link to an Observation, annotation target, or Evidence reference.
- Support soft-locking for Insights: locked Insights are read-only for normal editors, but discussion can continue and authorized users can reopen them.
- Version Dashboards, Custom Metrics, and Alert Rules with automatic Revisions on every saved change plus named Snapshots.
- Restoring historical state must create a new Revision instead of mutating past history.
- Archive Workspaces before deletion and allow full Workspace Restore, including dashboards, subscriptions, alerts, and historical state.
- Provide a Dashboard Time Range with optional widget-level overrides.
- Keep Dashboards workspace-owned; clones are independent copies and not live-linked templates.
- Expose realtime product behavior through REST APIs plus Socket.io events rather than GraphQL subscriptions.
- Build a user-visible Activity Feed for collaboration, alert, and source-health events, distinct from the admin-oriented Audit Trail.
- Capture source failures as Source Health problems and failed Collection Runs instead of silently skipping data or carrying forward stale values as current truth.

## Testing Decisions

- A good test should verify external behavior and user-visible outcomes rather than internal implementation details.
- The primary seam should be the application boundary: REST API contracts, Socket.io realtime behavior, worker-triggered outcomes, persistence-visible revisions/history, and authorization behavior across tenant and workspace boundaries.
- A narrow secondary seam should exist at the source collector adapter boundary so each Source Kind can be tested against a stable collection contract without depending on live third-party systems.
- Test the tenancy and membership model through public auth, invitation, and authorization behavior rather than direct storage assumptions.
- Test Dashboard behavior through creation, widget layout, cloning, time-range defaults/overrides, versioning, archive/restore, and visibility rules.
- Test source ingestion through Collection Run outcomes, Observation creation, evidence capture, Source Health transitions, and source-subscription filtering behavior.
- Test Custom Metrics through formula validation, Metric Unit enforcement, acyclic dependency handling, asynchronous materialization, and historical query behavior.
- Test Alerts through rule evaluation, Alert Cooldown behavior, Alert Event creation, acknowledgement, subscription defaults, delivery fan-out, and realtime propagation.
- Test Insights and collaboration through evidence-link requirements, annotation anchors, comment threads, locking/reopening rules, and Activity Feed visibility.
- Test historical behavior through immutable Observation History, retention/downsampling query behavior, Revision creation, Snapshot restore, and Workspace Restore.
- Prior art in the current repository is effectively none because the codebase is still greenfield; the initial test suite should establish reusable patterns around high-level contract tests and source-adapter tests rather than low-level unit tests of framework plumbing.

## Out of Scope

- Full Google-Docs-style concurrent dashboard editing with live layout conflict resolution.
- Slack delivery in v1.
- Statistical or ML-based anomaly detection in v1.
- App store tracking in v1.
- Full template libraries with linked dashboard inheritance.
- Generic comments on every object in the system.
- Arbitrary code execution or unrestricted scripting inside Custom Metric formulas.
- Per-tenant schemas or per-tenant databases in v1.
- Separate microservices for each product capability in v1.
- Broad connector catalogs beyond RSS, price tracking, KPI ingest, and Manual Source.

## Further Notes

- This spec should be treated as the v1 product and architecture baseline for PulseIntel.
- The domain glossary in CONTEXT.md and the ADRs in docs/adr are part of the contract for future work and should be read alongside this spec.
- The implementation should favor preserving trust, provenance, and historical explainability over aggressively simplifying away domain history.
- The product differentiator is not just monitoring data, but helping teams collaborate around trustworthy evidence and shared interpretation.

items.title: # ISP-143: Multi-Tenancy — Two Cities Sharing One Deployment with Isolated Data vs Shared Indexer vs Per-Tenant Contracts and the Noisy-Neighbor Disaster

labels.name: Stellar Wave
labels.description: Issues in the Stellar wave program

items.body:
- Type: Integration + Spike
- Severity: P0/Critical
- Difficulty: Extreme
- Estimate: 24h
- Touch surface: 15 files

## 1. Background & Context (rich — at least 5 paragraphs, reference REAL repo paths and behaviors)

HelPhone was born single-city: one Soroban contract set (`contracts/emergency_vault/`, `contracts/helphone_dao/`, `contracts/maintainer_vault/`, `contracts/aegis_vault/`), one indexer pipeline (`server/indexer/daemon.ts` → `parser.ts` → Postgres via `server/db/poolManager.ts`), one dispatch route (`server/routes/dispatch.ts`), one history API (`server/routes/history.ts`), and one frontend monolith (`src/App.tsx` + `src/main.tsx`) with `src/lib/featureFlags.ts` toggling features globally. Now two cities want to share one Render deployment (`render.yaml`, `Dockerfile.hermetic`) to split costs, and every shared layer becomes a blending hazard: City A's incidents visible in City B's `CommunityMap.jsx`, City A's surge consuming City B's dispatch latency, City A's DAO proposal draining a treasury City B thought was theirs. Multi-tenancy is not a flag; it is a data-isolation, noisy-neighbor, and contract-topology redesign that touches every layer simultaneously.

The second paragraph is about the data-isolation fault line. Postgres access flows through `server/db/connection.ts`, `poolManager.ts`, `migrator.ts`, `partitioning.js`, `maintenance.ts`, and `indexOptimizer.ts`, with `migrations/` defining the schema. Today there is no `tenant_id` discipline: `parser.ts` writes incident rows without tenant scoping, `history.ts` serves them without tenant filtering, `sync.ts` replicates them to offline clients without tenant partitioning, and `syncManager.ts` + `crdt.ts` merge them without tenant-aware conflict domains. Adding tenancy means choosing row-level security vs schema-per-tenant vs database-per-tenant, backfilling every row, rewriting every query, re-partitioning (`partitioning.js`) hot tables, and proving via adversarial tests that no query path — including telemetry (`server/telemetry.js`), health checks (`server/routes/health.ts`), and the docs endpoint (`server/routes/docs.ts` + `swagger.json`) — leaks cross-tenant rows. One missed `WHERE tenant_id` in `history.ts` is a front-page privacy breach under `docs/privacy-policy.md`.

The third paragraph is about the indexer sharing dilemma. A single `daemon.ts` ingesting events for all tenants' contracts is operationally simple but creates fate-sharing: a spam storm against City A's `emergency_vault` fills the ingestion queue, delays City B's dispatch-relevant events, and `rentRenewer.ts` burns shared RPC quota renewing City A's bloated entries while City B's critical entries expire. The alternative — per-tenant indexer shards with per-tenant RPC endpoints selected via `src/lib/rpcHealth.ts` — multiplies operational cost and contradicts the cost-sharing motive. The spike must measure the noisy-neighbor blast radius with `server/tests/load.js` dual-tenant surge tests, design per-tenant ingestion quotas and lag SLOs, and decide whether tenancy is enforced at ingestion (separate cursors per tenant) or only at serving (shared ingestion, filtered reads), with failure drills proving City B stays green while City A burns.

The fourth paragraph is about contract topology. Options range from shared contracts with tenant-scoped storage keys (cheapest, riskiest — one contract bug or DAO vote affects both cities) to per-tenant contract instances with a shared factory (clean isolation, multiplied deploy/migration/rent burden via `scripts/deploy-local-contract.sh` and `scripts/export-contract-state.sh` per tenant) to per-tenant networks entirely. `soroban-contract.md`, `docs/soroban-footprints.md`, and `docs/gas-optimization.md` must be re-evaluated per topology because footprints, rent, and batching (`src/lib/txBatcher.ts`, `src/lib/footprint.ts`) scale differently when storage keys double. The DAO layer (`helphone_dao`) is the hardest: either a federated DAO with per-city sub-treasuries or two independent DAOs sharing only infrastructure — a governance decision with on-chain consequences that cannot be refactored after mainnet deployment without migration ceremonies.

The fifth paragraph frames the spike: stand up a two-tenant prototype on one deployment — two contract sets (or scoped namespaces), tenant-aware indexer with per-tenant lag metrics, tenant-filtered dispatch/history/sync APIs, tenant-switched UI (subdomain or path tenancy wired through `featureFlags.ts` + `env.ts`), and a noisy-neighbor drill where Tenant A is load-attacked while Tenant B's p50/p99 dispatch latency and map freshness are measured. The deliverable is the topology decision with migration math, not a `tenant_id` column added hopefully.

## 2. Current Broken Behaviour

- Zero tenant scoping: `parser.ts` writes, `history.ts`/`dispatch.ts`/`sync.ts` serve, and `CommunityMap.jsx` renders without any tenant predicate; enabling a second city today merges both cities' emergencies into one feed.
- Shared fate ingestion: single `daemon.ts` cursor and shared `poolManager.ts` pool mean Tenant A surge directly inflates Tenant B ingestion lag and API latency with no quota or bulkhead.
- Global feature flags: `featureFlags.ts` toggles apply deployment-wide; City A cannot pilot a dispatch-policy change without exposing City B to the same experiment.
- Single treasury/DAO: `helphone_dao` + `TreasuryPanel.jsx` + `treasury.ts` assume one treasury; two cities sharing it have no budget isolation, and one city's voters can drain shared funds.
- Telemetry blending: `telemetry.ts` + `telemetry.js` emit tenant-agnostic metrics, so per-tenant SLOs, billing splits, and noisy-neighbor attribution are impossible.
- Migration blindness: `migrator.ts` + `migrations/` have no tenant-aware rollout story; a schema change locks or breaks both cities simultaneously with no per-tenant rollback.

## 3. Desired End State

- Topology decision recorded: shared-vs-per-tenant contracts with rent/footprint math, DAO federation model, and migration reversibility analysis; prototype implements the chosen topology for two tenants on one `render.yaml` deployment.
- Tenant isolation proven: every read/write path (`parser.ts`, `history.ts`, `dispatch.ts`, `sync.ts`, `health.ts`, `docs.ts`) enforces tenant scope (RLS or equivalent) with adversarial tests asserting zero cross-tenant rows under fuzzed tenant headers, subdomain spoofing, and direct-ID enumeration.
- Bulkheads + quotas: per-tenant ingestion quotas in `daemon.ts`, per-tenant DB pool partitions in `poolManager.ts`, per-tenant rate limits in `rateLimiter.ts`, and per-tenant RPC budgeting via `rpcHealth.ts`; noisy-neighbor drill shows Tenant B p99 dispatch latency degrades ≤15% while Tenant A absorbs 20x surge.
- Tenant-aware UI + flags: tenancy resolved from subdomain/path with `env.ts` + `featureFlags.ts` namespaced per tenant; `App.tsx` shell renders tenant branding and filters `CommunityMap.jsx` pins without cross-tenant cache bleed in `service-worker.js`.
- Per-tenant observability + billing: telemetry carries `tenant_id` from client (`telemetry.ts`) through server (`telemetry.js`) to dashboards; cost attribution per tenant for RPC, DB, and bandwidth supports fair cost splits.
- Tenant-scoped migrations: `migrator.ts` supports per-tenant rollout with canary (Tenant A first, Tenant B gated on SLOs) and per-tenant rollback without shared downtime.

## 4. Files / Systems Involved (10-15 real paths)

1. `contracts/emergency_vault/` — tenant namespacing vs per-tenant instance decision and storage-key design
2. `contracts/helphone_dao/` — federated vs independent DAO treasuries per tenant
3. `server/indexer/daemon.ts` — per-tenant cursors, quotas, and lag SLO instrumentation
4. `server/indexer/parser.ts` — tenant-scoped ingestion with tenant attribution
5. `server/db/poolManager.ts` — pool partitioning and per-tenant bulkheads
6. `server/db/partitioning.js` — hot-table re-partitioning by tenant
7. `server/db/migrator.ts` — tenant-aware migration runner with canary support
8. `server/routes/dispatch.ts` — tenant-filtered dispatch with per-tenant policy hooks
9. `server/routes/history.ts` — tenant-enforced history with enumeration-proof ID scoping
10. `server/routes/sync.ts` — tenant-partitioned offline sync with per-tenant conflict domains
11. `server/middleware/rateLimiter.ts` — per-tenant throttle buckets
12. `src/lib/featureFlags.ts` — namespaced flags with tenant resolution
13. `src/components/CommunityMap.jsx` — tenant-filtered rendering with cache isolation
14. `src/lib/telemetry.ts` — tenant-tagged client metrics
15. `render.yaml` — single-deployment two-tenant topology (env, domains, scaling)

## 5. Reproduction Steps (numbered, with real commands)

1. `npm install && cat render.yaml | head -n 60; ls contracts/*/src/*.rs 2>/dev/null | head` — confirm single-deployment, single-contract-set baseline.
2. `rg -n "tenant|city_id|org_id" server/ src/ contracts/ migrations/ -i | head -n 20` — confirm zero tenancy discipline anywhere in the stack.
3. Seed two-tenant fixture: insert City A + City B incidents into Postgres via `server/db/connection.ts` helper or `psql $DATABASE_URL -c "select * from incidents limit 3"`; then `curl -s "http://localhost:3000/api/history?limit=20" | python3 -c "import json,sys; print(sorted(set(i.get('city', i.get('tenant','none')) for i in json.load(sys.stdin).get('items',[]))))"` — demonstrate blended feed.
4. Noisy-neighbor drill: `node server/tests/load.js --tenant city-a --rps 500 --duration 120 2>&1 | tail -n 20 & node server/tests/load.js --tenant city-b --probe-latency 2>&1 | tail -n 20` — show City B p99 degrades in lockstep with City A surge (shared fate).
5. `curl -s http://localhost:3000/api/dispatch -H "X-Tenant: city-b" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"incident_id":"city-a-id-here"}' -w "\n%{http_code}\n" | tail -n 10` — attempt cross-tenant dispatch reference; record whether the server rejects or obeys.
6. `VITE_TENANT=city-a npm run dev` vs `VITE_TENANT=city-b npm run dev` — confirm flags and map pins do not actually isolate (same pins, same flags).
7. Contract check: `bash scripts/export-contract-state.sh --network testnet --output /tmp/opencode/single-tenant.json 2>&1 | tail -n 5; rg -n "tenant|sub_account|scope" contracts/emergency_vault/src/ -i | head` — confirm no tenant namespacing on-chain.
8. Bundle blended-feed responses, drill latencies, and cross-tenant dispatch result as tenancy-missing exhibits.

## 6. Spike Investigation Plan

1. Decide contract topology: prototype shared-scoped-keys vs per-tenant instances on local sandbox (`scripts/soroban-local-node.sh` + `deploy-local-contract.sh`); measure footprint/rent per topology and DAO-vote blast radius.
2. Implement tenant resolution: subdomain/path/header → verified tenant context in middleware (`auth.ts`, `rateLimiter.ts`, `cors.ts`); fuzz with spoofed headers and enumerated IDs proving rejection.
3. Enforce data isolation: add tenant scoping to schema (RLS policies or tenant-partitioned tables), rewrite `parser.ts`/`history.ts`/`dispatch.ts`/`sync.ts` queries, backfill fixtures; run adversarial cross-tenant test suite aiming for zero leaked rows.
4. Build bulkheads: partition `poolManager.ts` pools, quota `daemon.ts` ingestion per tenant with lag gauges, per-tenant `rateLimiter.ts` buckets, per-tenant RPC budgets; re-run dual-tenant `load.js` drill measuring Tenant B SLO preservation.
5. Namespace flags + UI: extend `featureFlags.ts` + `env.ts` with per-tenant overrides; isolate `service-worker.js` caches and `CommunityMap.jsx` pin stores per tenant; verify no cache bleed across tenant switches.
6. Instrument per-tenant telemetry + billing: thread `tenant_id` through `telemetry.ts` → `telemetry.js` → dashboards; attribute RPC/DB/bandwidth costs per tenant for the cost-sharing agreement.
7. Prove migrations: extend `migrator.ts` for per-tenant canary (migrate Tenant A, hold Tenant B on SLO gate); drill a rollback of Tenant A without touching Tenant B.
8. Write the ADR: topology choice, isolation mechanism, quota numbers, migration plan, and per-tenant runbook; include the noisy-neighbor drill report as the decision's evidence annex.

## 7. Acceptance Criteria (8-12 hard checkboxes)

- [ ] Contract topology prototype running two tenants on one deployment with measured footprint/rent deltas and DAO isolation semantics documented.
- [ ] Zero cross-tenant leakage: adversarial suite (fuzzed headers, subdomain spoof, ID enumeration across `history.ts`/`dispatch.ts`/`sync.ts`/`docs.ts`) passes with 0 leaked rows (CI-blocking).
- [ ] Noisy-neighbor drill report: 20x surge on Tenant A while Tenant B p99 dispatch latency degrades ≤15% and map freshness SLO holds; graphs attached.
- [ ] Per-tenant quotas live: ingestion lag per tenant dashboarded, pool partitions enforced, rate-limiter buckets independent (burst on A does not throttle B).
- [ ] Tenant-aware flags: same deployment serves different flag values per tenant; pilot flag flipped for City A only with City B observably unchanged.
- [ ] UI isolation: tenant switch changes branding, pins, and cached offline data with no bleed (service-worker cache keys namespaced; verified by cache-dump test).
- [ ] Per-tenant telemetry + cost attribution: dashboards filterable by tenant; one-week cost split computed from real drill traffic.
- [ ] Canary migration proven: schema change rolled to Tenant A, gated, then to Tenant B; Tenant A rollback drill succeeds without Tenant B impact.
- [ ] Privacy review: `privacy-policy.md` + `security-architecture.md` updated with tenancy boundaries; DPA implications of shared infrastructure recorded.
- [ ] ADR merged under `docs/adr/` with topology decision, quota table, and rollback runbook; `TODO.md` reflects per-tenant rollout milestones.

## 8. Why This Takes 24h / Why It Is Extremely Hard

Multi-tenancy is a whole-stack invariant transplant performed on a running disaster-response system: every query needs a tenant predicate that was never there, every shared queue needs a quota that changes its fairness properties, every contract needs a topology decision that is irreversible after mainnet, and every cache needs a namespace that must survive offline-first service-worker semantics. The adversarial testing is genuinely adversarial — proving a negative (no leakage on any path, including telemetry, health, docs, and error messages) under fuzzing — and the noisy-neighbor drill requires orchestrating dual-tenant load with production-grade measurement while the single deployment wheezes. The contract-topology prototype alone demands local Soroban multi-instance deployment with footprint accounting, and the ADR must settle a governance fight (shared vs independent DAOs) that is really a political fight between two cities wearing technical clothes. Twenty-four hours is the minimum to produce evidence rather than opinions.

## 9. Risks & Blast Radius

- One missed predicate is a breach: tenancy retrofits fail open by default; any unscoped query (including analytics, telemetry joins, admin endpoints) silently re-blends cities with legal consequences under both cities' DPAs.
- Bulkheads mis-tuned starve the wrong city: per-tenant quotas that are too rigid turn a legitimate city-wide disaster surge into self-inflicted load-shedding; quota policy needs disaster overrides with audit trails.
- Contract topology lock-in: per-tenant instances multiply rent/migration burden forever; shared contracts make one city's governance crisis both cities' crisis — either choice compounds for a decade.
- Migration canary false confidence: Tenant A canary passing does not prove Tenant B safety when data distributions differ (dense urban vs sprawling rural incident shapes); canary gates need per-tenant SLOs, not global ones.
- Cost-sharing disputes: without airtight per-tenant cost attribution, the cheaper city subsidizes the disaster-prone city and the partnership collapses exactly when solidarity matters most.

items.title: [Phase 4] Implement OTel telemetry ingestion and Evidence Store
items.body:
## Goal

Implement the Phase 4 durable all-signal telemetry foundation used by later async analysis: applications export standard OpenTelemetry logs, metrics, and traces; Flaggo acknowledges valid OTLP requests only after appending them to a bounded Raw OTLP Inbox; a versioned asynchronous materializer produces selected, query-ready Evidence Store observations.

Parent: #25.

## Architecture

```text
application-owned OTel providers
  -> OTLP logs / metrics / traces
  -> bounded durable Raw OTLP Inbox
  -> versioned Evidence Materializer
  -> query-ready Evidence Store
  -> async analysis
```

## Scope

- Emit `flaggo.decision.received` after a successful SDK `decide()` response. The decision ID remains correlation metadata; the event does not claim the result was applied.
- Keep `flaggo.outcome.observed` as an optional convenience shape, not the definition of outcome or the only valid evidence source.
- Keep applications as owners of their OTel providers, resources, instrumentation scopes, exporters, flush, and shutdown. A Collector is optional.
- Implement OTel Ingestion, the OTLP Receiver, and the Raw OTLP Inbox in Rust. Replace and remove the existing .NET ingestion path rather than maintaining parallel implementations.
- Use a root Cargo workspace with a pinned toolchain and lock file; keep Contract Service and Decision Service in .NET during this slice while all processes share separately owned tables in the same SQLite database.
- Accept standard OTLP/HTTP logs, metrics, and traces at `/v1/logs`, `/v1/metrics`, and `/v1/traces` using Protobuf JSON or binary protobuf, with identity or gzip request compression and a configurable decompressed-size limit.
- Validate transport and the signal-specific export-request message, then atomically append the complete decompressed request plus receipt and integrity metadata to a bounded durable Raw OTLP Inbox before returning success.
- Return full-request OTLP success after durable enqueue. Reject malformed, unsupported, oversized, or unavailable requests as a whole; item-level semantic failures do not use OTLP partial success.
- Bound inbox replay by explicit age and byte policies. The initial configurable defaults are 1 GiB of retained decompressed payload bytes and a 24-hour hard retention. Reject capacity overflow with a retryable response rather than evicting non-expired telemetry.
- Compact successfully materialized batches only after checkpointing and the configured minimum replay window.
- Materialize asynchronously using explicit OTLP profile, decoder, identity, selector, and projection versions.
- Decompose one candidate per log record, span, selectable span event, and Gauge, Sum, Histogram, Exponential Histogram, or Summary data point.
- Support the complete recursive OTLP `AnyValue` surface and preserve resource, resource schema, instrumentation scope, scope schema, and selected signal context.
- Keep logical source identity distinct from canonical content digest. Make duplicate delivery idempotent and retain conflicting content under one logical identity with diagnostics.
- Always materialize canonical Flaggo events. Apply versioned contract selectors to ordinary OTel telemetry after enqueue; unmatched inbox telemetry may expire under the replay policy.
- Define a native OTel selector contract for metrics, logs, spans, and span events after the inbox receiver and before implementing contract-aware materialization. Current `learning.evidence.binding` selects only `flaggo.outcome.observed`.
- Provide storage-agnostic Raw OTLP Inbox and Evidence Store contracts with transactional SQLite implementations for the autonomous deployment.
- Keep Decision Service independent of ingestion, the inbox, and Evidence Store.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A successful SDK decision emits one `flaggo.decision.received` log event with decision ID, exact contract/executable digests, result, evaluation provenance, time, and available correlation attributes, independent of trace sampling.
- [ ] An app without the Flaggo SDK can export resource-scoped OTLP logs, metrics, and traces through standard exporters.
- [ ] All three endpoints accept both profile encodings and both supported compression modes, enforce the decompressed-size bound, and return standard signal-specific OTLP responses.
- [ ] A success response is impossible before the complete request is durably committed to the Raw OTLP Inbox.
- [ ] Inbox entries preserve signal, encoding, media type, compression, profile version, receipt time, byte length, SHA-256 hash, and decompressed payload and are immutable while retained.
- [ ] Receiver success is independent of current contracts, item-level materialization, and async analysis; no item-level partial-success response is emitted.
- [ ] Retained requests replay after restart, failed materialization remains diagnosable and retryable, and compaction never removes an eligible batch before checkpoint and minimum replay retention.
- [ ] Materialization is deterministic, versioned, checkpointed, and idempotent, with provenance back to retained inbox batches.
- [ ] Standard scalar, array, key/value-list, bytes, and empty `AnyValue` values decode recursively without rejecting valid siblings.
- [ ] Metric projection defines correct candidate identity and observation-time semantics for all five metric data-point kinds, including multi-point and late-arriving exports.
- [ ] Canonical Flaggo events always materialize; ordinary telemetry materializes only under an accepted selector snapshot, and newly accepted selectors can backfill the retained inbox range.
- [ ] Decision and outcome events carrying the same decision ID remain distinct observations; span identity includes both trace ID and span ID.
- [ ] Duplicate content materializes once, while conflicting content under one logical source identity is retained and diagnosed.
- [ ] Inbox health, replay boundary, capacity, materialization lag/failures, duplicate/conflict counts, and evidence freshness are observable.
- [ ] Focused contracts, SDK, inbox, materializer, Evidence Store, ingestion, and local example tests pass.
- [ ] Decision Service remains stateless and never reads telemetry, the Raw OTLP Inbox, or Evidence Store during runtime evaluation.

## In-scope remaining work

- [ ] Bootstrap the Rust workspace, pinned toolchain, dependency lock, CI gates, and cross-platform example launcher support.
- [ ] Replace the .NET OTel Ingestion host and synchronous raw-evidence path with the Rust OTLP Receiver and SQLite Raw OTLP Inbox.
- [ ] Implement bounded retention and capacity using the configurable 1 GiB / 24-hour defaults and retryable overflow behavior.
- [ ] Implement real-host binary protobuf conformance in addition to the existing JSON path.
- [ ] Define and approve native OTel evidence selectors before materializer implementation.
- [ ] Implement the versioned materializer, checkpoints, diagnostics, and compaction boundary.
- [ ] Complete recursive `AnyValue` decoding and per-candidate failure handling.
- [ ] Implement metric data-point decomposition, identity, and time indexing.
- [ ] Apply selector snapshots, deduplication, conflict handling, and Evidence Store projection.

Evidence query pagination and arbitrary SQL/query capability are deferred beyond this issue.

## Non-goals

- Async correlation, evidence interpretation, rates, aggregation, attribution, candidate generation, or activation; #54 owns that work.
- Treating every received decision as proof that the result was applied.
- Requiring app telemetry to use the Flaggo SDK or explicit outcome helper.
- Production telemetry authentication, tenancy, distributed deployment, Kafka, object storage, or a permanent raw telemetry archive.
- Attribute redaction and sensitive-data policy.
- A general-purpose Evidence Store query language in this phase.

items.title: Daily Content Summary 2025-04-28
items.body:
# 📰 Daily Content Summary - 2025-04-28
### Executive Summary

**Key Insights**

*   **Offline Education:** Internet-in-a-Box provides crucial educational resources in remote areas, demonstrating the potential of localized Wi-Fi hotspots to bridge the digital divide.
*   **Security Vulnerabilities:** A vulnerability in iOS, triggered by a specific Darwin notification, could effectively soft-brick devices, highlighting the importance of robust security measures even in established operating systems. Apple addressed this in iOS 18.3.
*   **Founder Dynamics:** Non-technical founders often struggle to attract technical co-founders due to an overvaluation of their own contributions and an undervaluation of technical expertise. Demonstrating business acumen through customer acquisition is key.
*   **Creativity Boost:** Reading obituaries can enhance creativity by exposing individuals to diverse life stories and fostering the ability to make remote associations between seemingly unrelated concepts.
*   **AI Code Generation:** While AI can generate code easily, it often lacks the understanding and quality necessary for effective software engineering, emphasizing the continued importance of human reasoning and abstraction.

**Emerging Patterns**

*   **Bridging Gaps:** Several articles focus on bridging gaps: the digital divide (Internet-in-a-Box), the gap between business and technical founders, the gap between industry expertise and academic achievement (SNATIKA), and the gap between existing business systems and modern AI capabilities (Ambassador's Blackbird).
*   **Security Concerns:** Security vulnerabilities are a recurring theme, ranging from iOS soft-bricking to IMSI catcher vulnerabilities in cellular networks, highlighting the constant need for vigilance and innovation in security measures.
*   **AI Integration:** AI is both a problem and a solution. AI-generated code can be problematic, but AI is also used to discover new functions of genes related to Alzheimer's disease and is being integrated into NASA's knowledge management systems.

**Implications**

*   **Decentralized Education:** The success of Internet-in-a-Box could lead to a wider adoption of localized, offline educational resources, empowering communities with limited internet access.
*   **Enhanced Security Protocols:** The iOS vulnerability and IMSI catcher issues will likely drive stricter security protocols and continuous monitoring in mobile operating systems and cellular networks.
*   **Evolving Founder Roles:** The challenges faced by non-technical founders may lead to a shift in startup dynamics, with a greater emphasis on demonstrating business traction before seeking technical partners.
*   **AI-Augmented Creativity:** The connection between reading obituaries and enhanced creativity suggests that AI could be used to curate diverse content and stimulate innovative thinking.
*   **AI-Human Collaboration:** The limitations of AI-generated code emphasize the need for a collaborative approach, where AI assists human developers rather than replacing them entirely.

**Notable Quotes**

*   "The key to success lies in building a strong network and proving their value in customer acquisition and relationship building." - (Article on non-technical founders)
*   "Third-party credibility is a form of life hacking that doesn't always require hard work." - Jonathan Roseland (on letters of reference)
*   "The Stasi aimed to disrupt activist groups and individuals by creating conflict, sabotaging activities, isolating groups, and undermining personal confidence." - (Article on East German political activists)

How can we better balance the benefits of AI-generated content with the need for human oversight and quality control? What innovative solutions can be developed to address security vulnerabilities in increasingly complex technological systems?

items.title: Spec: two Agents live, Bantuson first

labels.name: ready-for-agent
labels.description: Fully specified, ready for an AFK agent

items.body:
Collapses the closed map [Map: two Agents live, Bantuson first](https://github.com/mfanafuthimhlanga/wchats/issues/4). Every decision below links to its ticket, which holds the detail and the evidence. Words are `CONTEXT.md`'s.

## Problem Statement

W Chats promises a business owner an Agent that is defensible: grounded in their Corpus, evaluated, and red-teamed before it goes live. After fourteen weeks, no Agent has ever been live. The Harness had never invoked an Agent until 2026-08-22; no `ship` Verdict has ever existed, and the recommendation that would produce one is written by a model, not computed; every model call is unpriced and its served model unrecorded; the deploy plan was sized at about $204 a month and never applied; and the eval subsystem grew to 7,193 lines of which the one observed run executed 41%. The owner cannot show either finish-line Agent to anyone.

## Solution

Refactor in place to the smallest system that takes one Agent from signup to a public URL through an honest gate, then do it twice: the Bantuson portfolio support Agent first (provisioned entirely through a new MCP server, embedded on the portfolio site), then the Mellow Transactional Agent (through the admin UI, against Stripe test mode). Dead subsystems are deleted; the run's numbers become frozen domain types written once and computed nowhere else; the Verdict becomes a pure function; every model call lands in a ledger with tokens, served model and derived cost in USD and ZAR; the platform moves to one DPA-backed provider on an owned tool loop; and the stack runs on Railway under a hard spend cap.

## User Stories

1. As the platform owner, I want the Harness to invoke the Agent and produce a Verdict from real scores, so that "evaluated before live" is a fact and not a sentence.
2. As the platform owner, I want the `ship` or `block` decision computed by code from typed inputs, so that no model-generated label ever gates a deploy.
3. As the platform owner, I want every `block` to carry typed reasons naming the signal, the observed value and the threshold, so that I know what to fix without reading logs.
4. As the platform owner, I want the golden set to gate absolutely and the exploratory set to gate on a confidence interval, so that my own contract is never averaged away.
5. As the platform owner, I want `ship` refused while the Judge identity is uncalibrated, so that an unmeasured Judge cannot approve an Agent.
6. As the platform owner, I want the Judge's agreement with my golden references measured on every run, so that self-preference bias is a number I can see.
7. As the platform owner, I want a fifth of Judge calls shadow-scored on a second provider, so that a drifting Judge flips a run to warnings instead of shipping quietly.
8. As the platform owner, I want the Attacker to try every vector three times independently with full coverage required, so that one lucky refusal never reads as robustness.
9. As the platform owner, I want every model call recorded with tokens, requested and served model, so that a run, a Verdict and a Customer turn each carry a measured spend.
10. As the platform owner, I want cost derived from a versioned price table in USD and ZAR with windows in CAT, so that a price change re-prices history without a migration and I read costs in my own time and currency.
11. As the platform owner, I want the platform on one DPA-backed provider with the SDK harness replaced by an owned loop, so that Tenant data has a lawful home and sessions survive ephemeral containers.
12. As the platform owner, I want the stack on Railway with a hard $20 limit and staging and production as two environments, so that a runaway bill is structurally impossible while I validate.
13. As the platform owner, I want to provision the Bantuson Agent entirely from Claude Code through MCP tools, so that the provisioning surface is proven by dogfood before a Tenant touches it.
14. As the platform owner, I want the finish-line test written as twenty Gherkin Scenarios before the run, so that acceptance is observer-independent and repeatable.
15. As the platform owner, I want the trace of the finish-line run to record what the Harness generated unprompted, so that gaps in the automatic gate become findings, not surprises.
16. As the platform owner, I want the labelling loop to run on the Agent that will actually serve, so that my two hours of labels are never spent on retired responses.
17. As a Tenant, I want my Agent evaluated nightly and red-teamed weekly only after it is deployed, so that I am never billed for measuring an Agent nobody can talk to.
18. As a Tenant, I want the widget to say where my Customers' messages are processed, so that my own privacy obligations are dischargeable.
19. As a Tenant, I want my documents to become a grounded Agent through one upload path with visible enrichment failures, so that a silent ingestion defect cannot masquerade as success.
20. As a Customer, I want answers grounded in the Tenant's Corpus with refusals for anything outside it, so that the Agent never invents facts about the business.
21. As a Customer, I want personal data in a response deflected by the firewall identically in evals and live turns, so that the measured Agent is the Agent I talk to.
22. As a contributor, I want frozen domain types on an import rung that cannot reach the database, so that core concepts are values I can construct in any test.
23. As a contributor, I want the complexity gate to be a per-function baseline that fails on unpinned, grown and stale entries, so that the worst function shrinks with every touch.
24. As a contributor, I want tests forbidden from reading app source as text or AST, so that a green test always means behaviour survived.
25. As a contributor, I want the gates themselves pinned by a test with an observed mutation proof, so that loosening a threshold goes red somewhere.
26. As a contributor, I want the checklist to trigger the eval and the red team and wait for both before deciding, so that a Verdict never reads a stale signal.
27. As the platform owner, I want per-unit economics measured from the ledger after the first public URL, so that pricing decisions rest on observations.

## Implementation Decisions

Each decision was made on the linked map ticket; the ticket holds the evidence.

- **The Harness cut** ([#6](https://github.com/mfanafuthimhlanga/wchats/issues/6)): the observed eval path survives; the decision-eval service, the label queue, trust-tier resolvers, promotion-to-verified-QA and Neon branch isolation are deleted with their tests. The eval task owns the run's numbers; readers compute nothing. ADR 0003.
- **Ingestion and retrieval types** ([#7](https://github.com/mfanafuthimhlanga/wchats/issues/7)): frozen `Chunk` (id derived from document and ordinal; `is_table` gains a column), `ChunkMetadata` (enrichment failure visible), `IngestionJob` (the chain's seam), `RetrievedChunk`/`RetrievedContext` (JSON to the model; the repr-and-literal_eval seam goes), `ToolResult` (outcome enum `ok | denied | requires_human | error`). All in a new domain package on a new bottom rung of the import-layers contract; the domain imports nothing above it.
- **Harness types** ([#31](https://github.com/mfanafuthimhlanga/wchats/issues/31)): frozen `EvalResult` (identity, requested and served models, counts, an `invocation_status` enum, per-dataset metrics each `{value, observations, measured}`, cost; an unmeasured field is absent or `measured=False`, never a default), one Judge record per call (dimension, score, `binary_verdict` with its threshold on the row, Judge identity, ledger reference), and `Verdict` produced only by a pure `decide(eval_result, red_team_result, calibration)`. The Orchestrator's model turn writes prose from the Verdict and cannot change the outcome. ADR 0007.
- **The `ship` rule, version 1** ([#19](https://github.com/mfanafuthimhlanga/wchats/issues/19)): a Scenario passes when every measured dimension passes; golden gates absolutely, with a floor: fewer than ten authored golden pairs blocks with its own reason, so an empty contract can never pass vacuously (amended 2026-08-24, on the ticket); authoring the golden set is a mandatory pre-deployment step of Provisioning; exploratory gates on the pass-rate CI (lower bound 0.85 to ship, upper bound under 0.70 blocks, between warns; both provisional until re-derived from the labelled corpus); `ship` refused without a `calibrated` Judge identity; red team k=3 across all seven vectors with coverage complete and any critical breach blocking; at least 90% of attempted Scenarios scored. The checklist task sequences: trigger eval and red team, await both terminal, then `decide()`.
- **Calibration's code path** ([#31](https://github.com/mfanafuthimhlanga/wchats/issues/31)): the calibration harness writes a `CalibrationStatus` artifact beside its sheets; the app loads it per Judge identity; absence is `not_calibrated_yet`, which blocks.
- **Schedules arm per Agent on deploy** ([#6](https://github.com/mfanafuthimhlanga/wchats/issues/6)): nightly eval and weekly red team stay scheduled; every fan-out selects deployed Agents only (the eval beat currently selects on readiness instead, issue #32).
- **Cost and the served model** ([#22](https://github.com/mfanafuthimhlanga/wchats/issues/22)): one client factory with a response hook yields a frozen `ModelCall` per call, including through instructor and Ragas; the owned loop reports per-turn usage. A per-tenant `model_calls` table with a daily control-database rollup. Tokens are the stored fact; USD and ZAR are derived by pure functions over a versioned price table (windows declared in CAT) and a dated `usd_zar` rate. Timestamps stored UTC. Langfuse mirrors the same `ModelCall`, never the source of truth.
- **The provider and the loop** ([#34](https://github.com/mfanafuthimhlanga/wchats/issues/34)): OpenAI `gpt-5.6-luna` for the Agent turn (effort none by default), the Judges and all direct-API calls; the Agent SDK harness is replaced by an owned bounded tool loop on the OpenAI SDK with session state in the existing conversations and messages tables; a random 20% of Judge calls are shadow-scored on Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite (EU) and the paired delta rides on `EvalResult`; DeepSeek serves only until cutover. The factory takes provider and credentials as inputs, never hardcoded at a call site. ADR 0008.
- **Eval egress equals live egress** ([#16](https://github.com/mfanafuthimhlanga/wchats/issues/16)): no firewall on the eval path; the eval turn crosses the same seam as a live turn, so the firewall's deflection is what gets scored; the run record names the served provider. A one-line processing notice ships in the widget for every Agent. ADR 0006.
- **The MCP surface** ([#10](https://github.com/mfanafuthimhlanga/wchats/issues/10)): fourteen tools, each a one-to-one wrapper over an existing route, served inside the API at one stateless endpoint; the tenant API key as a static bearer header, no OAuth; trigger tools return a job id and the caller polls; the portfolio embed is replaced by the snippet the embed tool returns. ADR 0004.
- **The Corpus and the finish line** ([#11](https://github.com/mfanafuthimhlanga/wchats/issues/11), [#12](https://github.com/mfanafuthimhlanga/wchats/issues/12)): the portfolio page and three project READMEs through the real ingestion; nine Scenario categories, four of them refusals; an owner-written golden set of about ten pairs; twenty Gherkin Scenarios written before the run, driven over the public widget routes plus five by hand on the live page; all twenty pass; one trace records commit, agent id, Verdict id, job ids, screenshots, spend, and what the Harness generated unprompted.
- **The host** ([#14](https://github.com/mfanafuthimhlanga/wchats/issues/14)): Railway, four services (api, worker, beat, managed Redis), one Dockerfile built on push with the pipeline extra only in the worker image, a $20 hard limit, staging and production as two environments; the Terraform, systemd and Caddy trees are deleted; object storage is R2 or B2 through the existing endpoint seam. ADR 0005.
- **The gates** ([#8](https://github.com/mfanafuthimhlanga/wchats/issues/8)): lizard at CCN 15 and 60 lines with a per-function baseline that fails on unpinned, grown and stale entries, never-add; one rule bans tests reading app source as text or AST with its own shrinking baseline; both run in the static tier; one test pins the gate, with an observed mutation proof.
- **Build inputs carried from the map**: owner credentials (Railway, R2 or B2, Clerk production, platform key, Actions cap, Voyage and OpenAI keys), the k=5 re-capture of 100 turns run after the owned loop lands and before labelling, the owner's 30-row double-blind labelling, the owner-authored golden sets registered per Agent with human provenance (a file-or-MCP path suffices for the two finish-line Agents; the Tenant-facing authoring screen is out of scope), and the per-unit economics measurement after the first public URL.
- **Breakage issues** #23 to #30, #32, #35 and #36 are absorbed where their subject is rebuilt; each closes with the change that fixes it, citing its trace line.

## Testing Decisions

A good test drives a seam with concrete inputs and asserts on observable outputs; it never reads app source, never asserts a mock was merely called when a value can be asserted, and a guard is proven by mutation: break it, observe red, restore, observe green, record the output.

- `decide()` is tested as a pure function, table-driven across the rule's edges (golden failure, CI straddling a bound, uncalibrated Judge, incomplete coverage, critical breach).
- The client factory is tested with a fake transport; assertions are on `ModelCall` ledger rows and on derived USD and ZAR from pinned price and rate tables.
- `run_agent_turn` is tested with a fake client injected at the factory; live and eval callers cross the same seam, so firewall parity is one test, not two suites.
- `run_eval_suite` is tested against a fake agent seam; the single assertion target is the frozen `EvalResult`.
- Ingestion tasks are tested at their `IngestionJob` interface; `Chunk` construction is pure and property-testable.
- Routes, including the MCP endpoint's fourteen wrappers, use the existing route-test pattern.
- Prior art: the calibration harness's tests (behavioural, falsifiable, the best in the repo) are the standard; the transactional tool tests' concrete-outcome style is kept and their source-string assertions are deleted with the ban.

## Out of Scope

The Mellow region's specifics (the Actor gate's calibration, the transactional Scenario set, the storefront embed, write-capable evals and their isolation), console polish, the A2A runtime surface, Paystack, BYO Agent providers (anchored in the map's fog; the factory's shape already permits it), and local AWS emulation.

## Further Notes

The map ([#4](https://github.com/mfanafuthimhlanga/wchats/issues/4)) is the index of record; each decision's evidence lives on its ticket. ADRs 0003 to 0008 are written as part of this build, one commit each, before the code they justify. The definition of production readiness is unchanged: two Agents live on their deployed Vercel URLs, and this spec carries the first half plus every shared foundation the second half reuses.

items.title: Bound term windows by retention instead of a compiled 90/365 cap (allow longer terms where data exists)
items.body:
### What

Every term window is validated against `MaxWindowDays()`, a compiled per-plugin constant: **90** for container, namespace, node, vm, gpu and hcp, **365** for pvc. Nothing in that path consults retention — not ROS's own digest retention, not Cost Management's, not the per-tenant setting added recently. The result is that a deployment keeping six months of digests cannot answer a 120-day question, and a PVC term can claim a year against six months of data.

This issue asks for the bound to follow **what is actually retained**, with the current 90/365 numbers kept as guidance rather than a hard rejection.

### Why it matters

Retention in play today, and whether the window cap sees it:

| Setting | Default | Governs | Consulted by the cap? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ROS_RETENTION_MONTHS` | 6 | ROS digest tables — the data a window actually reads (`internal/engine/retention.go`, per-plugin `SweepRetention`) | **no** |
| `ROS_HISTORY_RETENTION_DAYS` | 90 | history and quality tables | **no** |
| `RETAIN_NUM_MONTHS` (koku) | 4 in `settings.py`; 3 as the ClowdApp parameter | koku line items | **no** |
| `data_retention_months` (COST-573, per tenant) | 3, range 3–120 | `GET/PUT /api/cost-management/v1/account-settings/data-retention/` | **no** |
| `MaxWindowDays()` | 90, PVC 365 | the validation bound itself | it **is** the cap |

Two failure directions, both live:

- **90 withholds data.** Digest retention defaults to 6 months and partition drops are month-granular, so ~180–213 days exist while the cap stops at 90. Up to half the retained history is unreachable for windows.
- **PVC's 365 exceeds it.** A 200–365-day PVC term runs against ~6 months of digests. This is *not* silent — the engine records `DataDays` from the rows actually present and `ComputeConfidence` is `dataDays / windowDays`, which drives the low-confidence notification (`librobne/types/confidence.go`). But the term still reports `window_days: 300`, and nothing rejects or annotates the term itself.

The cap also cannot track operations: lowering retention below 90 makes every configured window potentially exceed available data, and raising retention does not move the cap at all.

### Why it is 90 today

Provenance, so the number is not mistaken for a data limit: `12dbe031` (2026-05-21) *"Implement per-plugin configurable recommendation terms"* added `TermProvider`, `MaxWindowDays()`, and the `400 window_days must be between 1 and 90 for container` response. The constant was the gate that made a user-editable window safe to expose. The value came from a **freshness** argument, stated in the plugin doc comments:

- container — "beyond ~3 months rarely add signal (workload behavior typically shifts at that timescale due to releases and config changes)"
- node — "workloads … change on release cycles … cluster autoscaler behavior, both operating on timescales under 3 months"
- gpu — "model/framework updates on a similar cadence"
- pvc 365 — "storage growth patterns are slow-moving and seasonal … a full year … can reveal quarterly or annual cycles"

Availability was never in scope. That is the defect: **availability and relevance are different ceilings, and only relevance is represented.**

### Proposed direction

1. **`available_days` — hard bound.** Derived from the digest partitions actually present, not from configuration: a retention change, a restore, or a partially backfilled tenant makes the config and the data disagree. Reject `window_days > available_days` with an error that names retention ("your deployment retains 182 days of digests") instead of a bare range.
2. **`recommended_days` — guidance.** Today's 90/365, exposed in `GET /settings/terms` and `GET /settings/capabilities`, plus the existing quality/confidence signal when exceeded. No 400: a tenant may have a reason, and the answer already carries how much data it actually used.
3. **One bound, everywhere.** The env path (`internal/engine/term_config.go:291`), the terms API (`internal/api/handlers_terms.go:149`), the VM settings API (`handlers_vm_settings.go:289`) and `robne` (`cmd/robne/terms.go:82`) must enforce the same number and fail the same way — see #792 and #793 for the places they already disagree.
4. **Contract surfaces updated in the same change.** `openapi.json` says "Maximum varies by plugin: 90 for container/namespace/node/gpu, 365 for pvc" on both request and response schemas; `docs-site/index.md` says "custom 1–90 day windows per term".

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `window_days` is accepted up to `available_days` for all term-bearing plugins, with `available_days` derived from partitions present at request time.
- [ ] A window above `available_days` fails with an error naming retention and the value it implies, not a bare `1-90`.
- [ ] 90/365 survives as `recommended_days` in `GET /settings/terms` and `GET /settings/capabilities`, and exceeding it produces the quality/confidence signal rather than a 400.
- [ ] The env path, the terms API, the VM settings API and `robne` enforce an identical bound with identical failure behaviour.
- [ ] `openapi.json` and `docs-site/index.md` describe the new rule; the plugin doc comments stop presenting 90 as a data limit.
- [ ] Tests: accepted at `available_days`, rejected at `available_days + 1`, and a retention-reduction case; the existing 90-bound tests updated to the new semantics.
- [ ] One demonstrated run — server or `robne` — of a term longer than 90 days on a deployment retaining six months, with the resulting `DataDays` and confidence shown.

### Non-goals

- Changing the default windows (1/7/15, PVC 7/30/90).
- Reading Cost Management's database directly. ROS consumes koku over HTTP (`effective_rates` today); a per-tenant retention value would arrive the same way.
- Changing koku/masu retention behaviour, including the refusal to process payloads outside retention (COST-6570).

### Open questions

1. **Which retention is the ceiling — ROS digests or `min(ROS, koku)`?** Digests outlive koku line items (they are written at ingest and swept by `ROS_RETENTION_MONTHS`), so ROS retention is the honest bound for a window; koku's bounds what may ever be *ingested*. If they diverge, the window bound should follow ROS.
2. **Granularity.** Partitions drop by month, so a 6-month setting yields 180–213 days. Report exact days, or months with the range made explicit?
3. **Retention lowered below a configured window.** Clamp stored terms at read time, invalidate them, or fail the read? Clamping silently rewrites a tenant's intent; failing breaks ingestion cycles.
4. **Retention raised.** Partitions only fill as data arrives, so `available_days` grows slowly. Is there a floor (the plugin's default long window) to avoid rejecting configurations that were valid yesterday?

### Close criteria

A decision on the four questions recorded here, then either the acceptance list implemented or split into implementation issues (env path → #792, CLI parity → #793).

---

Related: #792 (env path locks the term while ignoring the value), #793 (`robne` cannot configure HCP terms). Both are instances of "the bound exists in four places and they disagree".

Enable independent developers to register, create their own projects, and receive managed email notifications without database or server administration.

## Exit criteria / definition of done
- Verified signup → project → token → agent hookup → cloud email works end-to-end with tenant isolation; recruit ~20–30 real developers.
- All linked issues accepted with functional tests/documentation, unless explicitly moved by roadmap decision.
- Demonstrate end-to-end behavior and review security/operational impact.

Private-beta invitations; activate the landing-to-signup funnel; measure time to first notification and repeat sending.

## Sequencing / critical path
The tenant/resource model and account identities precede projects/tokens and authenticated dashboards. Deliverability precedes invitation volume. Abuse protections precede open signup.
