items.body:
> **Programme reconciliation (18 October 2026):** Delivery is coordinated by #1220. AmbulanceConnect is the citizen web/iOS/Android experience; EmergencyConnect owns dispatch and operations. Current stack: Expo/React Native, Zitadel, Valkey, Go and Postgres/OpenFGA. Any older recommendation below is subordinate to the programme's explicit safety, capacity-boundary and privacy decisions. Request receipt is not dispatch confirmation. Clinical protocol and India legal review plus #1222 operational launch gates are mandatory before live booking. This issue remains open until its own acceptance criteria are proved.

## Situation

Once #121 produces a triaged emergency case, nothing happens. There is no mechanism to choose a
vehicle, commit it to the case, route it, know where it is, or tell anyone when it will arrive. The
dispatcher's only tool would be a phone and personal knowledge of where the drivers are — which is
how most Indian hospital ambulance services are run today, and why response times are unmeasurable
and unmanageable.

The people affected are immediate. The dispatcher cannot see which of six vehicles is nearest, which
is already committed, and which is nominally free but actually stuck on a hospital ramp waiting for a
trolley. The ambulance crew receive a job by phone call, with an address repeated verbally, and no
digital record of when they were assigned or when they arrived. The receiving ED gets no warning — a
critical patient arrives with no resuscitation bay prepared, which is the single highest-value piece
of information EmergencyConnect can generate and today it is a WhatsApp message if it happens at all.
The family waiting with the patient are told "it's coming" with no ETA.

Response interval is the metric the whole product is judged on, and it cannot be improved without
being measured against a committed vehicle. Assignment must also be safe under contention: two
dispatchers on two consoles must never commit the same vehicle to two cases, and a vehicle that has
lost GPS signal in an underpass must not be treated as having disappeared.

There is a real integration surface here too. Ambulance GPS is listed as a platform integration:
most fleets already carry a third-party AIS-140 telematics unit, and the platform must consume those
feeds rather than assume every vehicle's position comes from the crew's phone.

---

## Task

### User or System Story

**As an** emergency dispatcher
**I want** to see every vehicle's live position and status, assign the most appropriate one to a
triaged case with a guaranteed-exclusive commitment, and track it through to hospital handover with
a continuously-updated ETA
**So that** the nearest capable vehicle is committed within seconds, the receiving department is
pre-alerted, and every interval in the response is measured.

### Scope

**In scope**

* **Live vehicle position ingestion** from two sources — the crew app (#124) and third-party
  telematics/GPS units — normalised into one position stream with source and accuracy recorded.
* **Dispatch recommendation**: ranking available vehicles for a case by travel time, capability
  match (BLS/ALS/neonatal), crew skill and current commitment, presented to the dispatcher as an
  ordered list.
* **Exclusive assignment** with a database-level guarantee that one vehicle holds at most one active
  dispatch, and an accept/timeout/reassign cycle if the crew does not acknowledge.
* **Dispatch lifecycle orchestration**: assigned → acknowledged → en route to scene → on scene →
  transporting → at destination → handover complete → clear, each transition timestamped and
  attributable to crew, dispatcher or system.
* **Continuous ETA** to scene and to destination, recomputed from live position and published as
  events for the requester app, the dispatcher board and the receiving facility.
* **Receiving-facility pre-alert**: a structured notification to the destination ED (#119) on
  transport commencement, carrying case number, priority, patient condition summary and ETA, with an
  acknowledgement from the ED that is visible to the crew.
* **Dispatcher map console** in Next.js 16 showing open cases, vehicle positions, status and
  assignment, with a geofenced arrival check that prompts (never silently sets) an on-scene
  transition.
* **Position history retention** per dispatch for incident review, with a defined retention period.
* **Destination reassignment** mid-transport when the intended facility cannot receive the patient.

**Out of scope**

* The crew mobile app itself — job acceptance UI, offline clinical recording and handover capture
  are owned by #124; this issue defines the contract it speaks.
* Vehicle roadworthiness, equipment readiness, oxygen levels and duty rostering — owned by #126;
  this issue consumes the availability state #126 publishes.
* Locating the patient precisely at the scene — owned by #125.
* The ED track board, triage and clinical record on arrival — owned by #119; this issue delivers
  the pre-alert into it.
* Turn-by-turn navigation rendering — the crew app hands off to the device's installed navigation
  application; the platform does not build a routing engine.

---

## Recommended Solution

A `dispatch` package in the EmergencyConnect Go service, with a **Temporal** workflow per dispatch,
PostGIS for spatial queries, Valkey for the live position index, and NATS JetStream for the event
fabric.

**Why Temporal.** A dispatch is a multi-hour, multi-actor orchestration with mandatory timers
(acknowledgement timeout, on-scene overdue alert, handover overdue alert), external signals from the
crew app, and compensating actions on reassignment. Modelling it as status columns plus a cron
sweeper is how vehicles end up silently stuck in `assigned` at 4 a.m. The workflow ID is the dispatch
ID, which also gives idempotent signal delivery from a flaky crew device for free.

**Why Valkey for positions and PostgreSQL for history.** A fleet emitting a fix every five seconds
produces write volume that has no business touching the clinical OLTP database, and the dispatcher
board only ever needs the latest fix per vehicle plus a radius query. Valkey `GEOADD`/`GEOSEARCH`
serves both in sub-millisecond time. Positions are batch-flushed to a PostgreSQL partitioned history
table for incident review only.

```sql
dispatch (
  id uuid pk, tenant_id uuid not null, emergency_case_id uuid not null,
  vehicle_id uuid not null, crew_ids uuid[] not null,
  origin_facility_id uuid, destination_facility_id uuid null,
  assigned_at timestamptz not null, acknowledged_at timestamptz,
  en_route_at timestamptz, on_scene_at timestamptz,
  transport_started_at timestamptz, at_destination_at timestamptz,
  handover_completed_at timestamptz, cleared_at timestamptz,
  cancel_reason text null, workflow_id text not null unique,
  status text not null
);
-- one live dispatch per vehicle, enforced by the database
create unique index dispatch_one_active_per_vehicle
  on dispatch (tenant_id, vehicle_id)
  where status in ('assigned','acknowledged','en_route','on_scene','transporting','at_destination');

vehicle_position_history (
  tenant_id uuid, vehicle_id uuid, dispatch_id uuid null,
  location geography(Point,4326) not null, speed_kmh numeric,
  heading numeric, accuracy_m numeric,
  source text not null,                 -- crew_app | telematics
  recorded_at timestamptz not null
) partition by range (recorded_at);

facility_prealert (
  id uuid pk, tenant_id uuid, dispatch_id uuid not null,
  destination_facility_id uuid not null,
  priority text not null, condition_summary text, eta_at timestamptz,
  sent_at timestamptz not null,
  acknowledged_at timestamptz null, acknowledged_by uuid null
)
```

The partial unique index is the core safety control. Two dispatchers racing on the same vehicle
resolve at the database, not in application logic that a retry can defeat.

**API surface**

```
GET  /api/v1/emergency/dispatch/recommendations?case_id=
POST /api/v1/emergency/dispatch                        -- assign; Idempotency-Key required
POST /api/v1/emergency/dispatch/{id}/acknowledge       -- crew signal
POST /api/v1/emergency/dispatch/{id}/status            -- en_route | on_scene | transporting | at_destination | clear
POST /api/v1/emergency/dispatch/{id}/destination       -- reassign receiving facility
POST /api/v1/emergency/dispatch/{id}/cancel            -- reason required
POST /api/v1/emergency/vehicles/{id}/positions         -- batched fixes, crew app or telematics gateway
GET  /api/v1/emergency/vehicles/live?bbox=             -- dispatcher map
GET  /api/v1/emergency/dispatch/{id}/eta
POST /api/v1/emergency/prealerts/{id}/acknowledge      -- receiving ED
```

**Events published.** `AmbulanceDispatched`, `AmbulanceAcknowledged`, `AmbulanceOnScene`,
`AmbulanceTransportStarted`, `AmbulanceEtaUpdated`, `AmbulancePreAlertRaised`,
`AmbulanceArrivedAtFacility`, `AmbulanceDispatchCancelled`, `VehicleUnreachable`. Consumed:
`EmergencyCaseTriaged` (#121) to open the recommendation flow, `VehicleAvailabilityChanged` (#126),
and crew status signals from #124. `AmbulanceEtaUpdated` is rate-limited to one event per dispatch
per 30 seconds — a raw ETA recomputation on every GPS fix would flood the bus and the requester's
push channel to no benefit.

**ETA.** Computed by a routing provider behind an interface, with a straight-line-plus-factor
fallback when the provider is unavailable or the vehicle is outside covered geography. The ETA
carries a `confidence` field and the UI never presents a low-confidence ETA as a precise minute
count — an ETA the family relies on and that is wrong by fifteen minutes is worse than a range.

**GPS loss.** Absence of position is treated as a first-class state, not as absence of the vehicle.
After the configured gap the vehicle renders as "last seen HH:MM at <location>" and a
`VehicleUnreachable` event alerts the dispatcher to voice-contact the crew. A vehicle in a tunnel
must never be dropped from the map or auto-marked unavailable.

**Authorisation (OpenFGA).**

```
type dispatch
  relations
    define facility: [facility]
    define assigned_crew: [user]
    define dispatcher: dispatcher from facility
    define receiving_facility: [facility]
    define can_view: assigned_crew or dispatcher or supervisor from facility
    define can_assign: dispatcher
    define can_update_status: assigned_crew or dispatcher
    define can_view_prealert: clinical_staff from receiving_facility
```

The receiving facility gains access to the case through the pre-alert relation and only from the
moment the pre-alert is raised — a hospital does not get to browse another facility's inbound
patients.

**Sequencing.** Depends on #121 (case record) and #126 (vehicle master and availability). #124
consumes this contract; #119 consumes the pre-alert. #125 improves scene location accuracy but is
not blocking.

**Risks.** (1) Double assignment under dispatcher contention — resolved by the partial unique index
plus an idempotency key on assign. (2) Position spoofing or a misconfigured telematics unit — fixes
are validated against plausible speed and accuracy bounds, rejected fixes are logged with the source,
and telematics gateways authenticate per device. (3) Pre-alert never read by the ED — the pre-alert
requires an explicit acknowledgement, is escalated to the ED charge nurse's alert queue if
unacknowledged within the configured window, and the unacknowledged state is visible to the crew so
they can telephone.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

### Primary Scenario

**Given** a P1 emergency case triaged at a facility with four available vehicles, the nearest ALS
unit being 2.4 km away
**When** the dispatcher opens recommendations and assigns that vehicle
**Then** a dispatch is created with the vehicle exclusively committed, a Temporal workflow started,
the crew notified and acknowledging within the timeout, `AmbulanceDispatched` published once, an ETA
to scene published within 5 seconds, and on transport commencement a structured pre-alert delivered
to the destination ED which appears on its track board (#119) and is acknowledged by the charge nurse.

### Failure or Validation Scenario

**Given** two dispatchers on two consoles simultaneously assign the same vehicle to two different
open cases
**When** both assignment requests reach the server
**Then** exactly one dispatch is created; the losing request receives a conflict response naming the
case the vehicle is now committed to and is presented with refreshed recommendations; no second
Temporal workflow is started; and no `AmbulanceDispatched` event is published for the losing request.

### Edge Cases

* The crew does not acknowledge within the timeout — the workflow alerts the dispatcher and offers
  reassignment; the unacknowledged assignment stays on the case timeline rather than being erased.
* The vehicle loses GPS for eleven minutes in an underpass — it renders as last-known with a
  timestamp, `VehicleUnreachable` fires, and it is neither removed from the map nor marked available.
* The destination ED is on divert mid-transport — destination reassignment updates the pre-alert,
  cancels the original facility's inbound entry, and raises a new pre-alert with a recomputed ETA.
* The routing provider is unavailable — a fallback ETA is published with `confidence = low` and the
  console renders a range rather than a precise minute.
* A telematics unit reports a fix implying 260 km/h — rejected as implausible, logged with the
  device identifier, and the previous fix retained.
* A dispatch is cancelled after the crew is on scene because the patient refuses transport — a
  reason is mandatory, the case timeline retains all intervals, and the vehicle returns to available
  only after the crew signals clear.
* A dispatcher at Facility A requests live positions and receives a vehicle belonging to another
  tenant — must be impossible; verified adversarially.
* Position batches arrive out of order from a device that buffered while offline — history is
  ordered by `recorded_at`, and the live index only advances on a newer fix.

---
## Engineering Guardrails

Complete the applicable items before the story is closed.

### Code Quality

* [ ] The change is limited to the agreed scope.
* [ ] Existing behaviour remains backward-compatible unless explicitly approved.
* [ ] Code follows the team’s agreed standards and architecture.
* [ ] No temporary code, debug output or unnecessary complexity remains.
* [ ] Error handling is explicit and does not silently ignore failures.

### Test-Driven Development

* [ ] Acceptance criteria were converted into test scenarios.
* [ ] New or changed business logic was developed using Red–Green–Refactor where practical.
* [ ] Bug fixes include a regression test that fails before the fix and passes afterwards.
* [ ] Tests validate behaviour rather than private implementation details.

### Automated Testing

* [ ] Unit tests cover new and changed logic.
* [ ] Positive, negative and important boundary scenarios are covered.
* [ ] Integration or contract tests are updated where service boundaries change.
* [ ] Critical user journeys are covered by Playwright or an equivalent E2E framework.
* [ ] Existing tests pass.
* [ ] No new flaky or skipped tests are introduced without justification.

### Security and Access

* [ ] Authentication and authorisation are enforced at the appropriate layer.
* [ ] Users and services can access only the data and actions they require.
* [ ] Input is validated and sensitive information is not exposed in logs or errors.
* [ ] Secrets and credentials are not stored in source code.
* [ ] Security and dependency scans pass.
* [ ] Tenant, account or customer isolation is tested where applicable.

### Accessibility and User Journey

* [ ] The primary user journey works from start to completion.
* [ ] Loading, empty, success and error states are handled.
* [ ] Keyboard navigation and focus behaviour work correctly.
* [ ] Controls have clear labels and accessible names.
* [ ] The change meets the team’s agreed WCAG accessibility level.
* [ ] The experience works across supported devices and browsers.

### Performance and Reliability

* [ ] The change does not introduce unnecessary API calls, database queries or processing.
* [ ] Timeouts, retries and failure behaviour are defined where applicable.
* [ ] Duplicate requests do not create inconsistent data.
* [ ] Performance-sensitive changes are tested against an agreed threshold.
* [ ] Partial failures do not leave the system in an invalid state.

### Observability

* [ ] Important failures are logged with useful diagnostic context.
* [ ] Logs do not contain sensitive information.
* [ ] Metrics or traces are added where the change affects a critical workflow.
* [ ] The team can determine whether the feature is working correctly after deployment.

### Documentation

* [ ] Relevant README, API or technical documentation is updated.
* [ ] Configuration or environment changes are documented.
* [ ] Deployment, migration or rollback steps are documented where required.
* [ ] Known limitations are recorded.

---
## Result

* **Expected user or system outcome:** a dispatcher commits the most appropriate vehicle in seconds
  from a ranked list, the whole response is tracked live with a continuously-updated ETA, and the
  receiving department is warned and has acknowledged before the patient arrives.
* **Expected business or operational outcome:** response intervals become measurable and therefore
  manageable; resuscitation bays are prepared in advance rather than on arrival; the fleet's real
  utilisation becomes visible for the first time.
* **Success metric or validation method:** p95 case-triaged-to-vehicle-assigned under 60 seconds;
  p95 dispatcher map position freshness under 10 seconds for vehicles with signal; ETA within ±20%
  of actual for 80% of dispatches with a routing provider available; 95% of transports generating a
  pre-alert acknowledged by the receiving facility before arrival; zero double-assignments across a
  90-day window; `POST /positions` sustaining 200 vehicles at a 5-second cadence with p95 under
  100ms.
* **Monitoring period:** 90 days on the pilot fleet, tracking assignment latency, acknowledgement
  timeout rate, GPS gap frequency and duration by vehicle, ETA error distribution, pre-alert
  acknowledgement latency, and rejected-fix volume by telematics device.

---
## Pull Request Evidence

The pull request should include:

* [ ] Link to this story.
* [ ] Summary of the change.
* [ ] Test evidence.
* [ ] Screenshots or recordings for UI changes.
* [ ] Security, accessibility or performance evidence where relevant.
* [ ] Deployment and rollback notes for higher-risk changes.
* [ ] Known risks or follow-up work.

---

## Definition of Done

The story is complete when:

* [ ] All acceptance criteria pass.
* [ ] Required tests pass locally and in CI.
* [ ] No critical or high-severity security or quality issues remain.
* [ ] The critical user or system journey has been validated.
* [ ] Documentation is updated.
* [ ] Code review is complete.
* [ ] The change has been deployed or is ready for deployment through the standard pipeline.
* [ ] Post-deployment validation is defined or completed.
* [ ] Any exception is documented with an owner and reason.

---
## Exceptions

None — all guardrails apply. The story ships a dispatcher map console alongside high-throughput
server-side ingestion and orchestration, so accessibility of the console, tenant and facility
isolation, sustained-load performance, partial-failure behaviour and observability obligations are
all in force. Position history is treated as personal data under retention policy, not as
throwaway telemetry.

items.body:
### Where to start (status 2026-10-02)

**Storage layer.** Segment store: done (#1661 on main). Qdrant and Milvus: #1733 -> #1734 -> #1735 -> #1736 in review (SQL collection registry, an incarnation per collection life, fenced handles, claimed purge); they close #1524, #1525 and #1563 on merge. SQLite stores: #1536 stays with the SQLite store fixes (#1460 to #1675), and they are HOST or PROCESS scope by declaration (#1757).

**Above the stores**, in priority order. Each is a tracking issue with a one-glance table (what is wrong, best fix, order) and a PR split, and each child issue shows its tracker at the top.

1. #1755 Session lifecycle: the `sessions` row as registry plus durable jobs. Tracks #1543, #1571, #1575, #1576, #1577, #1600, #1655, #1728, #1749.
2. #1756 Background work: one claimable-job primitive for provision, delete, ingestion and purge. Tracks #1745, #1749, #1699, #1738, #1722.
3. #1757 Concurrency scope per component, so declarative memory and short-term memory stay available for single-replica deployments without a routing layer. Tracks #1748, #1753, #1745.
3. #1758 Replica-safe defaults in one change. Tracks #1746, #1747, #1730, #1750, #1751, #1752, #1754.

Design reference: #1579 (deferred as a whole; its vocabulary and target shapes are what the tracking issues cite).

**Labels.** `horizontal scaling`: wrong or unsafe with more than one server process on the same backends. `concurrency`: wrong under concurrent requests or processes regardless of replica count (races, lost updates, unarbitrated read-then-write). `recovery`: a failure or crash leaves durable state nothing repairs (partial writes, lost jobs, no retry or terminal state). An issue carries every label that applies.

### Why this issue exists

The issues linked below were filed one at a time, most of them as bugs. Read individually they look like an accumulation of unrelated defects in the storage layer. Read together they are one change of model: the codebase was built for **sharded** horizontal scaling (each logical collection or partition owned by exactly one process, and separated from other tenants by a physical structure of its own), and the requirement is now **non-sharded** scaling (any process serves any tenant, and tenants are rows or values inside structures they share). This issue states that change once, records why the previous model was there, classifies each linked issue against it, and tracks what remains.

### The model the codebase was built on, and why

Two decisions, both explicit and documented when they were made.

**1. Ownership by process sharding.** #1201 (merged 2026-04-02) set the `VectorStore` contract that is still in `common/vector_store/vector_store.py` today:

> A given logical collection identified by a (namespace, name) pair must be managed by at most one process at a time. The consumer is responsible for sharding names across processes.

Its description states the guarantees plainly: "safe concurrent usage on a single process" and "safe concurrent sharded usage (one node per logical collection) on multiple processes". With ownership fixed per process, lifecycle operations (create, open-or-create, delete) could be read-check-write sequences guarded by per-process `asyncio` locks, and backends without transactions or unique constraints (Qdrant, Milvus) could keep their catalog of logical collections inside the backend itself. The multi-process guarantee was correct under its contract and was never broken: strict sharding always worked. The restriction itself is what became the limitation (#1524, #1525).

**2. Per-tenant physical structures.** #1205 (merged 2026-05-08) scoped the event memory "by partition key: should allow sharding and horizontal scaling", and on PostgreSQL gave every segment-store partition its own pair of child tables under LIST-partitioned parents, created and dropped by per-tenant DDL. #1292 (merged 2026-05-02) gave every SQLite vector collection its own tables, for a stated reason: "Partition keys are avoided in favor of per-collection tables, since sqlite-vec ANN indexes may not support them." Qdrant's `is_distributed` flag gives every logical collection its own shard key. The payoff was real: deleting a tenant was one `DROP` rather than a row-scanning `DELETE`, one tenant's rows never interleaved with another's in a heap or index, and backend index limitations were sidestepped. Note that #1201 already rejected one native collection per tenant ("most vector databases recommend against one collection per tenant, and empirical tests show that many collections induces significant overhead"); the per-tenant structure was the shard key or child table beneath a shared native collection, not the collection itself.

Both decisions fit the deployments they served: a single server process, embedded SQLite as a first-class backend, an opt-in pre-GA event backend, and tenant counts at which per-tenant DDL was cheap. Nothing below should be read as those decisions having been mistakes at the time.

### What changed

Two requirements the sharded model does not meet:

- **Multiple server processes must serve the same tenants.** Any replica handles any session; routing by session affinity is not a requirement a hosted deployment can carry. This is the horizontal-scalability problem as restated in #1524 and #1525: multiple processes working the *same* collections and partitions, not more processes each owning their own.
- **Tenant counts of tens of thousands to millions**, with individual tenants ranging from tens of thousands to tens of millions of rows (`design/segment_store_shared_tables.md` in #1545).

### Why the sharded model fails them

Measured, in the linked issues and in the design doc:

| Cost of the model | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Per-tenant DDL on shared PostgreSQL parents | #1544's second half, and the design doc in #1545: create and delete DDL deadlocked with writers and with each other, on upstream and on every intermediate fix, in two cycle shapes; the class has nowhere to live once there is no lifecycle DDL. (#1544's first half, a `CASCADE` that removed the shared foreign key, is a plain bug; see the classification below.) |
| Per-tenant partitions and prepared statements | #1546: after five executions PostgreSQL switches to a generic plan that locks every child partition per read: 9 locks per read with a custom plan, 319 with the generic plan at 316 partitions, HTTP 500 `out of shared memory` at 128-way concurrency. Each per-tenant table also costs about 5 catalog relations and disk files, which does not survive the required tenant counts. |
| Per-tenant shard keys on Qdrant | #1564: 450 ms per tenant admission, 45 s for 100 tenants against 0.3 s with payload partitioning, 505 segments against 5, and cluster mode required. |
| Per-process ownership | #1524, #1525: the moment two processes manage the same name, lock-guarded read-check-write lifecycle has no arbiter. #1566 (folded into #1564): the in-process lock table was a leftover of that serialisation. |

The comparison that settled the segment store (raw asyncpg, 40 tenants x 2000 row-pairs, pgvector:pg16, 2 CPUs; full table in the design doc):

| layout | ingest | seed read | tenant create | catalog cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `PARTITION OF` children | 8.7-9.2k pairs/s | 0.43-0.46 ms | ~12 ms DDL | ~5 relations/tenant |
| shared tables | 15k pairs/s | 0.21 ms | 0.006 ms | none |

Per-tenant tables won only small-tenant removal latency (9 ms drop against 58 ms row delete), which does not justify their catalog cost at the required tenant counts. This is the industry's pool model: O(1) logical deletion via a registry plus asynchronous batched reclamation; O(1) physical drops exist only in per-tenant-resource (silo) architectures, which the tenant-count requirement excludes.

### The target model

The layer above the stores that ties these together (a tenant record with a step table and a reconciler, UUID-only store keys minted per tenant lifetime, a single tenant handle, and prompt purge as best-effort) is proposed in `design/tenant_lifecycle.md` under #1579, with the resource-level contracts the stores expose to it. The bullets below are the store-level targets that proposal builds on.

- **A tenant is a row, not a relation.** One registry row per live tenant, carrying a random `incarnation` minted at creation; data rows and records are keyed by the incarnation. Creating a tenant is an insert.
- **One physical structure per backend, shared by every tenant**: shared tables on SQL; payload-partitioned native collections on vector backends, with native collections shared by config as #1201 already did.
- **Lifecycle arbitrated by the database, so any process may perform it**: unique constraints decide create races, row locks serialise delete against in-flight writers, `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` lets concurrent purgers split a backlog.
- **Deletion is O(1) logical** (registry delete plus a purge-queue entry in one transaction); **physical reclamation is asynchronous**, bounded per call, safe to run from any process, and driven by a background purger.
- **Stale handles cannot reach a successor.** A handle carries the incarnation it was opened on. Where the backend can pin a registry row (the segment store, with `FOR SHARE`), a stale handle raises; where it cannot (the vector backends), a stale handle's writes land in a dead incarnation that nothing reads and reclamation removes, with lease validation against the registry as the remaining option (#1563, #1564). Either way a tenant recreated under the same key is unreachable from the old handle, on any process, without coordination.
- **The contract says what each store supports.** The blanket "at most one process" sentence goes; a store whose metadata moves to a cross-process authority says so, and a deployment can introspect what it may do instead of relying on out-of-band knowledge (#1524, #1525).
- **Native containers are provisioned, not created on the request path.** Creating a logical collection is one registry insert arbitrated by a primary key; the container it lands in already exists, shaped once per deployment (one schema per container, because a shared container cannot carry per-tenant schemas) and ensured by the same provisioning step that owns SQL schema (#1572, #1573, #1570).
- **Per-tenant physical isolation stays available as a tier** for an oversized tenant (Qdrant's tiered multitenancy, per #1564), never as the default.

### Status by component

Each row names the issues that carry the work; fixes and their state are tracked on those issues, not here.

| Component | Sharded model | Target | Issues |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Segment store, PostgreSQL | LIST-partitioned parents, per-tenant child tables and DDL | shared tables keyed by incarnation; registry and purge queue; writers pin the registry row | #1544, #1546, #1549 |
| Segment store, SQLite | shared tables keyed by partition key (never sharded), no fencing | same architecture on every dialect | #1549 |
| Vector store lifecycle, all backends | per-backend ad-hoc catalogs, per-process locks; contract forbids multi-process management | collection metadata arbitrated by a cross-process authority, so any process can create, open and delete; the contract states what each store supports | #1524, #1525 |
| Vector store create path and interface | native container created inside `create_collection` (a dual write across registry and backend, safe only because names are content-addressed); per-collection `VectorStoreCollectionConfig` promising per-tenant schemas | containers provisioned before serving; `create_collection` is a registry insert; collection shape configured per deployment | #1572, #1573 |
| Qdrant | `is_distributed` shard key per logical collection; native name re-derived from `sha256(config)` on every open; in-process lock table | payload partitioning; native name pinned at creation; lifecycle arbitrated by the cross-process authority; reclamation of dead partition keys | #1564, #1565, #1563, #1562 (#1566 folded into #1564) |
| SQLite vector stores | per-collection tables; stale handles reach the successor | incarnation-scoped native resources (per-collection tables stay; the store's stated reason is that sqlite-vec's index may not support a partition key) | #1536 |
| Milvus | per-record `partition_key` field filtered on queries (already value-based); catalog in a dummy-vector `__registry` collection | catalog moved to the cross-process authority | #1524, #1535 |
| Session data manager | read-then-write on session rows, safe only with one process per session | database-arbitrated create and update | #1543 |
| Schema provisioning | every process runs `create_all` at boot; no migration path for a layout change | one provisioning owner; migrations carry layout changes such as the segment store's | #1570 |
| Above the stores | process-local handle caches; no domain-error-to-status mapping | evict and re-resolve on a stale handle; explicit API status | #1571 |

Found along the way, not sharding-related, but blocking correctness on SQLite: #1568 (per-connection state registered per store on caller-supplied engines) and #1542 (engines built without WAL, busy timeout, or explicit write transactions). Contract issues that matter more once native collections are shared across tenants: #1534 (unbounded property-key cardinality, undeclared-property mandate) and #1535 (`indexed_properties_schema` is part of collection identity); #1573 narrows that to whether per-collection configuration belongs in the interface at all.

### How to read the linked issues

- **Plain defects, unrelated to the model**: #1544's first half (a `CASCADE` that removes a shared constraint), #1562 (config serialisation repoints data), #1568 (per-connection SQLite state registered late).
- **Handle bugs the sharded model could have fixed locally**: #1536, #1549, #1563. Each reproduces inside one process: an in-flight request holds a handle while that same process deletes and recreates the collection, and the handle reaches the successor. Real under any model, but not a failure of sharding: the owning process performs the delete and could invalidate every handle it issued at that moment, in memory. The target model removes that option, since the deleter may be another process, so invalidation moves into the data as the incarnation.
- **Costs of the sharded model that only surface at scale**: #1546, #1564, #1544's second half (lifecycle DDL deadlocking against shared parents), #1566 (in-process lifecycle serialisation), and the catalog cost per tenant. Not coding errors; the model's own behaviour under tenant counts and process counts it was not designed for.
- **Capability gaps the sharded model never had to fill**: #1524, #1525 (cross-process lifecycle arbitration), #1565 (reclamation, since a value cannot be dropped), #1543 (lost updates once two processes share a session), #1570 (a schema owner, once tenant metadata is rows and only the fixed boot-time schema is left), #1572 (a provisioning owner for native containers, once creating a collection is a registry insert).
- **Consequences of the target model**: #1571 (fencing makes staleness recognisable, so the layers above must handle it), #1573 (a shared container carries one schema, so the interface must stop promising one per collection), the asynchronous-erasure semantics (a deleted tenant is unreachable immediately and erased in the background, so synchronous erasure is a deployment's explicit choice).

### Done when

- The "at most one process" clause is gone from `vector_store.py`, replaced by a scope every store declares and honours.
- No backend creates a per-tenant physical structure by default; tenant creation is a row write everywhere, and the per-tenant tier is an explicit opt-in.
- Every lifecycle operation is safe from any process on the same backend: create races resolve by constraint, delete is idempotent and fences in-flight writers, purge is concurrent-safe and bounded.
- A stale handle cannot reach a successor tenant on any backend (raising where the backend can pin a registry row, landing in a dead incarnation where it cannot), and every backend has reclamation for dead tenants.
- Native containers are provisioned before serving and creating a logical collection is a single registry insert; collection shape is configured per deployment, one schema per container.
- Existing deployments have a stated path for each layout change: a migration through #1570's infrastructure, or an explicit recreate-schema statement of the kind the segment store overhaul makes for the pre-GA event backend.

### Out of scope

- The declarative (Neo4j and Nebula) backend: audited 2026-10-02 (#1753); kept for single-replica deployments by scope declaration (#1757), not made to scale.
- Cross-replica coherence of the process-local `EpisodicMemoryManager` cache: moved into #1755 (step 5, instances hold no per-session state once short-term memory is process-scoped, #1757). #1297, which rated it the main scaling bottleneck, is closed.

*Investigated and written by Claude (Claude Code), filed from the account of the user who commissioned the investigation.*

items.title: GitHub ingestion: compile deliveries into change sets in accounts — cursor, branch/path filters, ancestor checks, snapshot on force-push, blob-SHA ops, content tickets, periodic reconcile
items.body:
## Goal

Make GitHub-driven ingestion **correct under real delivery conditions** — private repos, branch and path filters, redelivery, out-of-order deliveries, missed deliveries, force pushes — and **cheap on re-sync** (only changed blobs are fetched). Accounts becomes the single place that turns a GitHub event into a **change set**; the document store only applies ops. This is the host half; the module half is the companion issue in `obin-ai/module-document-store` (linked below) and the runbook half is in `obin-ai/core-solutions`.

Design context: RFC-0004 §4 (`docs/authorization/2-proposals/0004-data-boundaries-and-installation-actors.md`), #473/#478 (boundary on the source), #474/#479/#486 (installation mint at lease time).

## Current state (verified on `main`)

Two paths exist. Only one works.

**Sync path (works, but re-fetches everything).** `pkg/business/datasources.go`:
- `SyncDatasourceSource` enqueues a `datasource.sync` / `datasource.github.sync.request` job (org-scoped, fresh idempotency key).
- The leased sync worker calls `RunDatasourceSync` → `runGitHubSync`: decrypts the token, `DefaultBranch`/`ResolveCommit`, `ListFiles(repo, ref, source.Paths)`, then `GetFileContent` **for every file** and `enqueueIngest` one `datasource` / `datasource.github.sync` job per file with the bytes inline (≤ `maxIngestPayload` = 960 KiB) and attributes `datasource.source_id`, `datasource.org_id`, `datasource.boundary_id`, `github.repo/path/ref/sha/commit/change_type`. Idempotency key = `sha256(source, commit, path)`.
- Only `last_synced_at` is recorded (migration 104). **No cursor**: nothing knows which commit was last ingested.

**Push path (not viable).** `pkg/datasource/handler.go`:
- Verifies `X-Hub-Signature-256`, enqueues the **raw delivery** to queue `datasource`, topic `datasource.github.push`, `JobScope_Global`, idempotency key = `X-GitHub-Delivery`, attributes **only** `github.event` and `datasource.source_id`. No org id, no boundary id → the module's consumer (`jobTenant`) resolves an **empty tenant** for push jobs.
- The module's push `Source` (`module-document-store` `pkg/infra/github/github.go`) is constructed **without a token** (`github.New()` in `work.go`), calls compare/tree/raw unauthenticated (private repos fail; 60 req/h), **ignores the delivery's `ref`** (any branch is ingested as the configured one), **ignores `paths`**, and diffs the delivery's own `before..after` — so redelivered or out-of-order pushes re-upsert old content as a *new* version, and a force-push whose `before` is gone fails the compare.

The credential must stay in accounts (vault envelope, `DatasourceConnectorSecretPurpose`). Therefore change detection belongs here.

## Proposal

### 1. Schema — migration `114_datasource_ingest_cursor`

```sql
ALTER TABLE datasource_sources
  ADD COLUMN last_ingested_commit TEXT,          -- head commit fully enqueued as a change set
  ADD COLUMN last_ingested_at     TIMESTAMPTZ,
  ADD COLUMN last_delivery_id     TEXT,          -- provenance of the last applied delivery
  ADD COLUMN reconcile_interval   INTERVAL NOT NULL DEFAULT '30 minutes',
  ADD COLUMN next_reconcile_at    TIMESTAMPTZ;   -- NULL = reconcile disabled
CREATE INDEX idx_datasource_sources_reconcile ON datasource_sources (next_reconcile_at) WHERE status = 'active';
```
Classify per `DATABASE_AUTHORITY.md` (tenant relation, existing RLS policy covers it; `app_control_plane` needs UPDATE for the worker). Cursor writes go through a store method `AdvanceDatasourceCursor(orgID, sourceID, commit, deliveryID)` that is **monotonic**: it refuses to move backwards (checked by the worker's ancestor test, see §3).

### 2. Receiver — keep it dumb, fix attribution

`pkg/datasource/handler.go` keeps: HMAC verify → persist raw delivery → 2xx. Changes:
- Resolve the source row (already done under `app_control_plane` for the secret) and stamp `datasource.org_id` and `datasource.boundary_id` alongside `datasource.source_id`.
- Change the **queue** from `datasource` (consumed by the module) to `datasource.deliveries` (consumed by the accounts worker below). The module must never see raw GitHub payloads again.
- Answer `ping` with 200 without enqueueing; answer non-`push` events with 200 `{"status":"ignored"}` (log the event name).

### 3. Delivery worker — the change-set compiler

New leased worker in accounts (same shape as the sync worker), queue `datasource.deliveries`, **one in-flight job per source** (partition/lease key = `datasource.source_id`; if the jobs platform cannot partition yet, take a `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext(source_id))` for the duration of the change-set build).

Per delivery, with the source's decrypted token:

1. **Branch filter.** `payload.ref` must equal `refs/heads/<source.Branch>` (or the resolved default branch when `Branch` is empty). Otherwise ack and drop (`disposition=ignored_branch`).
2. **Deleted ref** (`payload.deleted`) → ack, drop, audit `datasource.branch_deleted`. Do **not** delete documents; that is an operator decision (open question 1).
3. **Stale / duplicate check.** If `last_ingested_commit` is set and `after` is an ancestor of it — `GET /repos/{r}/compare/{after}...{cursor}` reports `status ∈ {ahead, identical}` — ack and drop (`disposition=stale`). This handles redelivery, out-of-order deliveries, and the receiver's at-least-once semantics.
4. **Base selection.** `base := last_ingested_commit` if set, else `payload.before` unless it is the zero SHA or `payload.created` is true. Diffing from the **cursor, not from `before`**, means a missed delivery is caught up by the next one.
5. **Compare.** `GET /repos/{r}/compare/{base}...{after}` (paginate `files`, `per_page=100`). Map `status`: `added|modified|changed|copied` → upsert; `removed` → delete; `renamed` → rename with `previous_filename`. **Apply the path-prefix filter** to `filename` (and to `previous_filename` for renames: a rename *into* scope is an upsert, *out of* scope is a delete). Each file row carries GitHub's blob `sha`.
6. **Divergence / force push.** If compare returns `status=diverged`, or 404 because `base` no longer exists, or the compare `files` list is truncated (GitHub caps at 300 files) → **snapshot** (§4) at `after` instead of an op list. Audit `datasource.force_push_reconciled`.
7. **Emit.** For each op, enqueue the per-file job (§5) in **path order**; then `AdvanceDatasourceCursor(after, delivery_id)`. The cursor advances only after every op of the set is durably enqueued; a crash mid-set replays the delivery and dedupes on idempotency keys.
8. **Audit** `datasource.change_set_compiled {source, base, head, ops, mode: compare|snapshot, delivery_id}`.

### 4. Snapshot (full reconcile without full re-fetch)

Used for: created branch, force push, truncated compare, the periodic reconcile (§6), and an explicit "Sync now".

- `GET /repos/{r}/git/trees/{commit}?recursive=1`; fail loudly if `truncated` (existing rule). Filter blobs by path prefixes.
- Enqueue **one** job: topic `datasource.github.snapshot`, payload = `{repo, commit, files: [{path, blob_sha, size}]}` (compressed JSON; if it exceeds 960 KiB, page it as `snapshot.part i/n` with a set id and let the module assemble). No content.
- The **module** diffs the manifest against its own bindings for `(tenant, boundary, repo)`: paths absent from the manifest → delete; paths whose stored `blob_sha` differs or is unknown → request content; identical → no-op. Accounts cannot do this diff (it does not know what is stored) — that is the whole reason the snapshot is a manifest, not a file list.
- Cursor advances to `commit` after the snapshot job is enqueued.

### 5. Per-file job shape (extend the existing `datasource.github.sync` payload)

Keep queue `datasource`, keep `SchemaVersion` bump to **2**. Payload:
```json
{"repo":"o/r","path":"docs/a.md","prev_path":"docs/old.md","ref":"refs/heads/main",
 "commit":"<head sha>","blob_sha":"<git blob sha>","change_type":"added|modified|removed|renamed",
 "content":"<base64, ≤ 960 KiB>","content_ticket":"<opaque, when content omitted>"}
```
Attributes unchanged plus `datasource.delivery_id` and `datasource.change_set` (base…head). Idempotency key = `sha256(source_id, head_commit, path)` (already the rule; a revert A→B→A therefore re-delivers, and the module dedupes by content hash).

**Large files.** When a blob exceeds the inline cap, omit `content` and set `content_ticket`. Add an internal RPC `DatasourceService.ResolveContentTicket(ticket) → bytes` (`EXPOSURE_INTERNAL`, streams up to a hard cap, e.g. 25 MiB) that re-fetches `GET /repos/{r}/git/blobs/{blob_sha}` with the source's token. The token never leaves accounts. Tickets are `(source_id, blob_sha, expires_at)` signed with the internal key, not stored.

### 6. Periodic reconcile

A scheduler (reuse the existing worker tick) selects `active` sources with `next_reconcile_at <= now()`, enqueues a **snapshot** at the current branch head **only if** `ResolveCommit(branch) != last_ingested_commit`, and bumps `next_reconcile_at`. This is the production safety net for lost webhooks and the **local development mode without a tunnel**. Expose `reconcile_interval` on `AddSource`/`UpdateSource` (min 5 min; `0` disables).

`SyncDatasourceSource` ("Sync now") becomes: enqueue a snapshot at head regardless of cursor equality.

### 7. Observability

Per source: `last_ingested_commit`, `last_delivery_id`, last change-set size and mode, drop counters by disposition (`ignored_branch`, `stale`, `ping`). Surface in `GetDatasourceSource` and the datasources admin panel status line ("head 3f2a…, 12 files, compare, 2 min ago"). Metrics: `datasource_change_set_ops_total{mode}`, `datasource_delivery_dropped_total{disposition}`, `datasource_snapshot_files_total`.

## Acceptance (each is a test)

- [ ] **Branch filter.** Push to `feature/x` on a source configured for `main` → ack, no jobs, disposition `ignored_branch`.
- [ ] **Path filter.** Compare returns `docs/a.md`, `src/b.go`, source paths `["docs/"]` → exactly one op. Rename `docs/a.md → src/a.md` → a delete for `docs/a.md`; rename `src/a.md → docs/a.md` → an upsert.
- [ ] **Redelivery.** Same delivery id twice → receiver answers `duplicate`, worker sees one job.
- [ ] **Out of order.** Deliveries for A→B and B→C arrive as C then B: C compiles `cursor…C`; B is dropped as `stale`; cursor ends at C; the file content is C's.
- [ ] **Missed delivery.** Deliveries A→B (lost) and B→C: compiling C uses base = cursor (A), so B's changes are included.
- [ ] **Force push.** `before` unreachable → snapshot at `after`; a file removed by the rewrite is deleted downstream (module test); cursor = `after`.
- [ ] **Large file.** A 2 MiB blob produces a job with `content_ticket`; `ResolveContentTicket` streams the bytes with the source's token; an expired or foreign-source ticket is refused.
- [ ] **Cursor monotonic.** `AdvanceDatasourceCursor` refuses a commit that is an ancestor of the current cursor.
- [ ] **Reconcile.** With head == cursor no job is enqueued; with head != cursor one snapshot job is enqueued; `reconcile_interval=0` never schedules.
- [ ] **Private repo.** All GitHub calls in the worker carry the source token; the receiver and the module make **no** GitHub calls.
- [ ] Schema classified and RLS gate green; `AUTHZ_MATRIX.md` and the generated catalogs updated for the new internal RPC.

## Open questions

1. Branch deleted: keep documents (recommended, operator decides) vs delete.
2. Should the worker also compile `pull_request` / `release` events later? Out of scope; the change-set shape does not preclude it.
3. Snapshot paging above 960 KiB: page, or lift the inbox cap for this one topic?

## Related

Companion issues: module apply side (obin-ai/module-document-store), runbook (obin-ai/core-solutions) — linked in comments. #473, #478, #474, #479, #486, #470.

items.title: infra: replace TypeORM synchronize with explicit migrations
items.body:
## Background

The backend currently uses TypeORM with `synchronize: true` in `backend/src/app.module.ts`. That is convenient during early local development, but it is unsafe once the application moves toward managed PostgreSQL, Kubernetes deployment, or multi-tenant database provisioning.

Automatic schema synchronization lets the application mutate database schema at startup. In staging/production this creates several risks:

- schema changes are not reviewed as explicit migration files
- startup behavior can differ by environment depending on existing schema state
- accidental entity changes can alter or drop database structures unexpectedly
- multi-tenant database provisioning cannot reliably replay schema history
- Kubernetes rollouts may start multiple replicas that all attempt schema sync

This should be addressed before or alongside:

- #5 managed PostgreSQL migration
- #6 Dockerfiles and production images
- #7 Kubernetes manifests
- #8 database-per-tenant/control-plane architecture

## Proposed Change

Replace TypeORM schema auto-sync with explicit migrations.

The application should run with `synchronize: false` in normal runtime configuration. Database schema changes should be represented as migration files and applied with a dedicated command or deployment job.

## Tasks

- [ ] Add a TypeORM data source / migration configuration for the backend
- [ ] Create an initial migration for the current `billing_line_items` schema
- [ ] Set `synchronize: false` in `backend/src/app.module.ts`
- [ ] Add backend package scripts for migration workflows:
  - `migration:run`
  - `migration:revert`
  - optionally `migration:generate`
- [ ] Document local development flow in the README: start DB, run migrations, start backend
- [ ] Verify a fresh database can be initialized using migrations only
- [ ] Verify backend build still passes

## Acceptance Criteria

- Backend runtime no longer uses `synchronize: true`
- A fresh PostgreSQL database can be brought to the current schema by running migrations
- The current billing ingestion entity remains compatible with the generated schema
- Migration commands are documented and runnable from the backend package

## Notes

This should be handled before serious production/container/Kubernetes work. Docker images and Kubernetes deployments should not rely on application startup mutating database schema implicitly.

---
## Deutsche Fassung

## Hintergrund

Das Backend verwendet TypeORM derzeit mit `synchronize: true` in `backend/src/app.module.ts`. Das ist in einer frühen lokalen Entwicklungsphase bequem, aber unsicher, sobald die Anwendung in Richtung verwaltetes PostgreSQL, Kubernetes-Deployment oder mandantenspezifische Datenbankbereitstellung weiterentwickelt wird.

Die automatische Schemasynchronisierung erlaubt der Anwendung, das Datenbankschema beim Start zu verändern. In Staging und Produktion entstehen dadurch mehrere Risiken:

- Schemaänderungen werden nicht als explizite Migrationsdateien geprüft.
- Das Startverhalten kann sich abhängig vom bestehenden Schemazustand zwischen Umgebungen unterscheiden.
- Versehentliche Änderungen an Entitäten können Datenbankstrukturen unerwartet verändern oder löschen.
- Bei der Bereitstellung mandantenspezifischer Datenbanken kann die Schemahistorie nicht zuverlässig wiederholt werden.
- Bei Kubernetes-Rollouts können mehrere Replikate gleichzeitig versuchen, das Schema zu synchronisieren.

Dies sollte vor oder zusammen mit folgenden Issues umgesetzt werden:

- #5 Migration zu verwaltetem PostgreSQL
- #6 Dockerfiles und Produktions-Images
- #7 Kubernetes-Manifeste
- #8 Database-per-Tenant- und Control-Plane-Architektur

## Vorgeschlagene Änderung

Die automatische TypeORM-Schemasynchronisierung durch explizite Migrationen ersetzen.

Die Anwendung soll im normalen Laufzeitbetrieb mit `synchronize: false` laufen. Änderungen am Datenbankschema werden als Migrationsdateien abgebildet und durch einen eigenen Befehl oder Deployment-Job angewendet.

## Aufgaben

- [ ] TypeORM Data Source beziehungsweise Migrationskonfiguration für das Backend hinzufügen.
- [ ] Eine initiale Migration für das aktuelle Schema `billing_line_items` erstellen.
- [ ] In `backend/src/app.module.ts` `synchronize: false` setzen.
- [ ] Backend-Package-Skripte für Migrationsabläufe hinzufügen:
  - `migration:run`
  - `migration:revert`
  - optional `migration:generate`
- [ ] Lokalen Entwicklungsablauf im README dokumentieren: Datenbank starten, Migrationen ausführen, Backend starten.
- [ ] Prüfen, dass eine frische Datenbank ausschließlich durch Migrationen initialisiert werden kann.
- [ ] Prüfen, dass der Backend-Build weiterhin erfolgreich ist.

## Akzeptanzkriterien

- Die Backend-Laufzeit verwendet nicht mehr `synchronize: true`.
- Eine frische PostgreSQL-Datenbank kann durch Ausführen der Migrationen auf das aktuelle Schema gebracht werden.
- Die bestehende Entität für die Abrechnungsdatenübernahme bleibt mit dem erzeugten Schema kompatibel.
- Die Migrationsbefehle sind dokumentiert und im Backend-Package ausführbar.

## Hinweise

Dies muss vor ernsthafter Produktions-, Container- oder Kubernetes-Arbeit umgesetzt werden. Docker-Images und Kubernetes-Deployments dürfen nicht davon abhängen, dass der Anwendungsstart implizit das Datenbankschema verändert.
