## AI 系統從建置到上線：三段流程

閱讀順序只有三段：**先準備資料 → 再處理使用者請求 → 最後用線上結果持續改善**。底部三項是每個階段都必須具備的系統能力。

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph PREP["A. 事前準備：把資料變成 AI 可用的知識"]
    direction LR
    DE["1. Data Engineering<br/>收集、清理、治理資料"]
    DS["2. Data Science<br/>分析資料、定義指標與特徵"]
    ML["3. ML 基礎<br/>選模型、Embedding 與推論方式"]
    KB[("可檢索知識庫<br/>Chunks + Metadata + Vectors")]
    DE --> DS --> ML --> KB
  end

  subgraph REQUEST["B. 線上請求：使用者問問題時，系統實際怎麼跑"]
    direction LR
    USER["使用者 / 前端"] --> API["API 接收問題"]
    API --> RAG["4. RAG / LLM Application<br/>找資料、排序、組 Prompt"]
    RAG --> NEED{"需要執行動作？"}
    NEED -->|否| ANSWER["LLM 產生答案"]
    NEED -->|是| AGENT["5. Agent<br/>規劃步驟、呼叫工具、保存狀態"]
    AGENT --> ANSWER
    ANSWER --> USER
  end

  KB -->|提供相關資料| RAG

  subgraph IMPROVE["C. 上線後：觀察結果並持續改善"]
    direction LR
    OBS["6. Production AI / Observability<br/>記錄品質、延遲、成本與錯誤"]
    EVAL["7. LLM Evaluation<br/>Golden Dataset、Judge、Faithfulness"]
    FIX["修正資料 / Prompt / 模型 / 流程"]
    OBS --> EVAL --> FIX
  end

  ANSWER -->|留下 Trace 與 Feedback| OBS
  FIX -->|重新發佈| RAG
  FIX -->|補資料與品質規則| DE

  CROSS["所有階段共同要求<br/>8. Multi-tenant：租戶與資料隔離<br/>9. AI Security / Reliability：權限、PII、Guardrails<br/>10. Architecture：Queue、Cache、Scaling、Fault Tolerance"]
```

items.title: [FEATURE] Support PostgreSQL horizontal scaling

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
## Feature Summary

Add first-class support for horizontally scaling PostgreSQL read traffic — either by bundling a connection proxy (PgBouncer / PgCat) with read/write splitting, or by adding native read-replica routing to the app — so enterprise deployments can serve more concurrent users without vertically scaling the primary DB.

## Problem Statement

### Current Situation

TestPlanIt connects to PostgreSQL via a single `DATABASE_URL`. The app (Prisma + ZenStack) treats the database as a single instance for both reads and writes. A user can stand up a Postgres streaming replica for HA / failover, but the replica serves zero application traffic: all queries hit the primary.

Pain points observed during capacity testing (2 OCPU → 8 OCPU run on a single-node stack):
- App-tier throughput scales nearly linearly with added replicas (validated 1 → 4 app replicas).
- PostgreSQL becomes the bottleneck well before the app tier does. Going from 2 → 8 OCPU on the app tier only produced a 1.6× increase in sustained concurrent users, because the single Postgres primary ran out of headroom.
- User (e.g., large enterprises in finance) running tens of thousands of users have no in-product option to spread read traffic across replicas without building a custom proxy layer themselves.

### Desired Outcome

Users should be able to add read capacity by adding read replicas (and pointing TestPlanIt at them) without writing glue code. The product should "just scale horizontally" for the dominant read-heavy workloads (repository browsing, test run listings, search, reporting).

## Proposed Solution

Ship a supported way to split read and write traffic, via one of two paths:

**Path A — Connection proxy with read/write splitting (recommended):**
- Bundle PgCat (or pgpool-II, or a PgBouncer-based solution) in the reference Docker Compose / Helm chart.
- App continues to use a single `DATABASE_URL`; the proxy handles primary/replica routing based on SQL statement type.
- Expose config for replica endpoints, max lag tolerated, and failover behavior.

**Path B — Native read replica routing in the app:**
- Introduce a second Prisma client (read-only) wired to a `DATABASE_REPLICA_URL`.
- Add a thin wrapper in `lib/prisma.ts` that routes known read queries to the replica and writes to the primary.
- Handle replication-lag gotchas (read-your-own-writes) by pinning recently-written sessions to the primary for a short TTL.

### User Story

As an **enterprise infrastructure engineer**, I want **TestPlanIt to route read queries to Postgres read replicas automatically** so that **I can serve thousands of concurrent users without vertically scaling the primary or building my own SQL proxy**.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] TestPlanIt supports a documented way to configure one primary + N read replicas.
- [ ] Reads (`SELECT`) served by UI browsing, search, reporting, and listing endpoints are routed to a replica when configured.
- [ ] Writes (`INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE`) and transactions always route to the primary.
- [ ] Read-your-own-writes correctness preserved — a user who just created an object sees it immediately on the next read.
- [ ] Capacity test suite re-run shows sustained concurrent users at 8 OCPU app-tier + 1 replica scales above the single-primary baseline by a meaningful margin (target: ≥1.5× more users before p95 > 1s).
- [ ] Docs include a reference deployment diagram and failover behavior.
- [ ] ZenStack `@allow`/`@deny` rules continue to evaluate correctly across the split.

## Design Mockups

Suggested reference architecture:

```
          ┌─────────────┐
          │    Caddy    │  (LB)
          └──────┬──────┘
                 │
       ┌─────────┴─────────┐
       ▼                   ▼
  ┌─────────┐        ┌─────────┐
  │  App 1  │  ...   │  App N  │
  └────┬────┘        └────┬────┘
       │ DATABASE_URL     │
       ▼                  ▼
   ┌──────────────────────────┐
   │   PgCat / PgBouncer      │  (read/write split)
   └──────┬───────────┬───────┘
          │ writes    │ reads
          ▼           ▼
      ┌────────┐   ┌──────────┐
      │ Primary│   │ Replica  │  ← repeatable
      │   PG   │──▶│    PG    │     (N replicas)
      └────────┘   └──────────┘
```

## Alternative Solutions

### Option 1 — Ship PgCat in the reference stack

Pros: no app code changes; users opt in via config. Battle-tested in production at Instacart / OpenAI.
Cons: another moving part to operate; failover semantics are PgCat-specific.

### Option 2 — Native replica client in the app

Pros: full control over routing decisions; clean read-your-own-writes handling; no extra process to run.
Cons: higher engineering cost; ZenStack policy evaluation needs audit to confirm it works against a read replica; have to add a per-request "sticky to primary" TTL.

### Option 3 — Managed cloud DB

Defer the problem to AWS Aurora / Google AlloyDB, where routing is handled by the service. Document this as the recommended deployment for cloud hosted users.
Pros: zero engineering work.
Cons: locks out self-hosted enterprise users (exactly our target for this issue).

## Technical Considerations

### Dependencies

- [ ] Requires database schema changes
- [x] Requires API changes (internal — Prisma client layer)
- [ ] Requires UI/UX design review
- [x] Requires third-party integration (PgCat/pgpool, if taking Path A)
- [x] Other: ZenStack policy evaluation needs to work against a read replica

### Performance Impact

Positive. The capacity suite is expected to show a meaningful lift in sustained concurrent users per unit of app-tier OCPU once reads spread across replicas.

Risk area: replication lag. Must pin recently-written sessions to the primary or implement causal reads to avoid "I just saved it and it's gone" UX bugs.

### Security Considerations

- Replica endpoints must be reachable only from app replicas, not exposed externally.
- Credentials should support per-role (primary vs. replica) separation to reduce blast radius.
- Audit-log queries and write-side paths must be provably routed to the primary (otherwise audit tail could lag user-visible state).

## Business Value

### Priority

- [ ] Critical - Core functionality gap
- [x] High - Significant improvement
- [ ] Medium - Nice to have
- [ ] Low - Future consideration

### Affected User Groups

- [x] Test Managers
- [x] QA Engineers
- [x] Developers
- [x] Project Managers
- [x] Stakeholders
- [x] All users

(Operationally, the feature is owned by infra engineers, but every user benefits from the latency improvement under load.)

### Expected Usage

- [x] Daily

Always on once configured.

## Implementation Effort

- [ ] Small (1-2 days)
- [ ] Medium (3-5 days)
- [ ] Large (1-2 weeks)
- [x] Extra Large (>2 weeks)

Engineering scope: design + implementation + capacity validation + docs. Path A is the lighter of the two.

## Related Issues/Features

- Related to #
- Depends on #
- Blocks #

## Additional Context

Discovered during pre-sales capacity testing against an enterprise prospect. Capacity suite on a single-node stack:

- 2 OCPU (1 app replica, single PG): 217 concurrent users at p95 = 1s, 94 ingestion rps
- 8 OCPU (4 app replicas, single PG): 348 concurrent users at p95 = 1s, 203 ingestion rps

Scaling the app tier 4× only delivered ~1.6× more users and ~2.2× more rps. The single Postgres primary was the dominant bottleneck in that run. Users at the 5,000+ concurrent-user scale can't get there with our stack today without building a proxy themselves.

## Examples from Other Tools

- **Discourse** — documents read-replica routing via its own `multisite` config.
- **GitLab** — uses `database_load_balancing` (custom) + PgBouncer for read scaling.
- **Sentry** — routes reads via a PgBouncer layer.
- **Mattermost** — `SqlSettings.DataSourceReplicas` config for read routing.

## Checklist

- [x] I have searched for similar feature requests
- [x] I have provided a clear problem statement
- [x] I have described at least one solution
- [x] I have considered alternatives
- [x] This feature aligns with TestPlanIt's goals

items.title: upstream survey: 4 items needing a decision — 2026-10-04
items.body:
Weekly survey of the three upstream home-ops repositories, 8-day window ending 2026-10-04. **53 human-authored commits** reviewed (24 / 14 / 15; bot commits filtered out). All three clones fetched successfully. Verified against the live cluster throughout.

**No pull requests were opened this week.** Everything applicable that moved upstream is either already in place here, already further along than upstream, or hit a stop condition and appears below.

## Needing a decision

### 1. Narrow the gateway retry trigger to resets seen before the request is sent

Upstream: onedr0p/home-ops [#11766](https://github.com/onedr0p/home-ops/pull/11766).

A one-word change in the gateway-wide `BackendTrafficPolicy`: the retry trigger `reset` becomes `reset-before-request`. Under `reset`, Envoy retries whenever the upstream stream is reset — including after the request has already been handed to the upstream, which means a non-idempotent request can be replayed. `reset-before-request` restricts retries to resets observed before the request was forwarded.

**Why it might apply here.** The same policy exists here with the same single `reset` trigger and the same retry count, attached to both gateways by target selector, so the shape matches exactly. Confirmed that the Envoy Gateway CRD currently installed accepts `reset-before-request` as a trigger value, so this would apply cleanly rather than being rejected at admission.

**What the live cluster shows.** Retries are not theoretical here. The gateways performed a few hundred retries over the last day and essentially all of them succeeded, with none dropped for exceeding the retry budget. The two largest sources are both write paths — a webhook receiver and a log-ingestion endpoint — which is exactly where replaying a request the upstream already received has a visible effect: a duplicated trigger, or duplicated log lines.

**What blocks it.** It is a judgement call with a cost on both sides rather than a clear improvement. Narrowing the trigger removes the unsafe replays, but it also gives up the retries that today recover a reset arriving after the request was sent — and since nearly every retry currently succeeds, some share of those few hundred would become user-visible errors instead. Envoy Gateway is also in the "Protected infra" `packageRules` entry, and the policy is selected onto both gateways, so there is no small blast radius to test it in.

**Files it would touch:** the gateway-wide `BackendTrafficPolicy` in the Envoy Gateway app directory.

### 2. Declarative Postgres roles and databases, then client-certificate authentication

Upstream: jfroy/flatops [042f6bc6b](https://github.com/jfroy/flatops/commit/042f6bc6b), [ce9c5ba54](https://github.com/jfroy/flatops/commit/ce9c5ba54), [4b9143426](https://github.com/jfroy/flatops/commit/4b9143426), applied in that order.

Three commits that together replace per-app `postgres-init` init containers with CNPG's declarative `DatabaseRole` and `Database` resources (one tenant directory per app), then move every tenant from password to TLS client-certificate authentication, then split the single tenant Kustomization into one per app with health checks, so one failing database no longer blocks every other app.

**Why it might apply here.** The operator version running here is new enough, and both CRDs are already installed and entirely unused — nothing in the cluster declares a `DatabaseRole` or a `Database` today, while twenty apps carry a `postgres-init` init container instead. The `PushSecret` delivery pattern the upstream work leans on is already established here in two other places, so the mechanism is familiar rather than new. The TLS half is the weaker one: ten connection strings use `sslmode=require`, which encrypts but verifies nothing, three use `sslmode=disable`, and one app disables its runtime's TLS verification outright with a comment explaining that the in-cluster CA is not reachable from it. Certificate authentication addresses the authentication half and verified TLS addresses that comment.

**What blocks it.** Size and sequencing first — upstream shipped this as roughly five thousand changed lines across three commits, and CloudNativePG is protected infra. The prerequisites are also absent: the Postgres cluster here has no client CA configured and no `pg_hba` entry for certificate logins, and there is no trust-distribution mechanism of the kind the upstream pattern mounts for the server root, so that has to be chosen and provisioned before any of it lands. One of upstream's stated benefits does **not** apply here: no app namespace holds the superuser credential today, so for this cluster the case is declarative management and verified TLS, not removing a copied superuser password.

**Files it would touch:** a new tenant tree under the database namespace, the Postgres `Cluster` manifest, a shared component for the push grant, and the twenty app HelmReleases that currently run `postgres-init`.

### 3. Self-hosted pull-request review service

Upstream: onedr0p/home-ops [#11786](https://github.com/onedr0p/home-ops/pull/11786), followed by [#11787](https://github.com/onedr0p/home-ops/pull/11787), [#11788](https://github.com/onedr0p/home-ops/pull/11788), [#11792](https://github.com/onedr0p/home-ops/pull/11792), [#11795](https://github.com/onedr0p/home-ops/pull/11795), [#11796](https://github.com/onedr0p/home-ops/pull/11796) and several chart bumps across the week.

A new app: a self-hosted GitHub App that reviews pull requests, backed by its own CNPG cluster, running each review inside a sandboxed container runtime, with a Grafana dashboard and a PrometheusRule once the chart grew them.

**Why it might apply here.** The reviewer here is a GitHub Actions workflow scoped to dependency pull requests. This is a different thing — a persistent in-cluster service reviewing all pull requests — and it fits the pattern already used for rendering and diffing them in-cluster.

**What blocks it.** It is a new app, so an issue by default. Beyond that it wants the sandboxed container runtime, which is item 3 of #5440 and still open: upstream pins its review runners to that runtime class, and the only `RuntimeClass` in this cluster is the GPU one. It also needs a GitHub App registered with its private key and webhook secret stored out of band, an inference provider account and key, and its own database. The chart moved through roughly ten releases inside the survey window, so it is early.

**Files it would touch:** a new namespace directory holding the app and its database, plus a Renovate entry for the chart.

### 4. A dedicated arr dashboard

Upstream: jfroy/flatops [818e67994](https://github.com/jfroy/flatops/commit/818e67994).

Adds a dashboard app for arr services — app-template on Postgres with OIDC in front — where the services are configured through its own UI and stored in its database.

**Why it might apply here.** There is a large arr estate here and an OIDC provider already running in the cluster, so it would have both something to show and somewhere to authenticate.

**What blocks it.** New app, so an issue by default. It also overlaps the dashboard component already wired into apps here, which makes adopting it a question of whether a second dashboard is wanted rather than a gap to fill. Upstream's own commit message records that it deliberately left Kubernetes service discovery out, because the app lists Services across all namespaces with no way to scope the call — the alternative being a cluster-wide Service read grant.

**Files it would touch:** a new app directory and one line in a namespace `kustomization.yaml`.

## Looked adoptable, dropped after checking

- **Explicit health paths on two uptime checks** (onedr0p [#11767](https://github.com/onedr0p/home-ops/pull/11767)) adds a `path` to the uptime-check annotation on two apps. Both equivalents here are green: of 142 monitored endpoints exactly one is failing, and it is neither of them. Adopting this would change nothing observable, so it is a no-op.
- **Removing an app's session secret** (onedr0p [#11765](https://github.com/onedr0p/home-ops/pull/11765)) deletes an ExternalSecret upstream describes as unused. The equivalent secret does exist here, but whether the app still reads it could not be established from upstream's commit, and if it does, dropping it invalidates every session once. No benefit beyond tidiness, so it did not clear the confidence bar.
- **Switching the changed-files filter in CI** (onedr0p [#11798](https://github.com/onedr0p/home-ops/pull/11798)) replaces the filter action with a different one. The workflow here already carries the adaptation upstream was working around, with a comment recording it, so there is nothing to fix — and the replacement action is the one that was compromised in a supply-chain incident, which is not a direction to follow.
- **Broader h265 handling in the media quality profiles** (jfroy/flatops [d1ab19dd8](https://github.com/jfroy/flatops/commit/d1ab19dd8)) is a preference about what gets downloaded, not a correctness fix, so it is the owner's call rather than something to adopt by default.

## Status of the previously tracked items

Item 1 of #5440 — the storage key-type migration — **has since landed on `main`**. The key type, generation, retained-generation count and cipher restriction are all in the manifest now, the health-warning mutes are gone, and the live cluster reports clean health with an empty status-detail block rather than warnings hidden under a mute. That item looks closeable. Items 2 and 3 of #5440 are both still open and unchanged in the repository; neither is re-raised here.

items.title: Cloud automation Phase 5: Data + identity seeding — Neo4j restore Job, KeycloakRealmImport, secrets inventory

labels.name: phase
labels.description: Other work is specified against this; closure requires shipped/shipped-inert (harmonic-forge#642)

labels.name: shipped
labels.description: Closed producing output on real data; evidence in comments (harmonic-forge#642)

items.body:
Phase 5 of the cloud-automation toolchain (see epic; full research memo: `~/Harmonic_Projects/research/cymagraph-cloud-automation-toolchain.md`).

## Goal

A fresh environment reaches *usable* state with no manual steps: Neo4j data restored, Keycloak realm configured, secrets flowing. This completes "one command to a running app."

## Scope

1. **Neo4j seeding:** a restore Job — dump fetched from the Spaces bucket (same artifact family as `setup/neo4j.dump`), loaded via `neo4j-admin database load` into the Phase 4 instance. Plus the reverse: a CronJob dumping to Spaces on schedule (the durability story for single-instance Community Edition — documented accepted risk).
2. **Keycloak realm-as-code:** export the current realm to JSON, commit it, apply via the operator's `KeycloakRealmImport` CRD. Known limitation to resolve here: realm import is create-oriented; decide the ongoing-changes strategy (re-import policy vs keycloak-config-cli) and document it.
3. **Secrets inventory:** enumerate every secret the stack needs (Neo4j auth, Keycloak admin, SESSION_SECRET_KEY, Anthropic/Voyage keys, Google OAuth client) and route each through the Phase 3 SOPS flow. Values entered by the human key-holder only — agents never write secret values, per standing rule (real incident: #175).

## Acceptance criteria

1. From `tofu apply` on a clean account to a signed-in session viewing real graph data: zero manual steps beyond supplying credentials/key material at the documented points.
2. The scheduled dump lands in Spaces and a restore from it is verified once, live.
3. Realm JSON in Git reproduces working sign-in on a fresh environment (Keycloak/JWT for login, Google OAuth for resource access — the two must stay independent per ADR-015).
4. Secrets audit: `git grep` across infra repo finds zero plaintext secret values.

items.title: defect(quota): the commit lane's only org-limit gate was the session cap — removing the cap leaves /v1/sessions/commit total-unbounded (no points gate)

labels.name: P1-severe
labels.description: Beta SEVERE — breaks a promise to a real user; not ship-blocking on its own.

labels.name: lane:c1-capture
labels.description: Lane 1 Capture — install seam, capture path, the five write doors (obj 1).

labels.name: lane:c2b-extractor
labels.description: Lane 2b Extractor — the pipeline body and the write path (obj 2).

items.body:
## The gap, named precisely

`POST /v1/sessions/commit` writes `:Session`, `:Event`, a `:Document {documentKind:'transcript'}` and value Points, but its **only org-limit gate is `_check_org_limit(org, "sessions")`** (`tortoise/hosted_api.py`). There is no points gate on that path, and `_count_resource("points")` (`tortoise/quota.py`) counts only non-episodic `:Point` + `:Object`/`:Subject` — so `:Session`, `:Event` and transcript `:Document` nodes are counted by **no** quota.

Until #4010 that path was bounded **in total** by the flat `max_sessions = 1000`: 1000 sessions × a bounded payload = a bounded node count. With sessions unlimited for every tier (owner ruling on #4010 — **not** to be reversed, and no replacement cap on sessions), that total bound is gone. What remains bounds the **rate** (`RateLimitMiddleware`) and the **per-session** budget (`adjudicate_budget`, net-new ≤ 50), plus `included_write_ops_per_month`, which is metered and alerts at 80%/100% but **never blocks** (see #3873).

Concretely (all verified at `origin/main` + #4048's head): an authenticated free-tier `tt_` key can loop `POST /v1/sessions/commit` with a fresh `session_id` and a payload inside the caps (even `points: []`, which `test_empty_commit_ok_zero_budget` in `tests/test_commit_endpoint.py` proves returns 200), and every iteration mints nodes that no quota counts. On a shared multi-tenant graph that is a noisy-neighbour / disk-exhaustion surface, and the field's standard mitigation for exactly that class is a **per-tenant absolute storage bound** (see the noisy-neighbour and multi-tenant-storage literature).

## What is NOT the fix

- **Not** restoring a session cap — sessions are unlimited for every tier by owner ruling; a session cap here would be a quiet reversal of a recorded decision.
- **Not** a retention/eviction window — that contradicts the standing decision (#3853: no default retention window of any length on user content). Proposing it is a reopen, not an option.
- **Not** tiering of session counts.

## Candidate directions (for the owner/lane that takes this)

1. **Give the commit lane the gate the capture lane already has** — a pre-write `count_org_usage(org, "points")` vs `max_points`, exactly as `/v1/sessions` does. Cheapest, reuses shipped machinery, no new surface (#3863 freeze respected).
2. **Widen the points count** to include the node classes the commit lane mints (`:Session`, `:Event`, transcript `:Document`). More faithful to "total node growth", but it changes the meaning of `max_points` for every existing tenant and would need a migration/backfill decision.
3. **An explicit per-tenant node-count ceiling** independent of `max_points` — most honest about the bound, largest change (a new limit → a pricing/limit decision, i.e. an owner question).

Recommendation (labelled): **1** — it closes the path with the least new machinery and the fewest reversals. It is separable from #4010 and should land as its own PR with its own tests (a bounded-node-count assertion + a mutation).

## Why this is filed rather than fixed in #4048

#4048 removes an unapproved cap; it does not add a new gate to a billing hot path. Adding a points pre-check to the commit lane changes behaviour for every tenant and would need its own scope, tests and review — smuggling it into a cap-removal PR is how a directed change acquires unrelated risk. The security reviewer on #4048 raised exactly this, and it is recorded in that PR's body as a disclosed residual.

**Found by:** the `code-review` security reviewer on PR #4048 (tortoise #4010).

items.body:
## Four-priority implementation checkpoint — 2026-10-22 UTC

**Release controls, monitoring configuration and public brand/intake work are implemented. Customer-delivery readiness is partially closed:** PermitPlate passed its live first-customer operational gate in founder-curated, score-free mode; Recovery's private-host acceptance and CaptureBrief's full source-custody/recovery acceptance remain open. No real payment, subscriber delivery or recovery outcome is asserted.

### 1. Release protection — accepted for RETALLY main

[PR #582](https://github.com/P00NSMASHER/github-value-hunt-ledger/pull/582) moved all four scheduled writers onto guarded pull requests. The active [Main ruleset](https://github.com/P00NSMASHER/github-value-hunt-ledger/rules/25608380) requires a current, successful unique `release-gate`, a pull request, zero human approvals, and no bypass. [PR #585](https://github.com/P00NSMASHER/github-value-hunt-ledger/pull/585) proved normal protected merging after all applicable checks passed, including Windows encrypted backup. The subsequent Group inquiry release below also merged through this protection. These claims apply to this repository; sibling repository protection is separate.

### 2. Delivery readiness — PermitPlate operationally ready; private acceptance remains open

- **PermitPlate:** [#124](https://github.com/P00NSMASHER/permitplate-nyc/pull/124), [#127](https://github.com/P00NSMASHER/permitplate-nyc/pull/127) and [#128](https://github.com/P00NSMASHER/permitplate-nyc/pull/128) added fresh provider/public-build evidence, ordered research refresh before readiness, and prevented rejected workflow completions from cancelling the private research queue. The actual [curated refresh](https://github.com/P00NSMASHER/permitplate-nyc/actions/runs/39713183687) and chained [live readiness run](https://github.com/P00NSMASHER/permitplate-nyc/actions/runs/39713244752) succeeded on main `a97759783c4d4df5da89f1213cee448df5f29c35`. At 02:47 UTC, the controller reported `READY_FOR_FIRST_PAID_CUSTOMER`, `FOUNDER_CURATED_NO_SCORE_V1`, all 12 internal gates passing, no required first-customer external failures, and matching current/private research at 4,279 candidates. [Sanitized evidence artifact](https://github.com/P00NSMASHER/permitplate-nyc/actions/runs/39713244752/artifacts/12397024043). `commerciallyProven=false`: real paid-subscriber acceptance, provider-backed delivery and real next-run duplicate suppression remain unproved. Separate scored-opportunity diagnostics still fail and are not certified by this founder-curated acceptance.
- **CaptureBrief:** [PR #71](https://github.com/P00NSMASHER/capturebrief/pull/71) repaired the FY2027 source observer and retired obsolete Netlify live checks. The actual [FY2027 observer run](https://github.com/P00NSMASHER/capturebrief/actions/runs/39711219762) retrieved HTTP 200, 1,607,260 bytes and 1,104 CSV rows, with a fresh checksum receipt. This proves that specific public fetch, not full original-source/catalog custody, private indexing, independent restore or customer release.
- **Recovery/private workbench:** fresh read-only inspection still found no attached policies on the separate workbench Access app and no active account tunnels. The connected operator device was offline. Actual private-host installation, encrypted off-device recovery and buyer-specific source/access acceptance remain unverified. Existing inquiry-operator access is separate and was preserved.

### 3. Monitoring and automation ownership — configuration repaired

CaptureBrief's replacement monitoring passed its actual merged-source runs. The mis-scoped research task was corrected, and the current Executive, Engineering, Evidence & Reconciliation, Website, QA & Delivery, and Applied Research roles were preserved under the concurrent owner reset. First post-reset cycles have completed for Executive and Engineering; Website, QA & Delivery and Applied Research completed with recorded `no_update`. Evidence & Reconciliation remains `in_progress` at this checkpoint, with no current result; it is not counted as a successful run. Old Roblox/wholesale result text belongs to older runs and is not evidence about the corrected cycles. No additional recurring tasks were created.

### 4. Brand and contact intake — merged and verified live

- CaptureBrief [#72](https://github.com/P00NSMASHER/capturebrief/pull/72) and PermitPlate [#125](https://github.com/P00NSMASHER/permitplate-nyc/pull/125) unified RETALLY affiliation, navigation and contact details while preserving existing offer prices, checkout links and legal operators. Both public sites were rechecked after deployment.
- RETALLY [PR #589](https://github.com/P00NSMASHER/github-value-hunt-ledger/pull/589) merged at `c46b7405d8f766334b16aede807acdbf3f2604ff`. Cloudflare Pages production deployment `fa4cfbc0-a154-4b4a-95ac-4d4e05f16757` succeeded at that exact commit.
- The [live Group contact page](https://www.retallyrecovery.com/contact/) now collects name, email, optional company, selected business, message and explicit consent. The new shared intake path uses Turnstile, bounded input, existing rate limits, durable D1 storage before notification, idempotent retries and a truthful saved-reference response. Existing freight intake behavior is retained. The [privacy disclosure](https://www.retallyrecovery.com/privacy) and operator runbook were updated.
- Validation included 37 API/client tests, existing migration/operator reconciliation checks, all applicable final-head and merged-source checks, and [65 responsive page checks with accessibility and keyboard validation](https://github.com/P00NSMASHER/github-value-hunt-ledger/actions/runs/39712603696). Independent ordinary unbusted HTTPS reads at 02:49 UTC confirmed the new canonical and immutable contact/privacy pages, matching served JavaScript and `GET /api/group-inquiry` returning `online:true`.
- No real inquiry, notification email or payment was submitted in this pass. Production availability and code validation are not a fresh end-to-end mailbox/customer acceptance.

**History convention:** this checkpoint supersedes earlier technical-state claims where they conflict, including draft-only Group intake, disabled contact flags, unprotected RETALLY main and mandatory separate human code review. It does not erase real customer/source, private-host, recovery, financial or branch-specific commercial-proof requirements. Earlier dated evidence is preserved below.

---

## Current technical closure — October 21, 2026

**RETALLY main protection is now ACTIVE.** Provider readback of [ruleset 25608380](https://github.com/P00NSMASHER/github-value-hunt-ledger/rules/25608380) confirms the default branch requires a pull request and the unique GitHub Actions `release-gate` check (integration 15368), with strict up-to-date enforcement, **zero required human approvals**, no bypass actors, no deletion and no force push. Branch metadata confirms `protected=true`; the connected user has `current_user_can_bypass=never`. The earlier zero-ruleset finding below is resolved for this repository. CaptureBrief, PermitPlate and Resonance protections are separate repository checks, not implied by RETALLY's rule.

- [PR #582](https://github.com/P00NSMASHER/github-value-hunt-ledger/pull/582) merged at `6e01088dcbab261a33a035f2c5679eaa28ea516c` after exact-head release, source, security and all six RecoveryWorks jobs passed, including Windows encrypted backup. Every scheduled writer now uses the guarded PR path, with no direct-main feature-flag fallback.
- The next actual Technology Intelligence publication completed through [PR #584](https://github.com/P00NSMASHER/github-value-hunt-ledger/pull/584), producing `7ebe4c78aec21280a4b855f0413fb6b3553f9990`. This verifies working PR-only publication; it predates ruleset activation and is not the post-protection canary.
- **Protected-release canary ACCEPTED:** [PR #585](https://github.com/P00NSMASHER/github-value-hunt-ledger/pull/585), exact head `c9cfe1606c8ae1714c0d40fc6f8061c9ee9ae866`, passed all applicable hosted checks, including Windows encrypted backup, and merged normally at `10a46e59875398bb6d77a6d761927111ab17da19` with no human review and no bypass. Post-merge API readback still shows main protected and the active strict `release-gate` ruleset. The source manifest now matches actual enforcement.
- **Public contact intake is already enabled.** Current production configuration has `FREIGHT_INQUIRY_ENABLED=1` and `FREIGHT_INQUIRY_MAILBOX_VERIFIED=1`; the existing Resend credential is bound without exposing its value. The October 17 controlled Turnstile → D1 → Resend → Zoho acceptance supersedes the October 8/14 disabled-intake instructions. See [current inquiry readiness](https://github.com/P00NSMASHER/github-value-hunt-ledger/blob/main/freight/site/INQUIRY_PRODUCTION_READINESS.md). Do not send redundant mail or restore obsolete Cloudflare Email Sending requirements.
- **Private customer work remains unaccepted.** Fresh Cloudflare metadata still shows zero attached policies on the separate workbench Access app and zero account tunnels. A green code release, enabled contact form or synthetic test does not prove customer source rights, a working private host, independent encrypted recovery, actual payment, delivery or bank/carrier settlement.

**History convention:** all dated sections below preserve earlier evidence. Where they describe disabled inquiry flags, an absent Resend path, unprotected RETALLY main or an obsolete separate human code-review requirement, this newer source/provider-backed checkpoint and the current code release policy supersede those particular statements. Real customer/source/privacy/financial evidence gates remain distinct.

---

**Source-integrity and public-site work: largely ACCEPTED. Real-customer operations: NO-GO.** This is a dated evidence checkpoint, not an ongoing health monitor and not a replacement for the October 12 item-level scorecard preserved below.

items.title: core(tenancy): tenant-aware natural keys — conflict target and unique index include the tenant column; STI/custom-PK/report conflict alignment
items.body:
## Problem

A new object's `save()` upserts on `ObjectRegistry.getConflictColumns()` — default `['slug','context']`, STI `['slug','context','_meta_type']` (`core/src/object.ts:1877-1894`, `registry.ts:2733-2766`) — and slug defaults to the slugified name. The tenancy interceptor injects `tenant_id` into `where` for reads and populates it on save (`tenancy/src/interceptor.ts:290-297, 485-489`) but never touches the conflict target, and the generated unique index has no tenant column (`schema/generator.ts:693-704`, STI hard-coded `:1010-1015`, `:1246-1250`). The SDK's PostgreSQL upsert is `INSERT … ON CONFLICT(slug, context) DO UPDATE SET <every column>` — including `id` and `tenant_id` (`@happyvertical/sql/dist/index.js:2224-2236`).

**Probed with the real interceptor:** `withTenant(A) create({name:'Widget'})` then `withTenant(B) create({name:'Widget'})` → one row, `tenant_id = B`, a new `id`; tenant A now sees nothing, and every reference A held to the old id dangles (no DB FKs). Two towns publishing an article with the same slug and context on anytown's shared `contents` hit exactly this; anytown avoids it by writing the tenant UUID into `context` (its repair plan does `SET tenant_id = context::uuid`). `products/src/lib/models/Product.ts:53-68` documents the STI variant as a rejected insert — it is an adopted one.

Breadth: 60+ tenant-scoped classes with no custom `conflictColumns`; 118 tenant-scoped tables (49 STI) whose slug is unique across tenants.

Same code region, same class of bug (the #1165 class generalized):
- both STI paths hard-code `(slug, context, _meta_type)` and ignore `@smrt({ conflictColumns })`, while `getConflictColumns()` honours it → PG "no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification" on every save (products refrains from setting it for exactly this reason);
- custom-PK classes get no conflict index while `getConflictColumns()` still returns `slug,context`;
- `@report` classes derive `[tenant, …group cols]` at runtime (`registry.ts:2744-2760`) but the manifest CTI path emits `(slug, context)`; `ManifestBuilder.buildManifest()` also skips the report normalization pass the vite plugin runs (`manifest/generator.ts:336-342` vs `vite-plugin/index.ts:1189`).

## Change

- For tenant-scoped classes, the default conflict target becomes `[tenant column, ...natural key]` on **both** the build path (normalize `decoratorConfig.conflictColumns` in `manifest-generator.ts`, mirroring `normalizeReportObjects`) and the runtime path (`getConflictColumns()`), so schema and upsert agree by construction.
- STI and CTI generator paths derive the conflict unique index from the (normalized) config instead of hard-coding it; custom-PK and report classes get a unique index matching their runtime conflict target.
- **Keep the index name stable** (`<t>_slug_context_idx` / `<t>_slug_context_meta_type_idx`) so the differ's same-name shape-drift repair swaps columns in place; a renamed index would leave the old global unique in place and still block cross-tenant duplicates. Note the new index is a superset key, so creating it cannot fail on existing data.
- Decide and document the semantics for `mode: 'optional'` rows with NULL tenant (the SDK's null-aware PG upsert already dedups NULL-tenant natural keys through the model layer).
- Add a doctor/test assertion "live unique index == `getConflictColumns()`" so this class cannot recur (the same check covers #1165).
- Fix the products/Product.ts comment (or delete it once the framework fix lands).

## Acceptance

- two tenants can each create an object with the same slug/context on every tenant-scoped table; neither overwrites the other; the second create returns a new row
- STI classes with custom `conflictColumns` save on PG and SQLite
- report and custom-PK classes upsert against an existing unique index
- differ swaps the existing global unique index in place on an anytown-shaped PG snapshot; dry-run attached
- regression tests: cross-tenant create, STI custom conflictColumns, report default target

## Relationships

Touches `generator.ts` conflict-index blocks adjacent to the reference-index issue — rebase after it. Depends on the migrate-timeouts issue for rollout. Semantics change: ship in the schema release wave with an explicit release note (ingestion flows relying on cross-tenant natural-key dedup will now insert per tenant).

From the 2026-08-17 database-layer assessment (finding B1/A4).

---
**Part of epic #2382** (database-layer gap class; report in the epic's first comment). Rebase after #2359 (adjacent generator hunks). Rollout requires #2362. Related: #1165 (closed), #2372, #2368 (parity assertion "live unique index == conflict target").

items.title: Epic: Innovation Roadmap - Sovereign Ask, Influence Graph & Global Intelligence Layer
items.body:
## Task

Define and prioritize breakthrough innovations that establish MapleSpike as a sovereign Canadian intelligence platform with unique advantages over competitors like Katzilla.dev

## Context for Agent

Having established the Canadian baseline quality and competitive differentiation (Issue #549), this epic focuses on leapfrog innovations that play to MapleSpike's strengths: sovereignty, Canadian depth, self-hosted control, auditability, and influence-tracking capabilities.

## Innovation Areas to Develop

### 1. Sovereign "Ask" + Signal Engine
- Grounded natural language interface with verifiable citations
- Proactive signal layer (e.g., "new lobbying activity involving [entity]", "regulatory changes affecting [sector]")

### 2. Conflict-of-Interest & Influence Graph
- Real-time entity resolution across lobbying ↔ committees ↔ procurement ↔ GIC appointments ↔ international orgs
- Feature: "Show all influence paths for X"

### 3. Provenance-First Responses
- Every answer includes verifiable SHA-256 citation chains + full audit trail
- Cryptographic verification of data lineage

### 4. Self-Hosted + Air-Gapped Mode
- Full offline capability for classified/sensitive environments
- Zero external dependencies for high-security deployments

### 5. Multi-Jurisdictional Intelligence Layer
- Unified view across Canada + UN/WEF/WHO + Five Eyes + provincial data
- Automatic cross-border linkage and entity resolution

### 6. Policy Impact Simulator
- "What would happen to [sector] if this proposed regulation passes?"
- Uses historical data + entity graphs for impact scoring

### 7. White-Label / Tenant Mode
- Isolated instances for journalism orgs, law firms, NGOs, other governments
- Multi-tenant architecture with data isolation

### 8. Real-time Legislative & Regulatory Delta Tracking
- Canada Gazette + international equivalents with AI summarization
- Impact scoring and change alerts

### 9. Agent-Native Memory & Context Store
- Persistent long-term memory for agents built on entity graph
- Context retention across sessions and tool uses

### 10. Verifiable Compute & Zero-Knowledge Signals
- Future: Prove a signal was generated without revealing source data
- Advanced sovereignty feature for privacy-preserving insights

## Steps

- [ ] Detail each innovation area with technical specs and user stories
- [ ] Prioritize innovations by impact, effort, and strategic value
- [ ] Create implementation roadmap with milestones
- [ ] Identify dependencies on baseline quality work (#549)
- [ ] Define MVP versions for high-priority innovations
- [ ] Estimate effort and resource requirements
- [ ] Create success metrics and acceptance criteria for each
- [ ] Link to international expansion epic where relevant
- [ ] Document open questions and research needed

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Innovation roadmap defined with clear prioritization
- [ ] Technical feasibility assessed for top 3-5 innovations
- [ ] Dependencies on quality baseline work identified
- [ ] MVP scope defined for immediate-term innovations
- [ ] Success metrics established for each innovation area
- [ ] Roadmap communicated to stakeholders and contributors

## Workflow

- [ ] Single PR per task
- [ ] Worktree-based development
- [ ] Commit messages reference issue number
- [ ] PR body contains 'Closes #NNN'
- [ ] PR reviewed before merge
- [ ] Label with 'epic', 'roadmap', 'strategic', 'agent-ready'

items.title: research: Lakehouse backing store deep dive — ClickHouse Cloud
items.body:
**Parent: #15 — Production lakehouse adapter (BigQuery / ClickHouse Cloud)**

One of three deep-research sub-issues spawned from #15. Sister to the **BigQuery** deep-dive sub-issue; use a parallel structure so the two can be compared side-by-side. Architecture-level decisions (where the lakehouse lives, who writes to it) live in the **architecture / ingestion-contract** sub-issue.

## Goal

Produce a research packet that, taken together with the BigQuery counterpart, lets us pick a backing store with confidence and start implementation.

## Context

### Existing surface (recap from parent)

- `types/lakehouse.go::TraceLakehouse` — five-method interface backing today's CLI subcommands (`baseline`, `mine-failures`, `drift`, `compare-to-production`).
- `types/runtrace.go::RunTrace`, `RunRecording`, `ToolCallSummary`, `VerificationResult`.
- `types/metrics.go::TraceFilter`, `TraceMetrics`, `BaselineMetrics`, `DriftReport`.
- `eval/lakehouse/filestore.go` — the contract reference implementation. Note `parentOnlyToolCalls` (`filestore.go:239`) — sub-agent calls forwarded into the parent trace must be excluded from per-run aggregates (#55).
- `eval/cmd/eval/main.go` — the only consumer today.

### Read patterns the lakehouse must serve well

- **`Metrics(filter)`** — count, pass rate, mean turns, mean tokens, p50/p95 wall-clock duration over a window, optionally filtered by mode/model/outcome. Used by `baseline`, `drift`, and `compare-to-production`.
- **`QueryTraces(filter)` ordered by `StartedAt desc` with limit** — used to render recent runs and feed CI comparisons.
- **`QueryRecordings(filter)`** — only used by `mine-failures` today. Recordings carry full transcripts; this query touches a much heavier table.
- **Future: drift over arbitrary windows / cohort comparison.**

### Write patterns

- **`StoreTrace`** — one event per run completion, low-rate at first (10s–100s/day in early CP deployments), scaling toward 10k+/day as the agent product matures. Bursty (CI gate runs).
- **`StoreRecording`** — same per-run rate, but each payload is large (typical run: 5–20 turns, model input + output per turn, tool I/O captured verbatim). Easily megabytes.

### Constraints

- Cost-conscious early-stage deployment.
- Retain raw recordings for at least 30 days; aggregate trace metrics indefinitely.
- Schema evolution will happen. `RunTrace` already grew `RunID`/`ParentRunID` (#55).
- Compliance posture (#8): recordings are confidential by default; row/column-level access policy support is a plus.

## Research questions

1. **Schema design.** Which `MergeTree` engine is right — `MergeTree`, `ReplacingMergeTree` (idempotent ingest by `run_id`), `AggregatingMergeTree` for materialized rollups, or a small zoo across multiple tables? Sketch column types for `RunTrace`, including nested `ToolCalls` (`Nested`, `Array(Tuple(...))`, or the modern `JSON` type — note its current stability and limitations). How does the `parentOnlyToolCalls` predicate translate?
2. **`RunRecording` storage.** Wide row with a `String`/`JSON` column, or a separate `RunRecording` table joined on `run_id`, or external object storage (S3/GCS) with a CH-side reader? How does ClickHouse Cloud's tiered storage (hot SSD vs S3-backed cold) fit our retention shape — 30 days hot, indefinite aggregated metrics?
3. **Sort key & partitioning.** Order key choice (`(tenant_id, started_at)` vs `(started_at, run_id)` vs other) and partition granularity (month vs day vs hour). What gives us the smallest read sets for the `Metrics(filter)` and `QueryTraces` access patterns?
4. **Ingestion mechanism.** Async inserts (`async_insert=1`) vs the buffer engine vs Kafka engine vs ClickHouse Cloud's HTTP ingest. What does the control-plane Go writer look like — `clickhouse-go/v2` native protocol, the official HTTP client, or a Vector / OTel-collector in front? Backpressure, idempotency (`ReplacingMergeTree` with `run_id`), retry semantics.
5. **Cost model.** Estimated monthly cost at 10k runs/day and 100k runs/day. ClickHouse Cloud pricing has compute (per-replica per-hour with autoscaling), storage (per-GB-month), and data transfer; recordings as cold-tier objects vs hot. Where are the cliffs — minimum service price floor, autoscaling boundaries, query parallelism limits at small tiers?
6. **Query ergonomics.** Rewrite `computeMetrics` (`filestore.go:190`) as a ClickHouse SQL query. Use `quantilesTDigest` for p50/p95? Materialized views over `RunTrace` for the common drift / baseline queries — CH idiomatically loves them; how do they help here, and what's the staleness story?
7. **Schema evolution.** `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN` is cheap in MergeTree, but adding fields inside `Nested`/`Array(Tuple)` columns isn't free. What's the recommended migration recipe? Does the `JSON` type buy us forward-compat at acceptable read cost? Walk through a concrete upcoming change (e.g. multimodal `ContentBlock` variants from #103).
8. **PII / secret scrubbing & access control.** ClickHouse role-based access, row policies, column-level access. App-level AES-256-GCM with key from `SecretStore` is the realistic path for #8's RunRecording encryption — confirm or propose an alternative. How does ClickHouse Cloud handle CMEK?
9. **Multi-tenancy.** Database-per-tenant vs row-level policies vs separate ClickHouse Cloud services. What scales? Note that ClickHouse Cloud services have a per-service price floor — what does that imply at 100 tenants? 10k?
10. **Open-table interop.** ClickHouse Iceberg/Delta readers — useful here, or operational noise? Does writing *to* Iceberg through ClickHouse (when supported) make sense given our access patterns?
11. **Observability of the lakehouse itself.** `system.*` tables (`system.parts`, `system.async_inserts`, `system.query_log`), ClickHouse Cloud's built-in observability stack, alerting on async-insert backlog, "ingestion is stuck" playbook.
12. **Go client maturity.** `clickhouse-go/v2` — native vs HTTP, dep surface, batch insert ergonomics, testcontainers / `chmock` story for unit tests, auth flows for ClickHouse Cloud (TLS + password from `SecretStore`).

## Deliverables

A research packet covering, in parallel structure with the BigQuery sub-issue:

- **Recommended schema** (DDL sketches) with engine, order key, partition key, TTL clauses justified against the query workload.
- **Recommended ingestion path** (Go code outline using `clickhouse-go/v2` and `async_insert`, with retry / idempotency policy and observability hooks).
- **Cost model** at the two scale points above with the math shown (and your assumptions).
- **Query rewrites** for the four `eval` subcommands (`baseline`, `mine-failures`, `drift`, `compare-to-production`) — actual SQL, not pseudocode.
- **Schema-evolution recipe** that walks through a likely upcoming change.
- **Security posture** for the #8 encryption + classification requirements: which ClickHouse feature satisfies which line-item.
- **Multi-tenancy recommendation** with a clear growth path.
- **Operational runbook outline:** alerts, dashboards, dead-letter handling, async-insert backlog playbook.
- **Comparative honesty:** where would ClickHouse Cloud be a *worse* fit than BigQuery?

## Inputs the researcher should pull from

- **In-tree code:** `types/lakehouse.go`, `types/runtrace.go`, `types/metrics.go`, `eval/lakehouse/filestore.go`, `eval/cmd/eval/main.go`.
- **Related issues:** #8, #9, #13, #15 (parent), #55, #103. OTel exporter context from #100 is relevant for the wire format the control plane would consume.
- **External primary sources:** ClickHouse `MergeTree` and `ReplacingMergeTree` docs, async-insert reference, the modern `JSON` type announcement (and current limitations), ClickHouse Cloud pricing & autoscaling architecture, `clickhouse-go/v2` reference, the official OpenTelemetry ClickHouse exporter (relevant for the architecture sub-issue's question 2), public posts from teams running ClickHouse for LLM observability (Helicone is a notable example), ClickHouse "agent observability" reference architectures.
- **Cross-reference:** at least one public agent-platform write-up that names ClickHouse as their store, or a "we evaluated ClickHouse against X and chose…" post — both are useful signal.

## Out of scope

- The architecture / ownership question (covered in the sister architecture sub-issue).
- BigQuery (covered in the sister BigQuery sub-issue).
- Implementation work — this is research only.
